Reel 1

Washington, D. C.
March 1980

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
P R O C E E D I N G S
mt

I'm talking to Tom Whaley, great musician, one of the mainstays of music and musicians in New York City for many, many years and today is March 17, 1979 and I'm talking with a dear friend, Tom Whaley, and my name is Milt Hinton and Tom and I have been knowing one another way over 50 years, is that so, Tom. Way over 50 years you and I have been knocking around together and we're doing this for the Smithsonian Institute, Tom, and for oral history so that young people in the future will know about you because we are not really satisfied that our young people in America, black and white, know enough about their roots in jazz and in show business and you certainly are one of them. So from now on I want to keep my mouth shut and just ask you a couple of questions and you talk and elucidate as long as you like on it, Tom. You were born where?

I was born in Boston at the corner of Church and Melrose in 1892. And my father and mother moved to Boston after six months of living there, I mean to Everett, Massachusetts. It's about six or seven miles from Boston, just like from New York to Brooklyn. And well, the first thing I remember was in 1895 the subway opened and my mother and father went on the opening ride and the burglars broke in the house and my sister put us all in a room and told us to keep still and I think something
scared the burglars away because they never come in the house. Then that was when I was about three years old, and when I was seven years old my mother decided to give me piano lessons.
What was your mother's name.
Emma Foster.
Your dad's name.

James Thomas Whaley. And my mother was born in Richmond, Virginia and he was born in Fairfax County of West Virginia. I believe my father was an Indian because I went down there in 1902 and I saw this great big giant and my father said that was his father and he was a red man and he was a blacksmith and he could life a horse. That was in 1902 when we went down there.

But before that my mother gave me music lessons and she give me a teacher and the teacher used to sit there and eat candy and I'd make a whole lot of mistakes and I told my mother about it so we got another -- we got a German.
Where was this in Boston or Fairfax.

This was in Everett, Massachusetts and he used to give me piano lessons and I would go out to the Malden, to the church there and sing in this choir. We had a boy's choir out there and I had a high voice. I could sing E above the scale, and I was one of his leading boy sopranos and for quite awhile I used to walk about two or three miles to the church and have rehearsals and one winter I got my feet
wet and that was the end of my singing. That was in Malden, Massachusetts.
I forgot to ask you, did you have an brothers or sisters.

Yeah, I had two sisters and a brother. I had another brother but he died. I think that's -- my sister's name was -- one was Edna, she was the oldest. Viola was the next and then my brother he came next and he's the one that died and then there's me and then my brother Rudolph. He was the youngest.
You had two brothers, then. And two sisters.

Yeah. And we got along pretty good, and while I was in Everett I went to school there and during the school, during that term I used to take care of the doctor's horse and then I had a paper route, you know, sell papers go around there and then in the summertime I'd go in the factory, shoe factory and cut uppers. Oh, I was very industrious. Anyway I kept my music up and I remember when I was in the eighth grade, I played Beethoven's Opus 49 and my mother said why did you duck-bow and I said oh, them kids, they know. I didn't have to bow for them.
And then in the first -- I mean, freshman in high school, my mother died and my father had just built a house across the street and she didn't even live to enter it, and
that was my freshman year in 1910, 1908.
What kind of business was your father in.

My father, oh,he was headwaiter at the Belleview Hotel and then he went to the Young's Hotel and then from there he went to the cafeteria up in Boston. Anyway it was -- Pat Toy used to play there, Pat Toy Trio.
I could compare you to Eubie Blake You are one of the young men you weren't born in the South, so you didn't know anything about that southern thing.

The only thing I know about the south was when I traveled in it. See, I did a lot -- after I got in high school, see, I went to New England Conservatory for about six months and they didn't pay me no mind, see, so I quit there and I got a teacher, he perfected (at) the Russian Conservatory and he would sit down at the piano and run the scale like that, and I used to say do that again, because I thought I was kind of quick. I could run the scales but the man there, he was perfect. And he said that's 18 hours of practice.

So from then, I graduated from high school in 1911 and I took a post-graduate course because I didn't know nothing about grammar and I didn't know what a furrow was so I took about six months and then I got a job in Boston playing piano. I used to play on Dover and Washington Street, cabaret, a cafeteria and a beer joint where they would come and sit and
I'd play all different songs and those what do you call them, shucksters, they would be -- have a song and they'd come and put it on --
Hucksters, song --

Song pluggers, and they would put the song up and say play that in D and it was written in B flat and I'd say, man, that's in B flat, can't play it and he said you can't transpose it, and from then on I went home and started transposing everything I knew, up and down because I used to pride myself on being a good sight reader. Them guys up in Boston, they used to -- we had a club and they used to put music in front on the piano and say, when Tom comes in we'll stick him and they didn't stick me for a long while, and one day I came in there, probably was ____ and I sat down at the piano and they had this key to key rag. The first page was all right but when I turned the next page, they had a whole lot of triples there, and I said, uh, oh, and they said, oh, we caught him.
I said, no, you didn't. The tempo was too fast, that's all.

That's interesting to know because most people, we like to let the world know that all jazz musicians and all popular musicians didn't start just picking up their instruments, that some of them studied. You had good training.
Yeah, I had a good training and I used

to go around and listen to all the musicians and this is when Boston was noted for its piano players and some of the piano players, there's Leroy Tibbs, Joe Hubell and Freddie Tunstell, Willie -- oh, what was Willie's----
It's not too important.

But we had a whole lot of piano players there and they could play but I got with an orchestra and the man said "all you got to do is oompha, hold that tempo because I got violins, I got trumpets and I got all the other instruments in there to play off, you know, play the melody and all but all you got to do is play the oompha." I used to oompha all the time.
Now, oompha, the left hand, you play the bass and you play the right hand. Bass, left hand, right hand, left hand.

And we had a fellow named Walter Johnson and Leroy Johnson. They wasn't brothers but they would go and man, they could play. We'd go on a job. I'd be the piano player and when Wally would come in I'd ease out and he'd sit down at the piano and play and everybody would gather around him and he was a very good -- because in Everett we had a lot of people that were interested in music like the Faseoli, they were Italian people and they lived across the street from me and I used to go over there and they used -- we used to get together and play.
These were Italian piano players.

No, he was a leader. He had three sons, and he knew music and he'd stand up there with his baton and when you'd make a bad note he'd hit your hand and then across -- out the street there was this Walter Johnson, his father was a trumpet player, his mother was an organist and we used to go over there and play. I used to play the guitar or the banjo there.
So that's where you learned how to be so tough on us youngsters when we'd come along.

Oh, yeah, when I came to New York I used to tell everybody learn how to read. If you can't read, you can't read because up until the war in 1918 the white musicians weren't known in Boston, everything was colored. Colored musicians had all the jobs and then after the world war there was a -- the white musicians swept us away, but in 1912 I got a job out in Reading, Massachusetts, out at a road house and every Sunday when Enrico Caruso would come to Boston at the opera house, he'd come down there and Sunday afternoon at 2 o'clock and he'd stand up there and direct -- we'd play all the overtures. "Merry Wives of Windsor" and all those overtures, he would direct. He wouldn't sing, but he would direct.
And then we'd drink champagne and then when he'd get ready to go he'd give us $200 and divide it amongst the band. And 13, 14, Leroy Johnson was playing down to roadhouse
outside of Danvers and he called me up and said, 'hey, you want to come up here and play?' I said 'what?'
Where was Danvers.
Danvers was up outside of Wakefield.
In Massachusetts?

In Massachusetts. It was noted for an insane asylum in Danvers and this guy called me up and said 'you want to come up here and play.' That was in Lynnfield, Massachusetts. I said 'why, certainly' and he said all right, so that was a place where everybody wanted to go because that's where everybody, you know, all the big people used to come up there.
What year was this.

This was around 1914 and I went up there and I made an audition and I know I made a whole lot of mistakes but the man said you want the job. I said why certainly so then we had a violin player and guitar player and a drummer.
All of you were black.
Yeah.
And we used to entertain and if we didn't make 10, 20 dollars a night, we weren't doing anything. Sometimes we would make around $30 a night.
In them days, the average working person was making about that much a week.

Oh, yeah, we were getting $15 a week room and board, see, they roomed us out there. They had a nice bungalow for all the musicians but when we'd get in there, we'd get on the floor at 7 o'clock, start working and we worked till 12 and if people didn't give us any money, we'd go out to the bar and hang out at the bar and I remember Mrs. Eggleston she was the boss, she used to come out to the bar and say, Mr. Whaley, would you come and give us some music.

I said, them people don't want our music. They ain't interested in music. So after awhile I'd go back out and we'd get together and then you'd hear, people would come up or send the waiter up, here's a $5 bill, here's -- play so and so.

I remember one day a little short fellow, he was in all beard and he had a Prince Albert suit coat on and he came up and says, hey I want you to play 'Dixie'. I said okay and he went in his pocket and pulled out his wallet and give me a $10 bill. He said, 'play nothing but 'Dixie.' I said okay. So we kept on playing 'Dixie' and people hey don't you know anything else. This man is paying me $10 to play that, so then they started giving me money.
We used to make a whole lot of money.
Do you remember any of the songs other than Dixie was popular during that time?
Row, Row, Row, 'Oh, You Beautiful Doll.'
"Linger Awhile," & "Whispering."
You stayed up in Boston. What was your first chance to get down here to New York.
I played around, I went to war, see, in 1918.
Let's talk about that. How did you get to war.
I was playing down at this place, Suntaug Lake Inn and one Monday I went to work and there was greetings for me. United States Army has inducted me.
Where were you, in Boston.

This was in Boston -- no, this was in -- I was living in Everett then but I gathered my music up and told the lady I'm quitting. I got about five days before I have to go to the camp. I was inducted in August 31, 1917. Or 1918 what was it. 1918 and I went down and my father was working at the Haywood Hotel, that was it, in Boston, and I went down there and I told my dad, well, I'm inducted in the Army so they gave me a party.

And instead of me marching like all the rest -- I ain't going to march, what march, because I'm glad here I'm going into the Army, making $30 a month and I was making two, three hundred dollars a week. I was crying.
That's what the ARmy paid in those days, $30 a month.

Yes, $30 a month, well, anyway I got in the Army and we had a fellow -- we went to Camp Dix in New Jersey. First, we went to Devon and from Devon, I said to a guy on Labor Day night, the day before Labor Day, I said hey you know on Labor Day, we're going to leave here, let's go back to Boston. The cat said no, because I was ready to jump the ARmy right then.

So we got on -- they put us on board, Labor Day and went to Camp Dix and they had a fellow, he was in Dix, named Opal Cooper, big tall fellow and he could sing, he knew the words and music of 500 songs and they had a piano player in there but he couldn't read music and so I used to sit down and play for him and they used to throw shoes at me and everything because this guy would sit down and start singing and win all the money.
So then we went to France from Fort Dix and when we landed in France, San Jose --
On a troop ship.

We went over and we had a convoy see and we got about a couple days out, the convoy left us and the -- you could hear the water slushing against the outside of the ship and one day the lights went out. Now we're six decks down and I was seasick and the smell of the ship made me seasick and I was in my bunk, what do you call, the hammock and the cat hollered 'Oh, we're torpedoed,' and they all made a rush and here

I'm sick, I can't move and they all run up and then afterwhile the lights come back on so afterwhile I said to the guy, where do you think you're going. You're six decks down and we were torpedoed how are you going to get out. You can't get out. You're six decks down.

So then we landed in St. Jose (?) and I met a whole lot of the guys that were what do you call it, they were shell shocked over there, the Eighth Illinois. And they didn't know anything. They were vacant, had a vacant stare and they were gassed, you know.

And then we went to the camp, they call it sunny France, but it rained every day we were over there and you march all day long and you put your pup tent up and at night it would rain again and you'd have a wet blanket, oh, they were all wet and I remember we marched to -- I got in the band, see.
How did you get in the band?

See, I could read music, and this guy he was a singer, see, and I was in headquarters company, see when I went there, they put me in headquarters company and I could play the piano and this guy could sing, so then I went to the man and says, hey I want to get in the band, so they transferred me to the band and Bill Vodrey was the Army band leader.
What was the name of the band.
I was in headquarters company, Pioneer regiment and -- from New York.

Pioneer regiment, yeah, they turned it into a Pioneer regiment. We were a regular regiment, see and after we got over there they turned it into a Pioneer, see, we used to clean up. You go into a city and the people, the soldiers were sitting on the sidewalk, you think they were gassed and you would touch them and they would fall over and we had to pick them up.

And I went way back into the, about six miles outside and told the sergeant, that I wanted a job in there, so he put me down peeling potatoes. This was the mess sergeant. I used to peel potatoes and then I'd sneak off and go into my bunk and sleep. The Lieutenant would come by, what you doing, Whaley. I said, I just come off duty. That's all right.
You played piano in the band.

Yes, we had an orchestra, 14 pieces and we went from the -- I remember we were -- the band was going to be detached from the army, see and that's when I went to the Lieutenant and says, is my name on my list to leave. He said 'what's your name?' I said Whaley. He said, yep, so the next morning I picked my -- got up and took my tent down, and the man said, 'where are you going?' The sergeant. I said, 'I'm getting in -- leaving this, I'm going with the band.'
So we went to -- we traveled all over France, see,
we went to entertain President ______, he was the president at the time and when he got off the train the band played the 'Junkman Rag,' Lucky Roberts' 'Junkman Rag.'
Lucky Roberts was a piano player here in New York, wasn't he, and a great composer, too.
Right, and we played the 'Junkman Rag' for President ______, president of France.
And this band was called a pioneer --
Will Vodrey was the leader.
We got to talk about Will Vodrey a little later on, because he's another one of the greats like you.
I am going to tell you about -- you remember when he was down at the Cotton Club.
I was there, too.
You were there.
Yes, sir. We will talk about that, we don't want to forget about Vodrey.
Now this band wasn't called the 369th band was it.
No, that was Jim Europe. That was Jim Europe had the 369th.
You were in the Pioneer what.
I was in the Pioneer regiment.
And this was a --
And this was all black.
All black and we had white officers and one of the officers, the captain, he resigned because he said he didn't come over for no contraband band. He came over to fight so he resigned.

And well we stayed over there and went all over Europe playing. We'd go to the officer's mess and we'd play and you'd get money and Vodrey used to take the money and go to Paris so one day the Lieutenant says we're going to Leone now which way shall we go. Shall we go through Paris or go the other way. We said, let's go to Paris, so he took us into Paris and when I got outside of Paris, I said so this is Paris bring on the women.

And we went into a place they had there, half of the place was for dancing and the other was for rollerskating and we played in the dance section and I remember we had a fellow in that band, Louie Jones. He was a great violin player from New York and he was from Boston, but he was a very great violinist.
Can you name any other guys that were in that band around that time. Remember any of the fellows' names.
Oh, gee, fellow named Gulfport, he was in the band. He was a comedian.
Did he play anything.
He used to play oompha. Horn.
And Stafford, Joe Stafford, he was trombone player. Oh, we had quite a few New York boys there, musicians and I can't remember them all.
Well, you just go on with your story.
Anyway, where was I at.
You were in Paris.

Oh, yeah, we went to Paris and we played at the Ballroom and I remember a girl come up to Louie Jones and says, oh, you're beautiful and I said, see, I told you, Louie, you'd get all the gals and we left there --
You must have been a handsome dude in those days because you ain't bad now.
Who, me. Oh, I had plenty girls. The girl used to teach, I said, 'why don't you marry me' and she said 'no, if you come back here, then I'll marry you.'
I see from your complexion, you said your father was an Indian and I can see that sort of texture in your skin.
The redness is still here. I was telling Ruth about it --
Ruth who?
Ruth Ellington.
That's Duke's sister.
Yeah, and anyway the war was over, there was more people killed on that November 11th than there
was during the war because they got out there and start firing the guns.
1918, I guess it was.
Yes, it was in 1918 and when we got ready to come home, we went to Brest, and now Brest is way up on a hill and we went to - delousedus and they give us summer underwear.
How did they delouse you, give you some kind of chemical.

No, they put you under a shower and the guys would throw that stuff all over and that's how I lost my hair, I think, because all that stuff got in my hair but anyway we got deloused and got cold up there so I went to the commissary and I asked them for some heavy underwear, so I got the underwear and put it on and they called inspection one day, they called inspection and here I am with this heavy underwear on and the officer says go on and take that off and get yourself some underwear.
And we stayed up there on Brest for six months before we could get a boat to come back to New York.
After the war was over?

After the war was over and then we went into Newport News and I know we went down there -- in Virginia, we landed there and we went into camp there and the boss of the place he ordered us to go into the and hear a

lecture and one of our guys says we ain't going to have no lecture and he said we've been over there and serving in all that war and everything, you're going to lecture us and they put -- I says, let's go over there and don't have no argument because they'll put you in jail here and you won't get out because we're supposed to go back up to Dix --
Who is Richard, your buddy.
No, he was Chicken Richards. Used to be up at Small's and he --
What did he do, dance or sing or what.

No, he was in F Company, and I was in with the band and so we all got in Newport News and he wanted to go -- don't go to no lecture, so they put him -- they arrested him for disobeying and I told him afterwards, I said, man, you got an hour or so, listen. You ain't got to pay any attention what it is.
So about six days later we went up to Dix and then we were deloused again and discharged. I come back to New York.
You came back to New York.

Well, I went to New York -- this was in 1919 when I got back to Boston and I went back to my old job, but that didn't last long, see, at Suntaug Lake Inn, that didn't last long so then meanwhile I was sending guys out to Lake George, our trio, I used to send them out to Lake George every summer.
So you sort of got in the booking business, like, contracting.

Yeah, because I had a good job and I give them the job and they used to come out with $2,400 and all that and here I'm starving. So I went up there the next -- I think in '21 I went up there, Decoration Day they opened, May 30th and they keep open till Labor Day and I stayed out there and I made good money, but you know what, I had to borrow $50 from the boss to come back to Boston and the only thing I had to show for it was a trunk. I bought a trunk. I paid $125 for a trunk.
What did you do with your money up there.

Gambling, yeah, they gambled there, shucks, man, if you could win and I couldn't win and then they give me -- shoot $100 and I'd shoot it for them and fade out and I said aw shucks, every cent I got I used to gamble with. And so finally I got back to Boston and I started working again and Wilbur Sweatman came through.
Explain who Wilbur Sweatman is.

Wilbur Sweatman was a clarinet player. He used to play three clarinets at a time, see, and he had a group and he wanted a piano player so they picked me and I went with him. We traveled all over New England and then we come into New York in '21. The last part of '21, we came into New York and a fellow said Tom, I got a job for you, so I
went up to Larchmont, the Washington Arms. George Stevens, that was his name and he had the group. He was a singer. He used to be in the Shuffle Along show, he was a singer, good looking boy.
He was a singer.
Yeah, he was a singer with Shuffle Along.
Was Wilbur Sweatman in this band, too.

No, I quit Sweatman see, and went with George Stevens up at Larchmont. And we stayed there about a week or so and the man fired George because all the women were after George, see, and the man didn't want nothing like that, so when he fired George, we all quit and the man says, I didn't -- he said, where you going, and we said you fired us, didn't you.
So I went back to Boston then and hung around Boston and I owed eight months rent.
How much was your rent?
I was paying the lady about $10 a week, I think and didn't have no job, the musicians in New York would say, go on back to Boston, so around '25, the -- Lucky Roberts called me.
He was the great piano player we're talking about. He wrote that song.
He had a club up there, a liquor joint.

Up there at 149th Street and St. Nicholas Avenue and he used to have entertainers and everybody, the waiters were all singers, see, up there and so this night he called me and he asked me was I busy and I said no man, so I got together with him and his singer, see, Charlie Purcell and we went down to 666 Fifth Avenue and there was about six people, three couples and we entertained, played soft music and singing and I got $75 for that gig and that's when I started romping.
They tell me this Lucky Roberts was the society band man of New York in those days.
That's right.
He had all of the gigs, all of the good gigs, is that so.

He had all the gigs, like the Clef Club. If you get in the Clef Club, you are already made, but they didn't want no outsiders in there. They wouldn't let me in there, so finally I got the break with Lucky and I started doing a whole lot of things then. I got myself a band and used to play over in Brooklyn, Cat's Meow, I used to play all over and then I had a job on 131st Street at the -- the Italians had the place there and the night Gerald Chapman was electrocuted --
Who was electrocuted?
Gerald Chapman, he was a big gangster.
Did they put him in the electric chair.

Yeah, he was captured up there in Connecticut, see and I had never seen so many $100 bills come in a place, all that week trying to save this guy. They had so much money there, they couldn't buy him off, and so the night of the electrocution, the man said, play nothing but 'The Prisoner's Song' and that's all I played, 'The Prisoner's Song' and then from there I went -- I used to go up to 136th Street there, they had another joint where I used to go up there and play and get acquainted with the people and in '25 Small's opened on 135th Street.
What was the name of that place, Tom.
Casper's, you know the gangsters -- he was the head of the number racket there in New York. Casper. And they kidnapped him.
So what happened up there. Used to work up there.
Yeah, I used to go up there. Play up there for awhile.
Anything else you want to tell me about that. What happened around that era. How did you get into writing and meeting all these different guys.
I was going to --
Did you join this Clef Club you were telling me about.
No, I didn't.
How did you meet Lucky Roberts and all that.

I used to go up to Lucky's place, see, and listen to Lucky and everything and Lucky knew me so he asked me if I wanted a job and that's when I got it. But when Small's opened up, no, this is before Small. See, I had a band over there in Brooklyn and the guy owed me a week's salary and we opened up that Monday night and he said he was going to pay me and he didn't pay me, so I said well, it's no music. He said, no -- I said to the fellows, don't you play. He pay me, we play. If he don't don't. So I take all my music out and go back up and then I started rehearsing shows, up in the Lafayette Theatre, Lafayette Hall and I'm trying to think of that guy that danced. He had his wife and she was a singer and that's the first show I arranged for him at the Lafayette Theatre, that's in '28 and then I arranged for Ethel Waters. Earl Dancer had the group.
You weren't talking about Butterbeans and Susie.
No, not them.
Was it Brown or somebody and Brown.
Oh, this guy used to have a tall hat and a cane. I can never think of his name, but I arranged.
So that was your first orchestration job.
Yeah.
At the Lafayette Theatre in 1928.
And I told the fellows play just what I got on there and I'll correct it.
Just what you put on the table.

Yeah, play what I got on the paper and I'll correct it later on, and I used to go through all that music and play it and I used to tell the fellows, learn to read music, sight music. Learn that sight music and I want to talk about music now.

Music, jazz is not music. Jazz is tempo, see, years ago when Paul Whiteman was the king of syncopation, he used (sings) to play all that sweet music, see, 'Whispering' and 'I Love You,' see all that sweet music and that sophisticated swing, that's what it was. Paul Whiteman, he was the king of it. So you know, they get tired of that sweet stuff, so I used to say let's jazz this up, see, just jazz it up. Jazz was a bad word, see,
It meant something else.

Right. So I was saying let's jazz it up and the first thing you know everybody is saying jazz, play some jazz and I tried to tell -- when I was over in Europe there, I told the guy that had the paper, I said 'why don't you ask -- put a question in your paper, what is jazz?' and you find out everybody didn't know it, didn't know what jazz was,
because jazz is not music. Jazz is tempo. Swing. It was an era of swing. And everybody was swinging and then Paul Whiteman come along with his sophisticated swing and then --
Didn't we have a black band around at that time that was great too. The guy is still living. What's the name.
Around that time --
He went to Europe and stayed a long time. What's the name of this guy. He's here now in New York City. He's a piano player.
Oh, you're talking about Joe Turner.

No, not Joe Turner. He had a band, he's got a lady that sings with him now in his band and he left here in 1920 something and went to Europe. He's one of the first bands I think that went to Russia. I am trying to think of his name. Can you recall his name.

No, I don't. Well, I tell you, in 1919 Fletcher Henderson came to Boston and he was the greatest band in the world there, because he could play waltzes, and that's the Massachusetts -- what's the name of the hall up there. Horicultural Hall was crowded, people would come there to hear Fletcher Henderson play waltzes. He had Louie Armstrong in the band, he had Don Redman , oh, he had a whole -- what's the clarinet player. Buster Bailey. He had all them people and he could arrange and he used to arrange for the clarinet
player, the fellow now, Benny Goodman. Sure.
The man I was talking about, Tom, was named Sam Wooding.
Oh, Sam Wooding, yeah, he went out to Europe. He had a band. He's here in New York now.
But he had a great band, don't you remember that band.
Oh, yeah, and he came over -- when he came back he was up on 133rd Street at the Nest. He had a band up there. Sam Wooding.
Around the same time that Paul Whiteman has his great band, but they weren't giving black musicians, what I understand --
Who was the black -- Charlie Johnson had the band at Small's, he was great and this other guy was great.
Ray Noble.
No, he wrote (humming)
Vincent Lopez.
Vincent Lopez. Vincent Lopez had the greatest band. Charlie Johnson had the next.
Yeah, he used 'Nola' for his theme song.

Sontag Lake Inn. Yeah, I was there from 1912 to 1918 when they took me in the army and you know, I should be a millionaire, the money I made. I would take the money out and gamble, see, trying to be a gambler. I bought a car and I'd sit out in the car and wait for the guys to come out, you going to Boston and if they didn't come, I'd go in there and try to break the game up, oh, Mr. big, I want to shoot.
Used to be a lot of gambling around Boston. This is outside of Boston, though.

Yeah, this is outside of Boston. Now, Ferncroft is where they had a big gambling joint. Ferncroft is where they gambled, the guy used to come down after they'd win a whole lot, they'd come down to Sontag Lake Inn. A man would tell me, very bad tonight. We used to have a producer named Mr. Johnson, white head man, he was a producer here in New York and he used to come down there and he would have a companion with him, see, and when he come in, he'd come up to the piano and he would give me his pocketbook and I'd take

a $5 bill out for everybody in the band, see, so if he stayed there over an hour or longer, then I'd go up to him, the girl would say you just and I said I'm running this end of the town, now, when you get him over there you run it.
So he'd give me his pocketbook and I'd take $5 out apiece more. Oh, we used to make a whole lot of money.
You mean they allowed the blacks to gamble at the tables with the whites.
Shucks, do everything up in Boston. Gamble, they'd have a gambling down there, a man would say hey, shoot $100 Tom and I'd crap out. I know one day, I shot $300, 100, 100, 100.
We were talking about this place in Boston where you used to play, but you want to talk about some songs now.

Yeah, you see, all them guys used to come down and bring the lead sheet, the song pluggers and I used to try to get the guys interested in -- I had a song I said -- it goes like this (Humming) 'Japanese Sandman', see, I used to play that and didn't have a melody to it and I don't know how it got away from me, but first thing I know somebody come out with 'Japanese Sandman.' I said, man, I used to play that long while ago. And I got a number (humming) and no one stole that because it's too hard. Got somemore there. I used to write -- make up numbers and nothing happened until I came
here to New York and they started stealing all my music. The band would play in the theatre and the next week they'd be up the Savoy and you'd go up there that week and you hear my music up there.

Let's get back a little bit to Duke unless you got something else you want to say. I would like to talk about some of the guys in the band, you know all the guys, how did you get along with them, guys like Sonny was probably there the longest.

I got along with all of them. Ben Webster, he used to say, don't wake up Tom. Ben would have his beer and have a bottle and he'd sit there and drink all the time and he would get high but you wouldn't know it, see, he would get them sleepy eyes and go to sleep. The band --
How did you like his playing Ben Webster
Oh, Ben would rehearse and rehearse and then get on the stage and play something altogether different. (laughs)
Truly great musician, he was a dear friend of both yours and mine.
Oh, yeah. Toby --
Otto Hardwick, alto saxophone player.
Now, he was a great musician, see, he and Harry Carney on the baritone sax and his alto and they
were the great, they would -- you know, they would control the music, if it's going soft and oh, it was great.
All the dynamics was controlled by Toby and Carney.
That's right.

You know, in observing Duke's band, the guys that always seemed to me most reliable was like Harry Carney, you know, when they took intermission and the band came back out after intermission you could always depend on Carney to be back on time and you could always depend on perhaps in later years, the clarinet player that's down in the West Indies now.
Jimmy Hamilton.

Jimmy Hamilton and I think that's -- I remember once seeing that band, and after intermission Duke would play something, he made this little call -------- he made that little call to call off the men back and the guys were out socializing with the chicks and talking to the customers, Duke would be the only one on the bandstand and pretty soon you see Carney come up and he would start something like Mood Indigo where he only needed three or four of them to get it started.
Can you tell me something about that.
What do you call it, his -- Duke Ellington at the piano and he'd start a number like -------
what was it. (Humming)
"A Train."

The "A Train", see, and then go from the A Train he would go into a number for probably Cootie, see, and from then he would give a preparation for 'Mood Indigo' and that's three guys would come out and then he would go into Harry Carney on "Sophisticated Lady" and from Harry he would go into "Satin Doll" and that would close his performance. But he knew how to build up, you know, gradually build it up into man, they are jumping.
Oh, yeah, he had that ability to rise to the occasion and as you say to build it up.
Keep on coming up.
What did you say again, you started copying for Duke.

In 1940, you know, I was at the theatre and the girls in 1940, they wanted more money and the man wouldn't give them any more money so they closed them up and closed my job out also, so I was hanging around, so I don't know how, but I got in contact with Duke or Duke got in contact with me and sure, I says, I thought I was going to arrange, see, but he said he wanted a copier, so I said I'll go ahead and copy.
And in '42, we went to Hollywood and I was copying this "Black, Brown and Beige" and oh, this thing, "Come Sunday"

and I said, hey, what are you going to do with this, and he said nothing, but in 1963 he went to Chicago and included -- he made My People, that was the show and in that show was 'Black, Brown and Beige.' He had the people coming from the pit, they were in rags, my people, our people in rags coming up and then at the end, they were doctors, and lawyers and everything.
I never saw that show, that must have been beautiful. You copied that.

Yeah. Man, I used to copy and run out and listen to the shows, copy and listen to the shows and I said to Duke, you know, this should be in the World's Fair, you should take this out to the World's Fair. Never got there. That was a show, I think it was one of the greatest shows I have ever seen, so the topic was Negro, see.
What was the name of that?

My People. It was the education of the Negro through music. And he developed it and oh, it was beautiful and the last thing was 'What is Color? What is Virtue?' He developed that thing, he was working over in Detroit and he come over and fix a part and go back to the show, to his show, when we was in Detroit. That lasted -- we'd go on -- and I'd have to go out in the lobby and I said tell the band leader, don't go until I tell you, because the people are lined out there coming into the show. They would come there

two and three times a week to see that show. Butterbeans and Susie they were there looked like every day and Alice,oh, what's her name, the Whitman sisters, they were there all the time. That was a great show.
You'd have three and four thousand people at that show.
If you were there, you were copying for them, those were probably the greatest years of Duke's band, would you say. Most people have said that 1940 band --
That 1939 and '40 band was the greatest band, right.
Now, who were those guys. Ray Nance came in about that time.
Yeah, Ray Nance come in.
Tricky Sam was still there, right.
Right.
Who else, name some other guys.
Whetzel --
No, Whetzel was gone in 1940.
Johnny -- Jimmy Hamilton.
Rex Stewart was there.
Yeah, Rex Stewart, that's it.
And Ben was there. In 1940
Yeah. That was a great band.
That was one of the great bands and
the critics and most people in show business have always admitted that.

Yeah, to me that was a great band, see. Because the guys understood, you know, and they would play and bend a note, they could bend a note instead of playing it just as a quarter note or half note or eighth note, they would bend it and play it this way. Give it some color and everything. Interpretation of his music was great.
No question about that.
And what are some of the tunes that you think were some of his greatest masterpieces you copied for him.
Let me see, 'Black, Brown & Beige' I think was the greatest. That developed all that stuff in there.
Did that develop in My People.

Yeah, that came in with My People, but Ray Nance was in there on the violin. He had a part on his violin and man, he was great. Soul, really a soul man. He would play that violin and get on to one of them notes.
Ray and I went to high school together in Chicago.
In Chicago, yeah.
It was a great loss.
He was a great guy.
Now did you know in that band Blanton. Was that before you.
Blanton, Blanton was there just before I came in.
Talk about this young man who was so great and so brilliant.
They told me about it. I never heard him, but they used to tell me that Blanton was great. I say how could he be. Pettiford to me was a great.
Pettiford was fantastic.
Yeah, Pettiford and I were like brothers.
Is that so. Oscar Pettiford.
Oscar Pettiford and when he went to Europe.
Tell me about it, because he was a dear friend of mine.

I told Duke -- when Duke said he had Oscar Pettiford coming, I said Oscar Pettiford is a soloist. He said well, he's going to play bass in my band and I said okay and he came in and you know how it takes time for him to get in the groove and --
And he could do it.
And he got that cello, he could play that cello.
He's a fantastic player, a dear friend of mine. Fantastic player.
Who else in there that you really liked and who
impressed you, Tom. Do you know Joe Nanton-- Tricky Sam.

Yeah, he died while we was in -- up there in -- one of those shows, one of those roads coming from San Francisco. We had been out all night, see and I said to Tricky, I'm going on to bed, so he said all right and got up and I called him and he didn't answer, so it's time to go to the show and still he didn't answer and when they come in there and found --he had a hemmorhage, . He was dead.
I vaguelremember him and I knew him but he was always like a loner, wasn't he.
Yeah, he'd always have his bottle of whiskey with him in his case and he was the one that developed that waa, waa.
Absolutely. He would say Yah, yah, and so on. Tyree followed later.
Yeah, Tyree.
I can remember Tricky Sam from Beefsteak Charlie's. Do you know about Beefsteak's where we used to drink, down on 50th and Broadway. Remember that bar.
Oh, shucks.
I remember that Tricky Sam always used to be down there at the end of the bar by himself. He was just having a little taste. Who else in that band are you --
I'm trying to think. I used to try to get next to -- what's the drummer's name.
Sam Woodyard.
I tried to get him, but he was like a loner. All by himself all the time and I never knew when he was sober.
Did you know Barney very well.

I didn't know him very well but he and Tizol, they were two guys that left early, see. But Tizol -- Charlie Mingus, remember when Charlie Mingus was with the band. He died here recently and Charlie was with the band and he and Tricky -- I mean, what's the name the trombone player, Tizol, they couldn't get along.
They had that big fight at the Apollo Theatre. Were you there that time.
Yeah, I was there.
How did that thing go.
I told Duke you better get one of them off because Tizol is going to cut them down. That was awful. But I told Duke, Mingus' fault, Mingus was a agitator.
Go on and tell it. How did it happen.

I wasn't there when it started but I know they were agitating, see and Tizol was one, you were supposed -- like a director, see. Now they play it this way, because he copied the music and knew how it went. And Mingus and them got to arguing about something and I called Duke, I said, man Tizol is going to cut him down because Tizol was
really going to cut them I think.
Mingus had the fire axe or something, didn't he. Didn't Mingus have the fire axe after Tizol.
Oh, I don't know what they did. Anyway
It's in the record that perhaps the only person that Duke really ever fired was Mingus because he just hated to fire anybody. He would find some reason to get them out.
He didn't fire anybody.
But he told Mingus he thought he better go. That they couldn't get along. I remember reading that some place.

Well, I was down to a place where Earl Hines was playing and Mingus was on the side and Mingus got up to play and he was playing and you know, how parties sit down and start talking and Mingus took his horn and turned the table over.
His bass fiddle, you mean.
Yeah, his fiddle and turned the table over. And I had to go and get Earl back on the stage again. This was down at some club, nightclub.
Go on and talk, Tom.
That ended. Mingus was relieved. But they used to say Mingus was a great bass player. They used to tell me that Mingus was a great bass player, but --
I believe so, I really do.
Yeah.
Yes.
Well, I couldn't see it.

I think Mingus like, and this is in my humble opinion, Tom, of course, I'm not supposed to be talking but in my humble opinion I use him like Duke, he was so far ahead of the time and you know Duke was ahead of time, I think people are going to in the next few years, begin to recognize what a great person he was. It was like Duke's music was a little bit ahead of time.
But that's my humble opinion because I'm a bass player and I think perhaps I'm prejudiced.

Well, you see, Duke, he didn't like that word jazz either, see, he cut it out. There ain't no jazz -- I used to tell people, it ain't jazz, it's tempo. Jazz this thing up,mess the music up. That's what they do, mess it up. You would never know the melody.

You're right, Tom, in our day your and mine, we used the word jazz as sort of a sex symbol, like we would say, if you screw something up, it means it just mess it up. That's what we were saying about jazz, screw him, the heck with him. But we've had so many words changed now to, like, for instance, the word funky when you and I were young men, funky was a dirty word, right. Funky, the word funky
means somebody didn't smell good.
That's right.
They hadn't bathed properly. Had body odor. Now, funky means to play something that's --

Low-down. I used to tell everybody don't say eight bars of music, say I want eight measures of music, because eight bars of music doesn't fill out. It's always nine bars in an eight bar phrase. Eight measures phrase. And that's how they take liberties, you know.

There was a guy played in a symphony band in Cincinnati, he's a director of the Boston Conservatory now, but he wrote a book on jazz, supposed to be on jazz and he opened it, the first words was about jazz but then he went right into swing. See, he never did say what jazz was.

I have a record here which I read to you in 1974 where Duke was speaking about his music and perhaps a little bit later on, I can dig it up and we'll read it again. And I'll let you hear it. This is one of my old 33 records, it's a small -- not like an album but a 33 record that goes back quite sometime. We'll talk bout that a little later.
I could see Duke progressing every year it was something different and when he came into the sacred concert music, ah, that was my field. Oh, I loved --
You orchestrated all of that.
I loved that voice, the choir and when
we was up at Harvard I got more applause than Duke or anybody in the band, anybody. When they'd call my name out, oh, them people would yell.
That's when they struck the Duke -- Are we talking about at Yale.
Harvard, when he played the Sacred Concert up there, see, I rehearsed it and the director up there he wouldn't direct it. He said you direct it and that's what the kids all liked.
You conducted the concert there.

Yeah, I conducted up there and I said, I got more applause than Duke or anybody. Oh, them kids really applaud and we went down Texas the same way. Some church down there had it and the man said, no, you know it, you direct it.
When was that, Tom?
This was about in '65 or '66, somewhere around there. Let me see, the concerts started in '67, I think, his Sacred Concerts. The first one was out there in Grace Episcopal Church in San Francisco.
What year was that.
I think it was '67.
Then the rest of them must have been after this, '67 and '68 and '69. If this first on was in '67, the rest must have followed. Let me think.
Let me see, I think it was in '67 or '68, that first one was at Grace Episcopal. Oh, that place was crowded.
That's a matter of record, we could find that out very easy.

Yeah, and he -- I think that was a great concert, but then when we came here to New York, the 55th Street Theatre -- I mean, church, we did a concert there. And I thought that was great, and then we did at the St. John Divine, oh, that was a great concert, see. I tell you the greatest of all of them was when we were over in Spain, Barcelona.
You went over there with them.
Yes, I was over there with them.
What year was that.

That was in '68 and we did -- no, I think that was '69 or '70. We did a concert in Barcelona and I rehearsed the choir for ten nights and the night of the concert the place was crowded, the cathedral was crowded, people were standing and sitting all over the floor, all over everywhere and I had -- I rehearsed the band but the director, he directed it, see, and he knew everything, he remembered everything that I did and we had a number there that Tony Watkins, he started, 'Don't Get Down on Your Knees Unless You're Going to Pray.'
Who was Tony Watkins.

Tony Watkins was a singer with the band and in the middle of this number the choir came in and sang, 'Father, Forgive.' (Singing) and it was all that two words and when they got throught singing that, you could hear a pin drop and then pandemonium reigned, oh, they went wild. I was crying, Duke was hugging the director and oh, them people went crazy.
I said to Duke that is the greatest concert we've done. Oh, it was great, everybody enjoyed it and then we went to Paris. We did a concert in Paris. Oh, we did concerts all over, up there in Sweden.

It was beautiful. I enjoyed it greatly. When I started directing it was here in Brooklyn at this church over in Brooklyn, and I was up in the balcony and the band was below me and there was a little, just a little difference --
Time different, time lag we call that.

And then the next time we went over there, I got them all on the -- put them down on the level. But it was great. I enjoyed playing or rehearsing the group. I used to go all over New York and the country, I'd go all over Europe by myself.
You traveled alone.
I traveled alone and get to the group where they're going to have the concert and then rehearse them
and the band would come in so we'd have it all set up for them. Oh, it was great and I used to love them voices.
Used to love what.
Those voices. Those voices in Spain, they had something in them voice that youdon't have over in this country, oh, that was beautiful. Made me cry. It was so beautiful.
And you had orchestrated all of this, too, you orchestrated all of it.
Yeah, I knew every note. That's one thing, I knew every note in the choral group. I could tell the guy when he was singing the wrong note. I used to sing baritone in the group.
Whoever got weak, you'd jump in.
I said to myself that was great. That is one of the greatest concerts we ever did. I always told Duke that's the greatest concert you ever did and he never would say it was great, see.
What would he say.

He wouldn't say nothing. You'd tell him that's a great concert and then we went down here to Georgetown, I think I was blind then, I went down there with him and Mary McPartland was down there and we did a show down there.
You were blind before Duke died.
Oh, yeah.
I didn't know that.
I got blind in '72.
When did Duke die.
Duke died in '74.
I see.
And Strayhorn died in '68 or '67 somewhere around in there. Now, there was a beautiful guy.
Tell me about Strayhorn. Tell me your relationship with Strayhorn and Duke andyou guys, what was that like.
Oh, that was beautiful. Strayhorn was -- he could -- Duke could start something and he would end it, and you'd never know whether Duke started or stopped or Strayhorn started.

I remember in 1974 you told me about something about that Duke was in California and Strayhorn was someplace else and Duke wrote the one and three part and he wanted Strayhorn to write two and four sections, remember telling me that.
No, I don't remember that.
To some song, to some suite but you're saying that was true, right that you couldn't tell where it started.
That's right, Duke would start something

and let Strayhorn end it. You could never tell where Duke ended and where Strayhorn -- Strayhorn to me was a beautiful guy, he used to come by the house every Monday morning and I'd have a bottle of beer for him. That's all he'd have for breakfast and he'd sit down and talk and say what he's going to do and where he's going and he'd call me up when he finished his work and I'd go get him.
You scored his work too.
Oh, yeah, beautiful guy. prettiest
What was one / thing you think you scored for him.
That thing that Duke played, what's the name of it.
Not 'Chelsea Bridge.'
Yeah, that was a great.
There's an album I have here where I think it's after Strayhorn died that Duke made and his mother named him -- what was his name, Strayhorn.
Billy Strayhorn.
His mother named him Billy and Duke did an album on him. I'm trying to find out what tune did you think was a song, or a suite.
The thing that Billy wrote and I never learned was that thing that Duke played. And I was talking about it the other day.
Yes, I can remember vaguely.
Duke used to play it when he was at --
On the piano.
Yeah, on the piano. 'Lush Life.'

You liked that, that was a tough one. You know, to this very day, I'm supposed to know a lot of songs, you know, a bass player where I've been playing for a thousand years, I think I know a lot of tunes and anybody comesand sits down and says what do you want to play, a piano player, what do you want to play, he says I'd like to play 'Lush Life', I get scared to death, because even though I learned it a million times and played it with some wonderful people like --
Well, he was the only one that could play it and get something out of it. Billy, what's his name, the guy that died. Nat Cole. Nat did it, Ella did it, but no one did it like Billy Strayhorn.
The change is unbelievable. I freeze up because they're not just the usual run of things and I'm always afraid of it. Okay. I played it before but I don't think I know it now. Worried to death.
You know, I used to play it and look at that music, watch the music, and then I couldn't remember it afterwards, those changes.
Right, those beautiful changes. Took
a beautiful human being like Billy Strayhorn to think that way.
Yeah, that Lush Life was beautiful.
How did he get the name Sweet Pea. We all know how delicate he was and such a quiet young guy and had this beautiful smile on his face and stayed --
I never knew why they called him Sweet Pea.
I wonder did Duke give him that name or what.
I don't think so. I think he had that name.
Well, it sure fit him because he was a beautiful human being, gentlemanly and quiet.

And you know when he died I had got mugged at the bar on 125th Street. I was there, I had been to see Strayhorn at the hospital and I said I'll see you tomorrow and I went over there to the bar -- what was the name of that bar there.
On 125th Street.
Yeah, right below the theatre.
Was a restaurant there, too.

Yeah, well, I went there and Frank's Restaurant -- I went there and somebody was having a birthday party and they said, Tom, you're just in time. Okay, this is around 8 o'clock, so I sat down and they give me some birthday

wine or something like that and about 12 o'clock I says I'm going home now, and I remember putting my coat on and that's the last thing I remember. And at 5 o'clock in the morning the cop woke me up, I'm over there on East Drive, over there at 115th Street somewhere like over there, and the cop wanted to know what are you doing out there, and my pants were all torn, I had been cut and my money is all gone, and they brought me home, and I called the girl that lived across the street and I said, come in and help me. And she helped me and my face was all battered up. I had to go to the hospital, they had put a bandage allover my face and that's why I couldn't go to Strayhorn's funeral.
Oh man, that's --
I was so sad.
We were just sitting here talking and you were just telling me about, I used to smoke them good cigars.

Mercer Ellington, he used to buy me cigars, they cost $34 a box and I got to liking them see, and one day -- I liked my I.W. Harper also. 100 proof, if you ain't got 100 proof, I don't drink. I know I was down in Texas, Galveston, Duke and I and we went to this lady's house and I always used to carry a fifth of bourbon with me, so we went in this lady's house to have dinner or I guess it was dinner and she didn't have any bourbon so I went and got my

bourbon out of the bag and started drinking it and the woman says, how dare you bring that whiskey in my house. I said, well, I didn't want to insult you but I don't drink this whiskey you have so I had some and I thought I'd bring it in quietly and drink a little. So that was the end of that. She bawled me out. I said I'm sorry and I didn't mean any harm.
Well, how did you quit smoking them cigars.

So I was on a train going down to buy myself a box of cigars and I started thinking, you know, I can buy five fifths of whiskey for this $34 so that was the end of my smoking cigars. I bought myself a fifth of whiskey instead.
Great, and now you don't even bother with that.
I'll tell you another thing about, we was up there in British Columbia, you know where that is.
Yes, way up in Canada.
Way up in the northeast -- west part of the United States there, up there above Washington State. And we would -- we were doing a gig up there in what's the name of the town.
I can't tell you the town. There was a club up there that all the bands used to play there. Triangle Club or something like that.
And we got up there late, see, and we

didn't have time to eat or anything, sat up the band and go on to work and we got through, the band boy put the things on the bus and we were all waiting. We got down to the port of embarkation and we were all waiting around there so I'm about 20 feet from the bus, I'm by myself, because I'm waiting in a hurry to get back into town where I can get something to eat.

So one of these officers come up to me and says and what did you buy. I says what I did. He says, 'what did you buy.' I said, 'you know we didn't have time to eat anything. "Oh, what did I buy. I bought a million dollars worth of diamonds!" His face turned red, he turned around, take everything off that bus. Duke comes over and says, 'what did you tell the man?' I said the man asked me what did I buy and I told him I bought a million dollars worth of diamonds. I ain't had time to get a drink of water hardly and he asked me that.
So everybody laughed, million dollars worth of diamonds Whaley.
They named you that. Vancouver.
That's right, up there in Vancouver. Beautiful place.
Between the two of us, we can remember almost anything, Tom.
I remember that and everybody, even Steven James, he was there I think --
The singer.
No, Steven James, Ruth's son. He always remembered that.
Did you know Junior Ragland. He was one of the beautiful people that was in Duke's band.
I'll tell you about Junior, Junior would never put on a clean shirt.
Bass player, wasn't he.

Always a dirtyshirt. I said do you see Duke out there immaculate, and look at you. I said why don't you -- shucks, I remember one day, we were supposed to play the United States Bond Hour, and Ragland and Duke had rehearsed together, they were going to play a number and we went to -- after rehearsal we went to this club and I said 'Ragland, hey don't drink too much because you got to get up in the morning.' Shucks, you know, Ragland got drunk and everytime I'd look up the waiter was saying 'that man over there ordered a drink.' I said 'don't give him anymore.' So went to sleep, got up in the morning, we couldn't wake Junior Ragland up. We put him on some cold water, that didn't do him any good.
Junior was out. He sure was.

He was a natural bass player and a natural musician. Not to jump into your history but I knew him and we loved each other. He loved me dearly and I loved him, respect him as a bass player. But he was, as you say, he hadn't had the kind of background that we had about cleanliness

and his feet was always bare, he wore house shoes and Duke hired him because Duke was looking for talent and surely, Junior was a talent, so he hired and I can remember Junior used to bring me, he'd drink a drink called Junior Flip where you took gin and cherry juice and put it together and this one particular year during the wartimes Cab Calloway was at the Park Sheraton Hotel which is at 56th and 7th Avenue and Duke was at the Zanzibar at 49th Street and Broadway and during our intermission, they had intermission, Junior loving me so and respecting me so, he would fix a quart pitcher of this gin and put cherry juice in it and put a cover over it and in his house shoes, he would walk from 49th and Broadway up to 56th and 7th Avenue with this gin in a pitcher with a napkin over the top of it.

And I'm playing this very sedity club with Cab Calloway, Cab was most dignified in those days and his band was very dignified. We had white tails on and we were playing on the roof, the garden roof of the Park Sheraton Hotel and Junior Ragland would -- not up the service entrance, but right up the main entrance and he'd come up there on the elevator and he's a huge young man, he had a big bulk of a body and that very sad looking face, looked like it loved everybody like -- what are those dogs in Switzerland that people attribute to carrying the rum around their shoulders -- St. Bernard and he had that sort of St. Bernard dog look on his face and this huge

body and here he comes up on the elevator with this quart of gin and he gets off and he walks in this club and the maitre'd says sir, may I do something for you. He says no everything is cool. I just want to take this up to Milt Hinton and the maitre'd is trying to tell him that he should come up through the service entrance and he just walks right straight through the club and walks up to the bandstand and sits his quart of gin down on the bandstand with all the customers dancing and Cab Calloway looks at me, get your damn friends out of here.
That was the kind of beautiful human being that Junior Ragland Ragland was, besides being a truly great bass player.
Right, he was a great bass player. You know, in '48 when Duke went to Europe, he didn't take the whole band, see, so I used to go up to the Apollo Bar, that was on 25th Street --
125th Street, yeah.

Yeah, and I used to go to the man and say why don't you get some music in here so he says well, who should I get and I said get ahold of Johnny Hodges, so I went down and saw Johnny that night and I said go up to the Apollo bar and talk to the man about business. All right.

Johnny went up, the man hired Johnny and Johnny hired me as a manager and Junior Ragland Ragland was there and I wonder who else was there, anyway, he was one of the spots and Billy Eckstine was the other spot. We had Hibler on our -- singing,
and we opened and you couldn't get in there, man, they talked about Johnny Hodges is at the Apollo bar.
Oh, he was a sensation up there.

Sure, man, you couldn't get in that place and they'd pay $5 a head and Billy -- the second week Billy Eckstine came in and the opening night Billy wanted to quit. I said what's the matter, he said, man, they don't need me here. They got Hibbler and Johnny so finally he stayed but oh, that was a great spot and the man says, how long and I said oh, he'll stay. When Duke come back, Duke come up there and they gave a big party for Duke.
Duke talked to him -- I said to Johnny, you're going to Chicago and the man's going to double your salary. No, Que was the one that made him quit.
Que was Johnny Hodge's wife.

Yeah. Que said he got too much honor himself, he can't go. I said, he only had six people and he's making double the money. They were going to give him a whole lot of money up in Chicago and no, Johnny went back to Duke. I said, well, that's the end of that.
Then we went down to on 46th Street, I had Oscar Pettiford.
46th and what.
Between 6th and 7th, over the -- Louis Apozza had a place over there. And we had -- I had --
46th between 6th and 7th.

I don't know where it was now, but anyway it was over there and we used to fill them up and the man closed the place up to make it larger, see and then Oscar, he would get to the bar and instead of -- he'd tell me get the people out, I said they're waiting for you. He went back to Birdland, the man fired him and then he went back to Birdland. He was making a good salary up there.

He made some great records, Oscar Pettiford, I mean he was a bass player that really truly followed Blanton and carried Blanton, that Blanton could do, Oscar is the one that carried it on to bring bass up to where it is today, don't you believe that.
Oh, he could play that bass. I used to -- I told Duke when I heard about it, I said Pettiford is a soloist, well, he going to play in my band. Yeah, he and I, the Whaley brothers.
Is that what youcalled it.

Yeah, we used to go as the Whaley brothers. And we had a -- up there in Boston, I had a drummer, used to call the Whaley brothers, he and I. But that Apollo bar, that was a -- everybody used to come up there.
That was at --
It was on 8th Avenue near 126th, wasn't it.
No, it was -- the Apollo bar was below the Apollo Theatre.
Oh, yes, you're right.
Right at the corner of one of those -- of St. Nicholas, I think.
That's right, it was near -- on 125th Street near St. Nicholas. Nipsy Russell and Billy Daniels and everybody played there, didn't they. Even Pearl Bailey played there one time, didn't she.
Yeah, that was a good place.
It was a swinging joint.
I used to sit at the bar with the man, the man would put on -- put Cognac out there, I'd drink, I was drinking Cognac see, taking it easy.

Tom, you were really a big dog to us at the time because you had been therebefore all of us come there and you had controls, you really knew that town and you were the kind of guy that could give us all some work, just like you said, you told the guy at the Apollo bar, get Johnny Hodges. It was through you that a lot of us got little gigs now and then.
Yeah, I used to tell a lot of them people. I'd go around, I'd tell them -- they'd want to know who to get and I'd tell them. Man, you get this guy, he's great.
And they respected your opinion because it always proved out right.
Schiffman was the manager of the theatre, the Apollo Theatre.
What was his first name. I can't think of it now.
I can't think of his name. I always called him Mr. Schiffman.
But he owned the Apollo Theatre.

Yeah, he owned the theatre and he hired me as musical director. All I had to do was take the music that they brought in and orchestrate it and rehearse the girls with the producer, rehearse the show girls or the dancing girls.
And you tell them what you did there, Tom, because I did some of those things with you, with Eddie South back in 1933, it was down in the basement, wasn't it. You tell it.

We rehearsed down in the basement. They used to have a nightclub there before and I used to play there with that guy that had a trombone. Brownie, remember Brownie, Trombone Brown, he had the band there and I was his piano player and you know, we'd have to go downtown to these hotels and play a show and the man says it's a benefit and one day I went down there and there they had a car, you know,
an announcement that so and so's band was going to be there.
Yeah, a placard out in front, advertising.

And I told Joe, I think his name was Joe Warren that you got to pay me some money because I go in there at 6 o'clock at night and don't come out until 6 o'clock in the morning. I said I want more money and he wouldn't give it to me so I quit. I had been in a whole lot of places and Joe Warren, he owned that theatre, I mean, the downstairs, the bar downstairs, that was a nightclub down in there, the Apollo Theatre, did you know that.
I think so, downstairs, right. Because they had a little stage there.
Sure
Tell me some of the people that used to be down there. You would build a show around Eddie South. Who the -- the violin was Eddie South.

Yeah, the manager -- I mean the producer, he'd have the -- he'd have something in mind and he'd tell us to get together and make up something, see and we'd make -- I'd get the music, Paul Denniger used to write -- he was a writer and he used to write bits, Porter Grainger, remember Porter Grainger?
Yes, Porter Grainger, writer.
Donald Haywood.
Right, did some of that stuff for who.
He has that kid now, Leslie Uggams. Yeah, he and I used to rehearse Leslie Uggams.
Yeah, she was a little girl.
Yeah, little girl then and then she went with Miller's -- what's -- Miller had the chorus. She went with him.
And then she went with Cab on the road.
Now she's doing show bits, show business, she's out there in Hollywood.
She's a superstar now. What about the Nicholas brothers when they were little babies.
See, I used to direct the band and play the piano, so I went over to Philadelphia to Lee Whipper --
The great movie start. One of our own, he just died not too long ago.
That's right, 100 and some years old. I was over there--
Black man.

Yeah, and he told me hey, you direct the show and let Mrs. Nicholas play and her husband would play the drums. I said I'm not going to direct no show. This is when I first started, so sure enough I directed this show and let Mrs. Nicholas play the piano and her husband played the
drums and then the Nicholas brothers, oh, they were terrific. And did I tell you about Sammy Davis.
What about Sammy Davis.
Sammy Davis came into the Apollo Theatre with his uncle and father and didn't have any music and I fixed their music and they used to get Sammy in the middle and squeeze him. I'll never forget that.
Tell us about it, Tom.
Yeah, Sammy Davis. I arranged for him and his father when they first come into the Apollo Theatre.
Was that the Will Mastin Trio.
Will Mastin Trio, yeah. I will never forget that.
What kind of act was that.
Oh, that was a dancing act. They used to dance. I don't remember much about it, see, because that was a long -- that was when I first went in the Apollo.
I just want to have it on the record that you were there in the beginning with all of these superstars, these black actors or superstars now.
Everything started after I got in the Apollo Theatre. When I came to New York, the Connie's Inn wasn't there.
The what. Where was that at.
Connie's Inn was 132nd Street.
And 7th Avenue. It was near what theatre.

Right near the Lafayette Theatre. It was a college inn I think then and then they -- what was the name of the brothers, George and -- they bought the thing and turned it over -- I used to arrange music in there. Yeah. I've arranged music all over the -- I'll tell you about Jack Leg's Diamonds.
Jack Leg's Diamond, the gambler.
Yeah, he -- I used to play down -- I had a group down -- it's around 56th Street, there's a big building there and --
56th and What.

Broadway. They had lofts there and these guys, I don't know who they were but anyway, they opened it up as a nightclub and I used to have the band there, see, and they used to have colored entertainers and a colored entertainer, if they get a dollar, they give me 50 cents, see.
They got to split with the leader.

Yeah. Well, now we was -- one week we was doing great, we make a lot of money. Now, next week they fired a colored entertainers and put the white girls in and the white girls would only give us 10 cents on a dollar so I called Harry, I said Harry --
Who is Harry.

Harry was the boss, he was the boss -- I never knew his last name. Harry, I just said 'Harry, you know what, these colored entertainers used to give us 50 cents or split half and now these girls are only giving us 10 cents.' He said 'I can't help it.' So I think this is near the first of the week. I said, 'well, I'm getting through Saturday,' because our tips went from say, $15 a night to $3 and $4. I said 'we can't do that!'

So I quit. Now while I was there, this guy used to come over and sit in back with his hat on and always send a waiter up and tell the band to play such and such a number and he would never send any money so I told Harry, 'see that guy sitting down there, he's been here every night and he hasn't sent us a nickel.' He said 'you know who that is.' I said no. He said 'that's Jack Legs Diamond. He's a gangster. Let him alone.' So we quit that night and you know the next Monday night they raided the place and Alphonso Steele was the doorman, he got hurt. They shot the place up.

Another place I used to -- down to Mummer's Club, down on 33rd Street and one night, it was on a Saturday night and I was there and the place started fillingup and all these men come in and I said -- I don't know who it was, but I said so and so shouldn't let all these men in here, and I hadn't no more than said that then the cats jumped up on the table, little cat, he wasn't four feet and he had a great big pistol
and the bullets were pointing out the barrel, see, you could see them and he said this is a holdup. I said ain't this awful.
He stuck up the joint.

Yeah, they stuck the joint up and I had some tips in a bag and I eased it down and shoved it in my corner and they come to me and I said 'no, I ain't got nothing, ain't made nothing. It's been a bad night.' He said, 'yeah, we got to go up to Sing Sing with this money. We take up there to Sing Sing because they need some money.' So I went up to Small's that night and who do you suppose I saw them gangsters were up there.
Partying.
Yeah, they were partying.
Why.
They said they had to send money up to Sing Sing, and they robbed these places. Yeah, I had a colorful life.
You surely did, Tom. You deserve it.

I remember over at the Cat's Meow in Brooklyn, the gangsters run that place and they had a show, chorus girls and everything and the man owed me money for a week and he said he's going to give to me when I open up but he didn't give it to me so I wouldn't play there, no, you got to give us some money. We don't play. He took me in
the office and he hit me. I said I know you ain't going to get no more music now.
So I told the band don't play nothing.
That's fantastic.
That's --
Let's take a little rest now, Tom.
Okay.

break it in half Take it --/and then he'd play with the glass. Where you at?

So one day, this guy sent word up, tell that guy to break his clarinet. He sent five dollars up, see. So we did it.
What was this guy's name again, Tom?
