it on stage and getting plenty of money for it." Wow.
And I had another guy, I can't think of his name.
Did you ever know Cliff King and Wilbur Sweatman? They used to do that thing.

Well, Sweatman used to play three clarinets, played a -- Mother Machree, I think it was. He used to play something where he'd used three clarinets. And at this job, I used to go in there and they had 12:00 over there, at Beach Street and that was a restaurant where all the secretaries would come in for lunch. And we used to play from 12:00 to 2:00.
Oh, lunchtime.

Yeah, and then go back there at 12:00 at night, play for the dancers. Here I had two jobs and never made a nickel. I'd have to go to one job and collect some money and go to the next job and pay off. I was gambling, that's when I was gambling.
I was up in Boston. And Marva Louis, I arranged all her music, and she --
She was the lady that married Joe Louis, right?
Yeah, Marva Louis. She used to get $500 a performance. She went down to Philadelphia, and it was a small
room, and then people would try to tear her clothes off. But she went through with it. She made a bet with Joe, I think, or somebody, that she could last six months in show business. And she did.
Did she do it?
Yeah. She made a lot of money. $500 a week.
Did you ever know anything about Jack Johnson?

Jack Johnson? Jack Johnson I never met, but he was -- up in 1914, he was up there in Chelsea, Massachusetts. But I didn't see him, see. And I think Sam Langford -- see, I used to be a buddy of Sam Langford's.
Who was Sam Langford?
Sam Langford was a heavyweight fighter. He and Gus Smith used to fight each other.
What's the other guy's name?
Gunboat Smith.
Was he black, too?
No, he was a white guy. And they used to fight, put on a --
Exhibition.
No, this was a real fight. One would win this day and the next one would win -- I said, why don't you keep them -- he said, well, we've got to get along. Out

Revere Beach, I used to go out there with Sam Langford and walk with him, and Henry Armstrong. Henry Armstrong was in New York, and he used to come down to the theater there where he heard us, and watch us. Man, if I could play piano like you. I said, oh, you. If I could fight like you, I said.
We're just sort of skipping around now, but I'm just doing this to keep the conversation going with you. Now, what about Perry Bradford? Did you know Perry?
Perry Bradford. I'm going to tell you, Perry Bradford was one of the originals. He discovered Mamie Smith, he had Mamie Smith.
He said that, he told me that. I'm glad to hear you verify that.

Yeah, he had Mamie Smith and then Bessie Smith come on, see. And he couldn't use Bessie Smith, but he'd give her a dollar -- $100, I mean, for -- Bessie was an original, she was an original blues singer.
Right.
Bessie, she was up there at Carney's Inn. And she'd get in a high and start crying, and say, Tom, give me ten dollars, I want to buy some --
What, did Bessie Smith say that to you?
Yeah.
You knew her well, huh?
Oh, yeah. Shucks. Bessie Smith could
sing.
She could sing.
And Gertrude Saunders.
Who was that?
Gertrude Saunders.
What, she was singing?
Yeah. If she had kept her head, you would have never heard of Ethel Waters.
Is that so? What kind -- was she a good-looking chick?
Huh?
Was she a good-looking black woman?
Oh, yeah. She was a brown-skinned girl.
What kind of -- what was her personality like?
She thought she was the greatest. And she got arguing with the boss and --
Her ego got to her, huh?
Yeah. And the boss told the man to get another singer.
And so they got --
And that's when they went out and got Ethel Waters.
Where did they get Ethel from?
Ethel? From downtown somewhere.
Uh-huh. What about Ethel?

Oh, Ethel to me was a great -- I remember the first time I saw her, at the Lafayette Theater. And I said, Ethel, you need some music. And she said, my piano player would tell them all what to do. I said, no, you got too much to learn. You can't keep it in your head.
Anyway, she consented. I think she only give me 12 dollars.
Is that so?
Oh, yeah. But Ethel was a great -- I remember she was singing 'Supper Time'.
I'm lucky to be able to say that through the graces of you and MR. Eddie Mallory and Tyre and Benny Carter. I got to make some records with her.
Oh, you did?
Oh, a few of them, 'Bread and Gravy' and a couple of things that she did back in the '30s and the early '40s.
Did you -- did she do 'Supper Time' with you?
No, I don't think I did 'Supper Time' with her.
That's when she's talking about her old man won't come back anymore.
Yes, right, I remember that.
She did that at the theater. And you
know, if anybody would heckle her, she'd stop and fire right back at them. Alan Drew, you remember him?
Alan Drew, he sang -- yeah, tell me about Alan.
He was an M.C.
You ran into all these show people.
Oh, yeah.

That's what we really want to know about, Tom. The people that the people of the world don't know about now, because they're gone. And they don't know that these were the people that basically were before the Billy Eckstein's and the Lou Rawls and the Johnny Mathis and the Sammy Davis's. So you tell me now, who was this guy?

Alan Drew was an M.C. Milton Berle used to come up to the theater every day and sit there and listen to Alan Drew. The quickest repartee man in the world. But he was dirty, he didn't clean his stuff up. Milton Berle was dirty, but he cleaned it up when he went somewhere. Alan Drew was filthy. But he could -- somebody heckle him, he'd --
Today we got a guy, what's this guy today that we think is filthy but he's making a big name for himself? You know who I'm talking about?
Out there in Hollywood, that guy? Yeah. He heckled me at Basin Street.
You know who I'm talking about?
You're talking about that black boy.
Yeah, I know -- I can't call his name.
He's got a show on Broadway right now. Let's hold this tape just a minute, because I want to find out his name.
(Recording interrupted.)

-- you mentioned and a lot of other people. When he's great, he's very foul-mouthed; they don't even keep the children go see him. But it was a different era. Nowadays, you can get away with that stuff that Alan Drew couldn't get away with. He'd probably be famous if he were around today, with all of that foul talk. Like Redd Foxx and Richard Pryor is doing.
Oh, Redd Foxx --
Yeah, you know Redd Foxx. What about that?
When Redd Foxx left here, I thought he was through. And then the first thing I know, he's there doing things in Hollywood, up there in Los Angeles.
And he did all those records. You've got them here. Did you like them? You got those records.
Uh-huh, Redd Foxx.
Now, tell me about some of those other guys. Let's see, Alan Drew and we talked about --
Milton Berle.
Yeah.

Milton Berle used to come to the theater, as I say, every day to listen to Alan Drew. And instead of Alan Drew cleaning up his stuff, like Milton did, becoming the greatest -- Johnny Bigle was Milton Berle's mouthpiece.
Johnny Bigle?
Did you know of Johnny Bigle?
No, I didn't.
Clarence Robinson's partner.
Was he white or black?
Black boy. He used to drive Milton.
He was a chauffeur?

Yeah, he was a chauffeur, but he used to drive for Milton after he got out of show business, see. And he used to tell how Milton was so great. Oh, that's Johnny Bigle. Johnny Bigle used to tell them all that stuff. Drive him around nights and tell them all about how he and Clarence Robinson used to do things.
And perhaps he would tell them all of the stories.

Yeah, all the stuff. And when Johnny Bigle died, Milton Berle lost his mouthpiece. He tried to get a girl to do that, she couldn't do what Johnny Bigle -- and he lost a lot of precedence. But as long as Johnny Bigle was
living Show Milton Berle was the greatest.

George Dewey Washington.
George Dewey Washington.
When I met --
He was a singer, right?
Yep. I met him at the Lafayette Theater.
Tell us about him.
George Dewey Washington came in there with -- what's the lame guy that played violin.
From Buffalo?
Yeah. Smith, what's his name?
Leroy Smith.

Leroy Smith. He came here with Leroy Smith, at the Apollo Theater. And he would drink a whole glass of whiskey before he went on stage. Clear his voice, he said. And, oh, he could sing, George Dewey Washington, yeah. Great entertainer.
That 'Old Man River' was --
Oh, yeah.
He was famous even before Robeson sang that, isn't that right?
Right, he was before -- there was another guy, I can't think of his name. Before him.
Clarence Somebody?
Not Clarence. Oh, what is his name? He went out to -- he was out in Lake George.
But George Dewey Washington was quite a performer. He always had a cane, too, if I remember correctly.
Right, right.
And there was a dark man, I remember seeing him. And highly respected in the black community as a performer.
Yeah.
Is that right?
Paul Robeson to me was a great -- he's still great. He went to White Russia, Georgia*, and he married a woman over there, I think. Yeah, he married a white woman.
He did?
Yeah. But 'Old Man River.'
What about his artisticness.
His what?
His artisticness. What did you know about him? Did you ever know Paul or talk to him?
No, I never knew him. But the last time I saw Paul Robeson was when he was at 116th Street in the Square, and Duke had the band there. And he happened to come by. That's the last time I saw Paul.
*Georgia S.S.R.
I was just trying to get into some things of that era, some of the great performers. Can you think of any others that you knew? Did you know Josephine Baker?
Oh, my goodness, how could I forget her? Josephine Baker was in Boston. She was a Boston girl. Her and -- what's the guy that played trumpet?
Valaida Snow.

Valaida Snow. Her and Val da were on the same show together. And Josephine, she was doing a chorus girl, and she got out of step and lost that. And she started dancing. And the band kept on playing til she got off, and the man said, you keep that in. And Josephine Baker -- that was up in Boston.
Russell Smith was a trumpet player.
Uh-huh, Russell Smith. There were a few brothers --
Yeah, Joe Smith and John Smith.
Is that so?
Yeah.
A lot of good trumpet players.
All trumpet players. And Josephine --
Why do you mention Russell Smith in conjunction with --
Because Russell gave Josephine a car.
Oh, he did?
Yeah, he gave her a Pontiac or something like that.
I would have given her one, too, if I had been around. And she drove to New York, her and Valaida Snow. Valaida Snow was the girl trumpet.
She was a singer, too.
She was a performer. Oh, yeah, she was a performer. And I used to hang around with them.
You did a little more than hang around, Tom.
Oh, that's all. I'd hang around with them.

My wife was Sue Baker.
Beautiful lady.
1927 I married her. She married --

Yeah.
Yeah, my wife Mona and I knew her.

Hold it --

Yeah.

Yeah, --

How did you find out, Tom?

The doctor -- I asked the doctor, what's the matter with her? He couldn't cure her. He said, she's an epileptic. I said, what's that? He said, I don't know. Everyone in the family was an epileptic. Her sister went in a coma and her brother, same way. They all were epileptic, and went in coma and never came out of it.

So I was in -- I think I was in Chicago and she was in the hospital and they called me up and says, you'd better come back as soon as you can because I don't think she's going to live. And I came in early in the morning, and I think it was Sunday morning. The sun was rising when I left the hospital, and she died right after that.
A lovely wife, what was her name?
Sue, beautiful soul, all of them.
Yeah. You married again, didn't you?
Huh?
Did you marry again later?

Yeah, I married in '57. And the girl would always say, 'I'm going home to Ma,' when I'd be out and she'd want me to stay. I'd say, 'I can't make no money home.' So one day I came back and she sure was gone.
What was her name, Tom?
Mazie.
Mazie. So she split.
She was a West Indian girl, pretty girl.
Well, you always had pretty women because you're a sharp dude, man. Lord knows, you had your share. You ain't missed a thing, Tom.
Hey, I stop and think about all the girls I -- I was a terror, I must have been.
You were, man, I saw you. Remember me?
I had a girl in every town.

That was the era. Now, you wanted to talk about -- I wanted to get back to some of the things in the '30s and the '20s that was very important to you. And we haven't spoken too much about it. We spoke of it gradually last time. But go ahead and talk about Will Vodery, which I know you admired.
Oh, yeah. I met Bill Vodery here in New York, when I went in the Army in 1918, he was bandmaster.
And I wasn't in the band at the time, I was in headquarters' company. When I got transferred to the band, and Vodery was the bandmaster. And he used to rehearse us, and you know what I played?
What?
Flute and piccolo.
Wow, I didn't know that.
Yeah, I took up every instrument. They had enough but they didn't have no flute player, no piccolo player. So I had a French man there, and he taught me the flute.
Wow, I didn't know Tom Whaley was a flute player.
Yeah, I used to go out when they had parades and I'd play the piccolo. Man, I'd get a headache, I was walking like I was drunk, playing that flute. But, yeah, I --
So what about Vodery?

Vodery, he was terrific. But he was no good -- I mean, no good that way. He'd get -- we'd go out and play for the lieutenant, go in the lieutenant's office, the captain's bungalow and we'd play. And they'd give us money, we never saw any money. Vodery would take the money and go on to Paris and ball.
Well, wasn't that the usual procedure?
Yeah, they used to do it. And --
But what kind of musician was he?
Oh, he was great. He did a concert out in France there, he did a concert which the bandmasters had a -- what do you call it?
Reproduction? Reproduction of it?
You'd have to take a -- what do you call it, go to school, like.
Oh, take a course.
Take a course, yeah. And it would take the majority of them two hours to do, he'd do it in 20 minutes.
The examination, yeah.
Examination, yeah. Well, anyway, the man says, hey, you ain't finished. He said, man, it's all finished. He did in 20 minutes what it took the average person two hours to do.
He's the one that could write in score ink because he knew he was right.

He'd tell everybody, give me some manuscript papers, stand out in front of the band, and all that noise going on. And he'd write and throw a part to each one, and then says, ten dollars for every bad note. There was no bad note. He was the first man I ever seen do that.
He was the only person I ever saw do it,

too. And it's amazing, this is a black man and our young black children and young American children don't know about these kind of beautiful -- do you know where he was really from? He's gone now. Do you know what part of the country he grew up?
Baltimore. He went to Penn University.
Yeah, he graduated Penn College.
Penn University.
Yeah.
Well, I'm sure the records would be up there.
Yeah.
I must look that up.
Yeah. Man, he was great, to me. I'd make an arrangement down at the Cotton Club, there, with Cab. And I wrote an arrangement, -- and what was the trumpet player's name? He had a son.
Lamar Wright.

Lamar Wright. And I had Lamar hitting up there in E flat or F, and you know how Cab used to rehearse. He'd play that all the time. So Lamar Wright didn't play it, didn't go up there. He said, 'hey, what's the matter?' He said, 'man, got that single note up there?' He said, well, I can play it. And I said to Cab, man, you're rehearsing, he'd go up there. So he said, 'you put it on paper, didn't
you?" I say, yeah.
That's beautiful.
And Cab would say, play it.
Lamar could do that, too.
Oh, yeah, he could play it, the iron lip.
That's what they used to call him, the iron lip.
And Vodrey used to write some beautiful music.
Yeah, do you remember the thing -- he did scores for -- what show was that, it was --
Ziegfeld Follies. Man, Ziegfeld said he was the greatest musician around. Greatest writer.
He scored for Ziegfeld when Bert Williams was one of the comedians.
Oh, Bert Williams, comes to me, Bert Williams, up in Boston. I used to hang out with him on Washington and Pembroke. We used to come there, Bert Williams used to come there and I used to hang out.
Tell us about it. What kind of a guy was he? I never saw him, but I read about him.
He was -- I'm brown-skinned, Bud was a yellow man.
He was lighter in complexion than you.
Oh, yeah.
And you're a light brown skin.
Yeah, Bert Williams --
He was what we would call in our black society moriani. Is that right, would you say?
I don't know.
What would you call it?
I'd call him a yellow man.
Well, high yellow is the word we used, yes, okay.
And he would stand there at the bar and sip his beer and tell more jokes, man, he'd had everybody laughing. Bert Williams.
What bar was this in Boston?
This was up there in Washington Street, the corner of Pembroke.
Was this a black bar or was it an inter-racial bar?
No, it was an inter-racial bar.
Anybody could come in.
Sure, anybody come in.
What year was this?
Oh, let me see. This was way back in 1912, 13.
Maybe a little later, huh?
Yeah.
This was before he came to New York?
No, he used to come to Boston from New York.
After you (unintelligible) with Ziegfeld?
Playing in the show, yeah. He used to come in after he opened here and come to New York -- I mean, come to Boston. He and -- what's that other guy?
Eddie Cantor?
No.
Al Jolson?
No. Oh, I can't think of his name. Anyway, he was a great entertainer. But Bert Williams --
Harry --
No, that ain't the name. But they used to --
Bert Williams was in Ziegfeld's, too, wasn't he? He used to open the show, didn't he?
I think so.

He was there when Bill Vodeery was there. I listened to a couple of stories. I talked to Eubie Blake, and he told me a couple of stories that I wanted to see if you remember or if you can verify. That -- the name escapes me, the comedian we were talking about, what's his name?
Bert Williams.
Bert Williams used to open the show.
And because he was, as you say, a very light-complected black man, he had to --
He had to black up.
He had to black up. He performed in cork, in black.
Yeah.
Yeah. And he wore white gloves, is that right? Do you remember that?
I don't remember the gloves he wore.
Yeah. From what I heard from Vodery and from Eubie Blake and from Perry Bradford, that he opened the Ziegfeld show just sticking his hand with this white glove on --
Out through the curtain.
And the people would start laughing, even before Eddie Cantor or anybody came on. He was in some of the same shows.
He was a big man then.
Do you remember any of his records. "Nobody"
(Singing) Yeah, I used to imitate him.
You did?
Sure.
Do you know who wrote his music?
No.
Bill Vodery. Your man, your friend, Bill Vodery. I have the records here. Like I say, orchestra-
tions by Bill Vodrey. Because Bill was --
Big guy.
He was also writing for this Ziegfeld show, so it was no problem for him to orchestrate for the recordings, of all Bill Williams' recordings. Bill Vodrey is the musical conductor.
Yeah, I know, Bill Vodrey was a big guy. To me.
(Unintelligible.)
Joe Jordan.
Joe Jordan.
Did you ever hear of him?
Yes, he came from Chicago here, right?
Yeah, he used to orchestrate and have a band with Josephine Baker. He wrote all of the music for Josephine Baker when she was in show business.
Tell me about him.
Yeah, Joe Jordan. I was in his band when we was in the 46th Street Theater.
46th and what?
46th and -- off of Broadway. We did a show there.
What's the name of the show?
What was it?
If you can think of it.
Oh, we was --
Who else was in the show? If you can think of it.
No, let me go back to Will Morrissey. He was at the --
Who is Will Morrissey?
Morrissey was an old time comedian.
Black or white?

White man. He would have a high derby, a silk hat. And he would come out before the show and sit on the steps and entertain. And then he says, Tom, you ready? I says, all right. He says, let's go. That was stopping the traffic.
You were the musical director.
Yeah, I was directing the show.
And what was the name of that show?
Stopping the Traffic. Red Hot Harlem.
Red Hot Harlem.

Red Hot Harlem, that was it. Red Hot Harlem. That was back in -- it was around '28 or '29, '25, '27. Will Morrissey used to -- when I lived on 127th Street, he used to come up to my house, knock on the door at 4:00 in the morning, he and his wife. Li'l woman.
Will Morrissey.
Will Morrissey, I'll never forget him.
And he owned the show?
No, he didn't own the show. He was a --
Musical director, producer.
No, he was, like, an MC. He introduced the show.
It was a black show?
Yeah.
But he was a white man.
Yeah, Will Morrissey come on first. We had a skit in there, Walking the Last Mile. Roland Smith was doing it.
Who was Roland Smith?
Roland Smith was a singer.
Black man?
Yeah. And The Penalty of Love. And he --
The what of love?

Penalty. And he would sing this song and walk the last mile. And he'd go by the prisoners and they would holler, keep your head up, keep your chin up. And he would sing that. And he died. We had another guy do that same thing, and he died.
That was a bad luck role, wasn't it?
That was -- yeah. And I told the guy he should capitalize on this because it's two guys have died
doing that number, the Penalty of Love. And we had a girl singing -- oh, I can't think of her name. She's living. I met her recently. Barnes, Mae Barnes.
Mae Barnes. She lives out this way.
Yeah, Mae Barnes was in the show.
Mae Barnes. Great singer.
Oh, yeah, sure.
And Mae Barnes was in this show?
Yeah.
What did you say was the name of that show?
Red Hot Harlem.
Red Hot Harlem.
And then I went on the road with Dewey Wineglass in Stopping the Traffic.
Who was Dewey Wineglass? Was he a white--
Dewey Wineglass, a colored man.
Where did he get the name of Wineglass?
I don't know. Anyway, -- didn't you know him?
I think I did know him.
Sure, he was up at the theater, you know. He used to dance the Russian dance.
Dewey Wineglass, he was a dancer, huh?
Yeah. And then he produced this show,

And we went -- where did we go? Not at Baltimore. Was it Baltimore we went? And he was made an Elk. And I told him to do everything they tell you, don't fight them. No, in Pittsburgh. That's right, in Pittsburgh. I said, don't fight him. Man, he started fighting them people and, man, they put him in the hospital for six months.
Good heavens.
Yeah. And I had to take charge of the show, and we went on to Chicago, went to St. Louis, we come on back to Philadelphia.
This wasn't Red Hot Harlem.
No, this was Stopping the Traffic.
And what's a TOBA?
Tough on Black Ass.
That was our name for it, Tough On Black Ass. But the real name was what? It had to be something else.
I don't know.
There was a legitimate name for it.
TOBA.
This was a black show business circuit. And we called it Tough On Black Asses because it was so rough on us, on the road.
That's right.
But there was another name.*
And I remember in Pittsburgh, we was at
*Theatre Owners Booking Agency
this hotel, either the Top of the Hill or -- Wiley Avenue.
Wiley Avenue, that's it. And --
What year is this, now, Tom?
Oh, this is way back.
Not too far back.
No, it was around 24 or 25.
I see. What show are you with now?
That's Stopping the Traffic.
Stopping the Traffic.
Now, --
And you're the musical conductor?
Yeah.
Eubie Blake was the guy that did all -- conducted all them shows.

I used to conduct the show. That's -- I started when the Nicholas -- Mrs. Nicholas, she -- I was supposed to play the piano, see. I wasn't supposed to direct it. And I told the man -- he said, you go on and direct the show.
Lee Whippet was this great movie star, one of our first great-name movie stars.
Yeah. And Lee says, you direct and she will play the piano. Okay, I said.
Well, did he produce it or --
He was producing the show.
I see.
Yeah, and Mr. Nichols, he played drums.
Oh, is that so?
Yeah. Now, we go back to 1940, 1950.
Let's see, we're back in the '20s now.
Huh?
We're in the '20s now.
We're at what?
We're at the '20s in Pittsburgh. Because Mr. Nichols and them wasn't around in the '50s.

No. We're coming out of the -- that's Stopping the Traffic. And they put the man in the hospital and we went on to Chicago, St. Louis and then back to Chicago and on to Pittsburgh, and you know, the route, the TOBA circuit. Now, let me say, after I come out with Duke, see, in '40.

Name me some acts back in the -- now, we're back in the '20s. Before we get to the '40s, that's 20 years, we can just -- while we're in the '20s, on the TOBA circuit. Name me some of the acts all in there. Ethyl Waters played the TOBA, right?
No, I don't think so.
I thought I read someplace where she wound up in Wiley Avenue in Pittsburgh.
She may have been there but I --
Name me some more. Miller and Lyles.
Did they have anything to do with the TOBA?
No.
Well, I want to ask you because you were there.
They were on that big time show.
Phantages...
Yeah, they were -- no, they had, like, they went on a show --
(Unintelligible.)
Like, shuffling along. They were on that kind of an act. See, they had a show, see.
Well, what kind of people were on the TOBA?
Butterbeans and Sue.

Butterbeans and Susie. There was some act named Brown, something about -- some kind of lady and her husband, named -- not Cookin' Brown, but another name with Brown. A woman and her husband. Do you remember that?
Oh, I know. Yeah. Oh, what's her name? She had a sister. Flo Brown.
Yeah. Well, what about --
Flo and Cecil. They were on.
Yeah. Well, what about the Whitmans?
Were they ever on --
The Whitmans had their own circuit. They had their own --
Tell about these -- tell me about the Whitmans. They were some black sisters in there, their own show. What was that like?
Oh, they had -- what was the boy's name? They used to have two kids. They were from the orphanage, see?
Right.
And they did a whole lot of -- but, see, I forgot a whole lot of that stuff, because --
Well, name me just the things that you remember.
Let me see, --
Like the TOBA, like you were on the TOBA. Silas Green, was he on there?

I don't know. He may have been. There was a whole lot of people that was on that show, on that circuit. That was a big circuit, because when you come into town, the kids are right there waiting for you. I want you to see my act, see.
Right.
And you'd listen to them and you'd tell them whether it was good or not, see? And -- but they don't have anything like that nowadays.
But I just thought you'd remember some-
body. But if you don't we'll go on past that. What about the guys when you were talking about, now, in the '30s. We're going from the '20s, we'll go ten years.
The '30s was when I went in the theater.
The Apollo.
Yeah.
Now, we haven't named any comedians. You haven't told me about Willie Green. You name them, in your order.
Oh, Willie Green. Yeah, Willie Green. He was on the -- he was a comedian.
Right. Did you know him?
And Aphos.
Aphos and Estrelita.
Yeah, and -- oh, I can't think of this guy's name?

Two guys, it was. They used to do that thing to everybody (Unintelligible) You were there -- no, it wasn't, it was across the street. What was the name of that act? It had the controversial thing, where he would say, don't go there because you're going to get sick, and he would say, okay --
Open the door, Richard. Who was he?
That was Johnny --
No, not Johnny.
We'll get to him later.
Open the door, Richard.
Well, what about the guys before him?
The comedians before him. We'll get to him and I can call my wife, I'm sure she'll remember his name. What about Pigmeat? Pigmeat Markham. I'm trying to think of this other guy.
There were two guys at the Apollo Theater.
Yeah, I'm trying to think of that name.
I tell you what, let's take a break for a second.
(Recording interrupted.)
We're talking about comedians now. We wrote some names down. Who's that? Johnny Taylor was a comedian that used to work at Rochester before Rochester got with Jack Benny.
Yeah.
He had that baseball skit, right?
No, I don't know about that.
You don't know about that?
No.
Well, he came looking for Johnny Taylor because he was funny, and he couldn't find him and he took Rochester. Rochester had to take care of him for the rest of his life.
Yeah.
Now, who was the other comedian we were talking about?
John Mason.
John Mason. Yeah, he was one of these stalwarts on -- at the Apollo Theater, you know.
Appeared nearly every week there.
What was his skits like, do you remember any of them skits?
Oh, he had plenty of them.
I just wondered if you knew any one of them. And then there was Pigmeat.
Pigmeat Markham. He was a judge, he used to have that judge skit.
Here comes the judge.
Yeah. What you fall in that coalhoat for? Bang.
Right.
Fine you so much. And Dusty Fletcher.
Dusty Fletcher was -- who was he known for?
'Open the door, Richard.'
He had some guy that used to borrow his clothes. He would get drunk and come home and the guy wouldn't open the door for him.
Yeah.
And he says, I knows you're in there.
Yeah. I pay as much rent as you do.
Right. And then there was -- remember, there was a couple of ladies that used to be -- straight ladies. What were their names?
Virginia Harris, she used to be on the show. She used to be one of the ladies. And Edna Harris.
Edna Harris. Were they sisters?
Yeah. They were sisters.
And who else? We mentioned Pigmeat Markham, we mentioned Dusty Fletcher and John Mason. Who else was on there?
Alan Drew.
Alan Drew, we remember Alan Drew.
He was way early. And --
Any more? Anything else you want to talk about?
Aphos and Estrelita. (Unintelligible).
What were they like, Tom?
Oh, they were a funny team. Aphos was a funny guy. Estrelita was a straight girl.
Can you give me an example of what their skits were like?
No, they used to -- the same -- I never
paid much attention to comedians, because I was busy with that music.
You always (arranged) for the show.

I would tell the bandleader at the end of the show, now, this is your show. Friday, we open Friday 5:00. I say, this is your show, I'm gone. And I would go up, hit every bar in Seventh Avenue up to 145th Street, turn over and go up St. Nicholas to 149th Street. Land up in Lucky Roberts.
And then Sunday morning, I get home, tell my wife, hey, pay the taxi, I ain't got no money.

Well, look, Tom, now, this is kind of personal. And I want to ask you how you figure this out. And I've known you and I've talked about how you help me and what an important part as we've shown here in talking, your relationship at the Apollo Theater where all the black musicians, all the jazz musicians played, all the black show people played.

Now, we talked about back in Boston, before my time, you were a kid and your recollections with Johnny Hodges and Jefferson Hilton and all the great saxophone players that came out of Boston, including Tootsie Mondello, a white saxophone player. And we've talked about your deep relationship, of the great writer of music, Duke Ellington. How close you were to him and how he trusted you to decipher his scores.
You told me how certain other musicians would do it,
would give you a score and say -- Wille Vodery, he wrote for 23 years for the Ziegfeld Follies. He'd give you a score and tell you -- he'd trust you to add two trumpets to it or two clarinets to it.

And you've told me about -- we've discussed -- and I'm aware of this and I know all this, about all of these people that you've written for, the bands that you had, you were the musical director at the Apollo Theater for years. How does it happen that in books like -- Leonard Feather's Book of Jazz, Stanley Dance 's book. Nobody mentions your name. How does that --
You know what? I can't figure that myself. See, I was chairman of the board with Duke Ellington.
Absolutely.
Duke used to tell me, tell them all, I want you to meet my chairman of the board, Tom Whaley.
Right.

And I can't understand why no one would call on me -- a guy did come from Yale and try to get me, but I was sick, and I couldn't -- he came and I was sick that week and I couldn't do the thing. But I mean other people. They know how I -- how close I was with Duke, and knew everything and even Mercer, he don't even do nothing. Mercer -- oh, I don't know what's the matter, but --
Yeah, I don't understand, but I'm

trying to figure out, Tom, -- and I'm a part of this, I'm aware of this. This is the reason I'm so glad to be a part of talking to you and putting your-- having this go into the National Archives. That people will know the importance of one black man that was through all the jazz. You're 86 years old and this is 1979.
And I can't understand how this happened. And I was in Washington in 1970, for Duke's 70th birthday party. You conducted the orchestra which I was in, and Joe Williams to sing 'For My People.'
Right.

Now, how can -- and Leonard Feather was there and many other great dignitaries was there. How is it, when I look through the discography of musicians in the '70s or farther back than that, that I don't find the name Whaley? It disturbs me greatly.
I wonder why, just like Long John Nebel, see. Sy Oliver introduced me to him, see, and he says, I ought to have you on the show sometime, but never did.

Well, I'm so happy to have you on this one and have you tell your story. I just wish -- you've been the most literate of any person I've ever interviewed. Your dates, you're the brightest, chronologically you know how to bring it about, which I'm most grateful for.
I tell you, it's no -- we set here and you're 86
years old, you set here for three and a half hours with me, straight. And you've told me all these stories and we've gone through everybody from 18-something up to 1979.

And I have some personal tapes of mine here that we just listened to where you were visiting me in 1974. And because of my deep interest in you and my love for you, I was trying to tape and find out some of the things about you then. So now I've mentioned it, and I've very disturbed and I hope that this won't happen again, that in the annals of jazz, that your name will go down in the annals of American music, a man that's so deeply associated with Duke Ellington.

And another thing. When they put that book out with all the pictures of the people in the Apollo Theater, I said, where's my picture? Why ain't my picture on there? I'm just a part -- because I was there. Ralph Cooper brought me in there, see.
Absolutely.
From the Lafayette Theater.

Right. But in my basement right here, in Long Island on the wall, there's a picture of you on the wall with this great group in 1970, at Duke's 70th birthday party at the White House. Duke Ellington and President Nixon and you're standing next to Earl Hines.
Hey, what's the other guy from here, had the -- he was running the pictures?
Willis Conover, is that the one?
No, he was from here. He was from New York.
Joe Morgan?
No, he's in the picture business.
I don't know where or who he was. I know that Willis Conover was mainly responsible for M.C.'ing the show.
Yeah, he M.C.'ed it, yeah. But this guy, he was in the back of the pictures. Oh, I never thought I'd forget his name.
Did he ever send you copies of those pictures from the White House?
No.
He didn't?
No, I never got any. When he entered my house, I got the letter from the President inviting me. I think it's on there, I'm not sure. I know I had it there.
Yes, he had the invitations. It was a most remarkable affair. You were there, along with all the dignitaries, not people --
You know the Senator from New York now? Moynihan?
Yeah.
Well, he was there. He was sitting
right -- two seats from me. Yeah, at that table. And what's the singer, the blues singer?
[Marilyn Mayo.]
No, no, the girl that sings -- she don't sing in no theaters. She sings in churches. Joe Bostick's got her.
I can't remember him.
She sang -- what did she sing? She sang a song, down there.
At the White House?
Yeah. Didn't she sing a song down there?
I don't think she did.
No, no, she didn't sing.
I don't think so. [Marilyn Mayo] was the lady that sang -- Joe Williams sang, let my people go.
Yeah, Joe --
And [Marilyn Mayo] sang a couple of songs.
Joe was the one that made me direct the band.
Right. "Prelude to A Kiss" is what [Marilyn Mayo] sang, if I remember.
I'm trying to remember -- oh, she's an old time singer.
Not Mahalia Jackson.
Mahalia Jackson.
Was she there?
Sure, she was there, sitting at the same table with me.
But she didn't sing, I don't think.
No, she didn't sing. Yeah, Mahalia Jackson.
Mahalia Jackson, yes.
Yeah.
I don't want to tie you up. We've done a tremendous amount of work here.
No, I ain't tired.
And if there's anything you want to talk about, Tom, I would love to hear it. Because I don't have to say but two words and that's --
When are you going to record again?
Right now?
No, sir, we'll have to set a date for another time. We'll find out when your great nephew can bring you back. What's your great nephew's name that brought you out here?
Randy.
Randy. How is he your great nephew?
He's my nephew's son.
What relationship is your nephew to you?
He's my sister's --
Your sister's son?
My sister's son.
I see.

See, Randy's father had four boys. Randy and -- Randy's father's sister had four girls. And I think they're all living. One is up in -- up there beyond Detroit and one's up there in Marlin or Everett. She was with the Commissioner's office. And another one is up in Boston. And where's the other one? I think the other one is up in Detroit, too.
Well, we're going to knock it off, now, Tom. Your great nephew is here.
Oh, is he here?
Yes, sir.
Okay.
So, it's been just enjoyable.
I'm glad to come out here.
Well, listen, man, it's my pleasure and we're going to do it again whenever your great nephew can --
Remember, we got to do Venezuela.
Let me write that down.
This is December 2, 1979. This is a continuation of an interview with you, Tom Whaley. And how long ago was it since we had the last interview with you?
About six months, isn't it?
It's been about six months. And when I left you got a little ill. Tell me what happened to you?
What do you mean, my operation?
Yeah, yeah.
Oh, I had blood in my bladder, see. And I didn't know it and I went to the hospital on a Tuesday.
How did you happen to find out you had it in there?
You told me.
Right.

Because I know I had a little burning sensation in there and then you told me there was blood. So I went to the hospital on a Tuesday, and the man says, you've got to stay in here. So then my -- Mike, Ruth Ellington's son, he took all my clothes up to the house and I told her to have them cleaned and when I come out I'm going to get it, see.

And I had a money belt and I had $200 in there and I told her about it. So I stayed in the hospital there, a week, I think before they operated on me. And while they were -- they did one operation, then I had a hernia and they -- I think it was double, I'm not sure. But, anyway, they took one out anyway and I recuperated.
I was in the hospital for two months, over two months, see. When I come out in June and my nephew brought me my clothes back. I put them on. Shall I tell you about the
Yeah, sure.
Oh, they were rough, those nurses.
They have to be rough to get you straight. They got you walking, haven't they?
They really turn you -- "stand up". I say, wait a minute.
This is like the Army.
Yeah, this is the Veterans Hospital. They had no mercy at all. But, anyway, I got better, and --
It's not that they don't have any mercy, Tom. They can't cater to your illnesses, they want to get you up. So they have to do it along the lines of militarily.

Yeah. Then the lady that was in charge of getting me out of there, see, -- and my nephew was supposed to come and get me. And it was a mixup there, he didn't come til about 7:00 at night. And he come and he got me home.
Well, that's good. I'm glad you're home.
I'm glad to get home.

I know you're glad to get home. Then I got away, I was on tour, and we just couldn't get together. So here it is, Sunday, December 2. And we're back together again. It's a nice crisp December day here, the first Sunday of the month in New York City. And on the last tape that we did, you
were saying that we had to break because your great nephew came to pick you up.
You mentioned to me, now, when we start again, let's talk about Venezuela.
Yeah.
So tell me. What about Venezuela?
In 1950, we was in Chicago. I was with the band, see.
Yes, Duke Ellington's band.

With Duke Ellington's band. And I asked him for more money. He said he wasn't going to give me any more money, so I quit. I came back to New York. Al Sears quit the band also that same time I did, and we come back to New York.

And I was fooling around, and somebody says, hey, Norma Miller wants to see you. And I said, what's Norma And he said, -- whoever was the fellow that told me, he says, he's got a show and he needs somebody to arrange the music. So then I got in touch with her and we -- she took me down to her lawyer or the guy who was producing the thing. And we came to terms, and so I started writing her music, writing the show.

And I had a contract -- I got a contract with them, and I had nine men including myself, see. And we went down to Caracas, Venezuela. And while I was down there, that's when I started arranging the music. And there was one number that
became a big hit in the show. It was called Tropical Madness. It depicted how the weather was calm and nice, and then it went into a frenzy. And that was a big hit of the show.

And -- let me see, we stayed in Caracas about two weeks, and then we went touring Venezeula -- Maricabo, Madlin, and Maricabo, that's where they discovered oil. And had all those places, they had dance halls like they had up at the Savoy, but the only difference was, every girl that worked in the dance hall, she had a bed on the outside, and it was from 14 to 80, they'd take you on. Pete Nugent and I, we killed ourselves.
Who was Pete Nugent? He was a dancer, wasn't he?
Pete Nugent was a dancer, yeah. He was with the show, Norma Miller's show. We used to buddy around together. And we went from --
There must have been prostitution all over that place.

Oh, yeah, yes. You'd get a chick from 14 years old up to 80. Just want to know when. Come on. So we went from there to Bogota, Columbia. And in a brand new hotel, and all those performers on the show, they were crazy, get stark naked and run up and down the hall and hollering. And I used to tell them, man, you get put out.
But they didn't pay me no mind. They went on with
their wild ways. And we stayed in Colombia I guess a week. And from there we went to Barranquilla. That was a port of embar-kation, where we left from.
And before they left, the man paid me all my money and I paid the men off and we went to Miami. We landed in Miami and I think I stayed there a day or so and then I went on up to New York.
Who were some of the guys in your band there, Tom? How many pieces in the band?
Oh, I had --
How many pieces? Musicians?
-- two trumpets and a trombone, and three saxes. I think it's three saxes. And a bass and drums. I don't remember the guys in the band.
I see.
But they read music and they played very good. And the people --
Were the musicians from here?
Yeah, New York musicians, yeah. I paid them $100 a week, room and board. They -- we used to get a decent rate.
Good.
And the people down there, they followed us around and then a lot of the musicians down there, they used to come in and talk with me and they'd give me some music. And

-- oh, they could read, those musicians down there, they read good. And we used to play in a tent, a great big tent at 8:00, see. And at 6:00 every night, nearly, it would start raining, a big shower would come. And we'd have to wait and then it would clear up and then the people would come in and Saturday afternoons, we'd play in the afternoon.

And I had a fine time down there. They -- a lot of the natives, they were doctors who worked in the hospitals and things, and they would come around. And there was one fellow, his father was a drug -- big drug man. And he had a store down there. And he used to take me everywhere. I couldn't buy nothing. He'd just take me around, buy my food. He was a great --
Tom, do you remember any of the tunes in that show? Was there a tune in there called Clee Hops, a dance that Norma did? Clee Hops?
No, she did --
Anything like, 'I Like Music'?

Let me see, the big number was, Tropical Madness. And then we did Rhapsody in Blue. That was a number where the girls did all the -- and one day, -- I used to get drunk, see. Them guys would feed me, and I'd drink. And I remember one Saturday afternoon, I'd been out bowling since 11:00 in the morning and here it is, 2:00. And when it came to Rhapsody in Blue, I stood up and hummed it.
And the girls all -- they hummed their part.

Tom, I'd like to ask you to digress a little bit and get back to your and my era, about New York and some of the great people that you associated with. And since you are a piano player, you were telling me that you go to the Jewish Home for the Blind on Tuesdays.
65th Street, yeah.
Every Tuesday. And that you go up to senior citizens on 116th Street and sometimes you play for them.
Right.

And I know as a piano player -- I'd like to ask you about some of the piano players of your era. And then later we'll talk -- I want you to really talk about Duke and tell me how you -- and Duke's relationship. But let's start with piano players now.
George Rickson.
George Rickson.
He was one of the greatest.
Is that so?
Yeah.
I never heard his name before.
George Rickson. And then Joe Burrough.
Joe Burrough.
His brother was Eubie Burrough.
What did Eubie Burrough play?
He played piano.
Both of them?
Yeah, all these are piano players I'm naming.
Joe Burrough was a piano player?
Yeah.
And his brother what?
Eubie Burrough.
Eubie. Now, tell me about George Rickson.
George Rickson was -- he played for all the shows. See, when a man wanted a piano player for the show, they'd get George Rickson.
He was a good reader, in other words.
Oh, he could read.
How was he on jazz? Could he improvise?
Oh, yeah, he was one of the best. Dan Carey, he was another piano player. See, the majority of them didn't read.
These guys you met, did Dan Carey read?
No, Dan was an ear piano player. Eubie was -- I mean, Joe Burrough, he was an ear piano -- and then there was Freddy Tunstoll. Freddy used to copy music, and he'd -- just like printing.
Well, he evidently could read then, huh?
Oh, yeah, he could read. Oh, we made
Sabie Lewis.
Sabie Lewis, he was out of Boston, huh?
Yeah, they were all in Boston.
These are all names out of Boston?
Yeah.
That's George Rickson and Dan Carey and Joe Burrough and his brother Eubie Burrough, they were all Boston men.

Oh, yeah. Marion Cook, when he was in Chicago playing with the symphony band, he broke his violin and declared he wouldn't play no more, see. And when they wanted piano player, he said, I can go to Boston and get all the piano players I want, good piano players, all them piano players were good.
Since you just brought up Will Marion Cook, for the record, tell the people who Will Marion Cook was.
Will Marion Cook was one of the greatest violinists in the world. He was rated third amongst the great musicians.
He was a black violinist.
Yeah.
Baltimore, was he?
From Baltimore. No, he was from -- I guess -- no, he was from North Carolina, -- what's that place there?
Well, --
But, anyway --
But he was a great violinist. Where did he study?
He went to Europe. He studied over in Europe and came back and became a very great musician.
And he was a composer also, wasn't he?
Yeah, I think he was.
He wrote some things like Melinda Lou? Remember that, Melina Lou? His wife -- what was his wife's name? She was a great singer, Abb--
Abbie Mitchell.
Abbie Mitchell.
She sang that -- 'Won't you come with me in my great teepee and let me fold you in my' -- something like that.
She also sang a song of (inaudible) called, 'Linda Lou, honey, did you hear that mockingbird sing?'
Oh, yeah.
Honey, he was singing so sweet in the moonlight.
She sang --
Do you remember that?
No, I don't remember that. She sang in the show that Eubie Blake and Noble Sissle had.
What was the name of the show?
Won't you come with me in my big teepee? Oh, what was the name of that show?
Shuffle Along?
Suffle Along.
Shuffle Along.
Yeah.
And she was a singer in that show, huh?
Beg your pardon?
She was a singer in that show.
Oh, yeah. I remember that show.
And you mentioned him breaking up his violin. Why did he break up his violin? In Chicago, did you say it was?
In Chicago, yeah.
Why?
See, he was supposed to be first violinist.
I see.
And I don't know, some -- they wouldn't put him because he was a black man. They wouldn't put him first so he broke his violin up and said he wouldn't play no violin anymore.
I don't think he ever did, either.
No. He was a great guy.
He was also a friend of Eubie Blake. Eubie knew him very well.
Oh, yeah.

I remember my first recollection as a young man, of playing in a big orchestra. It was in 1933, in Chicago World Fair. And they had all of the -- they had a black evening there, a black achievement evening. And Eubie Blake and Will Marion Cook were two of the guest conductors. And it was my first chance to play in a big orchestra, under the baton of Eubie Blake.
Well, now, we were talking about these two piano players. You said he could go to Boston and get all the piano players he wants.
Oh, yeah.
Well, what about New York? You were some more in Boston? Did you have some more of the guys from Boston?
Oh, yeah. I named Sabie Lewis.
Sabie Lewis.

Yeah, Sabie Lewis. He was a very great piano player. He used to play around all the places. Well, you see, up til the First World War, there was nothing but black musicians. White musicians didn't have a chance. All the clubs everywhere had black musicians in there. Walter Johnson was one of the greatest.
What did he play?
Walter Johnson, pianist.
Walter Johnson.
Yeah. He used to have a -- say, a dance and I would start the dance. Walter would come in --
You'd start playing in the band?
Sure.
I see.
I used to play with all the places. I had a job playing down on Dover and Washington Street in a place -- and this is right after I got out of high school.
And what year would that be about?
1912. I played around there, and I lived in Everett.
That's in Boston, around Boston.
Yeah.
Then you come up around there?

Oh, yeah. I was born in Boston. Church and Melrose. And there was another guy I had mentioned -- Henry Bachelor, piano player. See, we had a whole gang of piano players around there and they all were working, too. All had a government job, and we used to get jobs. I used to go down to the St. Jordan marsh there and go up in the man's office and sit down and talk with him, and get -- about a job. We'd talk over all the conditions and everything.

And I was playing down on Beech Street, and a Harvard student came in one night and he says, 'hey, how much you charge to play down in Worcester?' I said, '$500,' just like that, see. Now, I didn't know -- I thought he was kidding, see, so I said $500. I had four men there. So about a couple of weeks later, this guy came in, hey, remember what we was talking about? I said, oh, yeah. He said, well, the job is on such-and-such a day.

Now, I had -- he give me a retainer, and I got somebody to take our places for one night. And we went down and hired a car to take us down to Worcester. And this was in May, see. And it was a colonial -- everybody was dressed as a colonial, see.
Oh, yeah.

MR. WHALEY: Colonial dress, and had the wigs on and everything. And you know what? We didn't do much playing down there. The steward came and said, now, you fellows will play over there, and he designated where we would play. And he says, they'll tell you when to play. Now, you want something to eat, you sit down here and eat.

And we ate and drank and played. Didn't play much, because they weren't interested, see. This was just for show, the band was, see. And we went back to Boston and I used to tell the fellows, oh, that was a great outing.
That was a good gig, wasn't it?
Oh, yeah, that was a good gig.
That was good money. A guy used to get ten or 15 dollars a night. You got $500 for five men.

Well, another time, a guy come up to me and asked me if I would play up there in -- oh, somewhere up in the northern part of Massachusetts. And I told him, yeah. I hired a car and we went up there and the man says, what are you doing up here? I says, well, didn't you tell me -- he said I got a telegram saying that everything was off. I said, no, I wrote that everything is on, be up there.

And, sure enough, we went down to the telegraph office and there was the telegram, everything off. I said, that guy was dizzy, whoever signed that. Because -- I came back to New York, I mean, to Boston and I got my lawyer. I had a lawyer from the federal government, Will Schotten. And he said, don't worry about it, Tom. I'll get -- so sure enough, I got all my money back.
That's good. You even remember the lawyer's name from that era.
Yeah, it just come to me, like that.
Sure. Well, okay, so you named all these piano players here. Do you think you missed anybody?
Oh, yeah, let me see.
George Rickson we talked about.
George Rickson.
And then there was Joe Burrough and his brother Eubie Burrough. Then we had Dan Curry --
Dan Carey.
Dan Carey, excuse me. Who couldn't read too well, and there was -- what's that guy, Walter Johnson.

Yeah, Walter Johnson. He was the greatest of them all. And there was another fellow named Skinny Johnson. Oh, he was about six feet two or something, and when he played he'd wrap one leg around the other and sit down there. Oh, he could really play.
Now, what type of feeling went into it? Was it jazz or was it --
Ragtime was -- I would call it swing music. That's what they were playing. They were playing swing music. You see, --
Well, did you have to stride like with the left hand or --
Oh, yeah. You wasn't a piano player if you didn't stride.
I see.
And make that left hand go.
Then you had Freddy Turner. You mentioned --
Tunstol.
Tunstol.
Yeah.
He also copied music.
Yeah, yeah. He wrote a number -- what was the name of that? Well, anyway, it became very popular. And I'm trying to think of this other guy.
You mentioned Sabie Lewis. You already told me about Sabie Lewis.
Sabie Lewis, yeah, he was --
And Henry Bachelor.
Henry Bachelor, yeah. Right, they were -- see, they all were --
And Tom Whaley.
And Thomas Whaley, right. Tom Whaley. They used to call me Fish Whaley, because they said I could swim underwater longer than anybody else.
Did you like to swim, Tom?

Oh, yeah. They threw me off -- I used to go down to the bridge where they would swim and see, my mother, she didn't want me to go in the water. One day they threw me in. I stayed away as long as I could so my clothes could dry. And I come home, mama says -- I say, they threw me in the water. Well, then I learned to swim.
What was your mother's name, Tom, again?
Emma.
Emma, that's right.
Yeah, she was --
So then you learned to swim.
Yeah.
You really did swim under water pretty good, huh?
Oh, yeah. We used to just put our faces down and go on through. But we had a great big playground there where we lived.
Where was that?
In Everett.
In Everett, Massachusetts?
Yeah. It's about six or seven miles from Boston. And my father bought a house there, and --
What did your father do, now?
Huh?
What was your father's business? What did you say?

He was in the hotel business, a waiter. He was head waiter of the Bellevue Hotel in Boston. Then he was captain in Young's Hotel, see, and then he became a waiter or a second waiter in -- oh, gee, in a cabaret place where they just serve drinks, see.
But my father used to make a lot of money. In the Bellevue Hotel, he was head water and they would give him money.
That's good.
Every -- when spring come along we'd have a new suit. And in the fall we'd have another suit. See, we were the best-dressed kids in the neighborhood.
How many of you were there?
My --
I'm just rehashing this now.
My -- I had a brother, I had two brothers, one died. And I had two sisters. So there was four of us, and -
That was a nice life as a child.

Oh, yeah. We used to go to school, went to school and I rehashed that, didn't I? Talked about my school days. Yeah. We used to -- when I went to high school I walked two miles. Did I tell you about -- in the choir the man gave me music lessons, and I sang -- used to go to the choir. I'd walk a couple of miles to the choir. And I got my feet wet one winter and I couldn't sing anymore.

I was a kid, about 12, 13 years old. And I could hit E above the staff. I was one of the kids -- the only other kid, he could sing as high as I could, but -- and then one summer we sang over in Trinity Church there in Boston.
That's beautiful.
But in -- I told you about Marva Lewis, I played for her.
Oh, yeah. Well, we're back to your childhood. Now, when you were a kid around Boston, your daddy
was a waiter. Did you live in -- what's this town you say?
Everett.
Was that a black neighborhood there?
No, it was only about three colored families around there, see. Let me see, in my class in grammar school there was only two colored, Rufus Snowden and I.
You even remember his name.

Yeah, I remember his name. And then later on, there was a girl named Harris. She moved to Everett and she came into high school. But there was very few, and that's why I had a fight. Them Italians and the Jews and the Irishmen, they'd all gang. When the bell rang in school, I tried to get in the front lines, see. And they'd try to head me off, try to block me. But I usually got in that front line. And when I got out that door, I was gone. Because if I didn't, I'd have to fight.

And I'd fight and I'd beat the kid up, and he'd go home and tell his mother and his mother would come up to my mother and say, your son beat my son. I said, well, he called me a nigger. I beat him up.
So we had that thing, even in those days.
Oh, yeah.
Even though the education was equal because you were getting the same kind of education they were
getting.
Sure.

Which in other parts of the world, black children weren't getting that kind of education so that means that this is why today that you are still a little bit ahead of the game, as far as culture and education is concerned.

My mother used to make us study and get our lessons. And when I'd get in school I could fool around because I had my -- and then high school, I became acquainted with the greatest football player in the world, Johnny Brinkley.
Johnny Brinkley.

Yeah, that was in high school. And he and I chummed together and he said, what's the lesson today and I'd tell him. When I got out of school, see, I started dabbling in stocks and he saw me down there one day, he said, man, get out of this. You want to get robbed?
How did you get involved in stocks, Tom?
Oh, buying stocks.
How did you get into that kind of thing?

See, where I played, after I got out of high school, I played down on this place in North Redding. It was a roadhouse, see. And these stockbrokers would come down and say, you got any money? Buy so-and-so. Bethlehem Steel was selling at -- I think it was $40

a share or something like that. And, man, I'll never forget it. Mr. Shepherd, he came down and said, boys, you got any money? Buy Bethlehem Steel and put it away. You know what? Bethlehem Steel went up to $700 a share.
And I said, look, why didn't I buy some steel? But I used to get some stock that was about 75 cents a share. I used to buy ten or 20 shares, and it would go up and sell it out.
Did you get involved in that? I never heard of too many black people being involved in that. That's because of the Boston culture, I guess, huh?
Yeah, they'd come down there and -- Caruso used to come down there every Sunday while he was in Boston.
Enrico Caruso?
Yeah, Enrico Caruso, the great tenor singer.
You knew him?
I used to play for him.
Really? You got to tell -- these are things I want to know.

He'd come down there every Sunday afternoon and sit down, and have dinner, and then he'd get up and direct us. We'd play the overtures of operas and all that stuff. Didn't play no dance music on a Sunday in Boston.
What was the name of this club?
North Redding -- I don't remember the name of the club but it was in North Redding.
It was in North Redding, Pennsylvania?
No, North Redding, Massachusetts. Just right outside of Wakefield.
Why would he be down there?

Well, he lives -- I guess the chauffeur used to bring him down there. It was a very popular roadhouse down there. And then from there, this fellow named Skinny Johnson called up one day and says, you want to come down here? That was Suntaug Lake Inn one of the greatest places in Northern Massachusetts. And it had the best of the people coming there, all the show people.
And I said, yeah. So I went down there and made an audition for the guy and the guy says, all right, the job is yours. Caruso, Eddie Cantor, Mission Elmer.
Mission Elmer, the great violinist?

Violinist, that's right. He'd come down there and bring his violin and say, now, I'm going to fool around and break all my strings until I get down to the G string. When the G string -- this is the end of a perfect day.
And you played this with Mitch Elmer?
Yeah. Oh, I used to play with all of
them. Rock & White. Remember the name Rock & White? : Who was he?

It was a vaudeville team. They had a show in Boston. See, I used to keep track of all the shows. If there was a show coming to Boston I used to be down there the first afternoon and catch it and find out what was a big hit.
So Rock & White came into town and I used to tell my --

You know what they did? They sent me $200 -- and I said to the guy, I said, "See that? I shouldn't give you guys any of this."
Oh, that's beautiful.
But all them people come down here today and they tip $10. Man, you know, we used to make $35 a night -- five of us, and we each made $35 a night.
Yeah? What year was that?

This was around '15 or '14. And we were, at first, we went down there, we were working for room and board -- $15 a week room and board. Then we got up to $45, room and board. And we used to make from $250 to $300 a week.
Do you remember any of the guys who were with you in those days?

Yes, there was Carl White -- he played the banjo and he sang. Leroy Tibbs played the tenor saxophone. Clarence Cummings, he played the violin, and Willie Lynch, he played drums. You probably know Willie Lynch, he used to play at the Savoy, he had that big band, you know, when the Savoy opened? Willie Lynch had the band.
I was just gonna ask you did any of those guys ever make it to New York?
Yeah, they came here to New York.
Willie came. But the other guys, I think they stayed in Boston.
That great tenor was down there. The tenor singer. Caruso. He used to come in this restaurant too?

Yeah. he used to come in there on Sunday afternoons, see, when he was in Boston. He'd come down there in the afternoons, and we'd drink champagne, and when he got through, he'd give us $200, to divide this among the group.

We used to make good money--if we didn't make $35 a night, nearly every night-- if people didn't give us any money, we'd go by the bar and hang out at the bar, and Mrs. Anderson would say--that's the lady owned it--she would come out and say, "oh, Mr. Whaley, would you please give us some music?" And I'd say, "Well, these people aint interested in--they're only interested in their own selves. They don't want our music." But I said, "Well, all right. We'll do it. We'll accommodate you." We'd go back there--shucks. Somebody'd start giving us some money. You see 2s, threes, $5.

We used to have this old man, he used to come down here. He was a sharp mother. He must have been five feet, and he'd have a frock coat on--big--and he would come in and, say, --and reach in his pocket and he'd have a billfold and he would whip it out and he'd be looking for a $10 bill. See, he'd give $10 bills, and say, "Play 'Dixie'." And we'd play "Dixie" a couple of times, see, and he'd come back and say "Play 'Dixie,' to give him some more, see, and all the people would do that much; they'd say, "Is that all you know?" and I'd say, "Well, this man's payin' for it!"
So every time he came in he'd give us a $10 bill to play "Dixie" again. Oh, we used to make money! Come in on Monday nights and I'd get off, and hire a taxi--oh, not
a taxi, but a car -- old Packard limousine and we'd go up to the north shore, all around there, and wine and dine and then come back to New York and let the girls go home ... oh yeah.

And the Harvard students, all used to come down that club, and any big night, I'd have my table with my music on it, and some of the Harvard students wouldn't have a table, and I'd say, "Okay, I'll take my music off and tell the waiter to put a napkin or tablecloth on there, and let you sit here" and man, they'd give me money.
Did any of these Harvard kids turn out to be famous that you knew of later?
Brickley -- he went to --
Who's that?

Charlie Brinkley. He went to Harvard -- I used to go up to the Gold Coast all the time, and they'd have two pianos up there and all the guys would have guitars and everything, and we'd jam every time I'd go up there. Oh, it was a great living up there, I tell you.
You know, it seems to me -- I guess Boston being such a cultural center, and you being from there, did you ever know anything about Johnny Hodges?

Yeah, I tell you -- I'll tell you a story about Johnny Hodges. I had a job at the Avery Hotel -- remember I told you about that? On Beech Street there -- and at the Avery Hotel, we'd play from six to eight every day.

And one day this fellow come up and says, "Can I play" and I'd say, "Sure, come on up!" We had a gallery, see, and that's where the band used to play, see. We had about three or four pieces, that's all, no drums then, just -- didn't have a bass player, even, just a saxophone, and this guy come up and I had known him, see, and he come up with a straight soprano sax, see, and he played -- and when I got the job down, he never came down there, but Harry Carney used to come down there.
Oh? You knew Harry Carney up there, too?

Oh yeah, Harry Carney used to come up there, and when somebody got off, and he would take their place and play up there. And then Johnny used to come up there, you know, every once in awhile and play ...
Now what year was this now?
This was around '14.
Yeah, '14 or '15.
So this tie that you had with Duke Ellington, in this association with these people in this band goes back 60 or 70 years, doesn't it?
Oh yeah, sure.
That's amazing.
Johnny went to New York, and he

came back, he said he played with Chick Webb, and he came back and he hung around again -- meanwhile, Walter Johnson had opened a nightclub up there on Dudley Street, around there, and so I had the band, see, and I used to play up there, and oh -- it didn't last long because they raided it.
Well, did you know Hilton Jefferson up there?
Oh yeah, Jeff? Jeff was up there. He's from Boston.
Yeah, all you New Englanders. Just a great bunch of piano players and a good bunch of saxophone players.
That's right.
And the others you mentioned, including yourself, and there's a Hilton Jefferson, there's Harry Carney and there's Johnny Hodges, and there's -- Toots Mondello, all from the Boston area.

Sure, Boston was a music culture place there. You know, I was -- I went to the conservatory, see, for about six months, but see, they didn't give me the attention, and a guy says, 'Hey, there's a teacher who has just come back from Russia, he had perfected at the Conservatory of Russia' -- and I went to him, and we -- I talked with him and I said, 'Well, I can come Sundays, Sunday at 1 o'clock' so
every Sunday I'd go to him, I'd give him $10 for an hour.
Do you remember his name?
Gold -- Gold something. Anyway, I never did -- he had a family, see.
What did he teach you, Tom -- what was he showing you?
He studied in the conservatory in Russia.
Did he show you chords or harmony or what?
Oh, he'd sit down and show me things --
On piano?

Yeah, and the hour was gone, you know, and after the hour was gone, his whole family would come in and they'd sit down and they'd talk music. Tell me everything. And I don't know, I took lessons off him for about six months, I think, until I got -- I had to go down, I had to work Sundays, see, and that kind of put me off.

But he set down and ran through it. He'd go vavoom! And I'd say, 'Do that again' when I first went there. Vavoom -- finger every note. I said, 'Oh, Lord' and I thought I was kind of a fast -- a good one for notes, but this guy would just rattle them off, varoom, varoom.
Just as a rehash again, because we separated these tapes, and I wanted to be sure that
we didn't miss anything -- what was your first teacher's name, or who first started you on piano?

I had a lady, I never knew her name, but she would sit there and eat candy, and I know I'd be making mistakes, so I told my mother, I told her -- "Look, she's eating candy all the time, and I make a whole lot of mistakes and she'll be saying that's very good" -- so then I got another teacher, a gentleman, his name was Fraley, and I remember him because he was a short, fat guy and he had a church choir up there in Malden, and he said he'd give me lessons if you'll come and sing, and he said he'd give me a tryout singing, and he found out I had a good voice, and I went up to the choir, had a robe, you know, one of these robes, black and white -- choirboy I was, and I used to sing up there all the time.
I'd go up there and he'd give me lessons, and he was very strict.
Did your mother play piano at all?
No, none of them did.
Uh huh.

And across the street from where I lived, there was an Italian. They had two sons, I know, and he was a teacher, see -- and he was teaching, and I'd go over his house, and sit down and play the piano and he had a
great big long baton, see, as long as this cane, and when I'd make a bad note, he'd hit my hands, so I told my mother, "I ain't going over there any more, the man hit my hand!'

And she'd say, "You go over there." And this Walter Johnson, his father was a trumpet player, see, and we used to go over his house and play. I'd play -- I had a mandolin then, and I played mandolin there.
Oh yeah.
I had one of those things, too. And you say he was pretty good, you say, he was about the best around, you said, right?
Who was that?
Walter Johnson.
Oh, Walter was terrific. He went out to California, see, and he died out there, but he went out there and played around.
When did you come into New York? Let's get into that.

I met Swetman. Wilbur Swetman, and Swetman was looking for a piano player, and I was out of a job -- well, I wasn't out of a job, but you know, it was coming on summer, and I just set three guys up there at Lake George, a summer place, so I said, "Yeah, I'll go" -- so then he ...
Wilbur Swetman, eh?
And then he used to play three clarinets at one time. And --
You came to New York with him?

Yeah, and first we toured New England and then we come to New York. When I first came to New York, George Stevens -- he was a singer, played banjo, and he got a job and asked me if I wanted to play with him, and I said, 'Yeah' so we went up there to New Rochelle right outside of New Rochelle there, and played there for about a week, and the man fired George.
Why did he fire him?

Wait a minute. The man said, 'Where you going' -- and I said, 'Well, you fired the boss.' So he said so what, and I said, 'Well, when you fire the boss, you fire all of us' -- so he said, the guy was getting fresh with the girls, with the women, with the people - and he was a good looking boy, he could sing, too.
So he let you all stay on, huh?
No -- we all quit and come on back. That's when I starved here for 8 months around New York, and --
Who did you meet? Who was the first piano player you met around here? Did you know anything about Jelly Roll?
Oh, Jelly Roll -- I was trying to think about that; I met Jelly Roll up here at the theatre, you know?
He used to pace around in front of the Lafayette Theatre, and Jelly Roll Morton -- so I'll come up to that later.
So I nearly starved here in New York. And then finally I got myself together, I got a band, and I used to play all around New York. But first, before that, Lucky Roberts called me ...
He was a club date man.
Yeah, and he said, 'Can you work tonight?' and I said 'Yep' and he said, 'Come up here and I'll brief you on some of the music.' Charlie Purcell was the singer. So --
Who was that again?
Charles Purcell, and we went down to 666 Fifth Avenue, and there was three couples, and we played songs, music, and he sang -- it only lasted a couple hours.
The party was brief, you know, and like I said, it'd be $35, and then -- that's what started me.
That's been the 20's, wasn't it?
Yeah, way back there in the twenties.
And the teens, too.
Wow.
I started rumping them; see, I got myself --
Lucky was a piano player, too -- what did he do?
Lucky was running that place up there.
: What place?
He had his own bar and grill.
: Is that so? Uptown?
A house on 149th Street, on St. Nicholas Avenue.
: On St. Nick?
Yeah.
: What did he call it?
The ... oh, what was it? I don't know, I forget.
: He wrote a couple of very profitable songs, too, didn't he?
Yeah, when I was in the army. 'Junkman's Rag' -- we played that for the President of France, President Pointcaire.
: And that was Lucky Roberts's tune.
That was Lucky Roberts's tune. 'Junkman's Rag.'
: Uh huh. You wouldn't happen to know where we could find some of that music, do you?
Well --
: How'd it go now?
Da, da, da, da ...
: Maybe I'll ask you to play me a couple bars of it later. Okay?
Right, I never played it -- it just came to me.
Uh huh. Now go on with the story.
Where was I?
You were talking about Lucky Roberts and how you got started when you went off by yourself.

Right. I started playing around these clubs, see, to get a job, and we went down on the -- on Broadway there, 1800 block, in there, between 56th and 57th Street. Or 55th and 56th Street, there's a big building there, and it was a loft, see, and they had a nightclub up there and I got a job there, and they used to have colored singers, Mary Strange was one of them --
Mary Strange?
Mary Strange, yes.
That's a wild name.
Yeah, and she could sing -- she knew a whole lot of songs, see, and she could entertain and pull her dress up and put it on the table and take a dollar bill off the table.
How do they do that? They put their legs up there and ...
Just go up there and put that dollar bill up there and take their what's it's name and bring it on back.
Yeah!
So they pulled the colored singers out and put whites in there. Now the colored singers

used to give us 50¢ -- if they got a dollar, they'd give us 50¢ of it. So the white singers came in and they gave us 10¢ on the dollar, so I told Harry, the boss, I said, "Say, you know what? The colored singers gave us 50¢ on the dollar, you know, they get a dollar and they give us 50¢, and now these people only give us 10¢ -- I can't make no money playing for them for 10¢" and he said, "Well, I can't do nothing about it" and I said, "Well, I'm quitting."

It was on a Saturday night, and I quit. Monday morning, they had another band in there and they got raided, they got shot up. The gangsters shot the place up, and that's where Jack "Legs" Diamond used to come in, and he used to sit way down there and tell the waiter to tell the piano player to tell so and so to play so and so.

And he never sent up any money. So I called Harry and I said, do you see that guy sitting way down there with Jack "Legs" Diamond, he always wore a derby. the derby on? ^ I said, "now he's been sitting up here every night asking for different songs and he never sends any money back," and he said, "Well, that's Legs Diamond" -- yeah, and then we went down, I got another job down on 33rd Street, the Mummers Club.
Huh? I never heard of that, the Mummers Club.
Mummer's Club, yeah, played down there, and the gangsters come in there one Saturday night and I'd see

all these guys coming in and I said to I don't know who was playing with me, but I remember I said, "Harry, who let these guys in?" I had one of them say that to the guy and he said, "Keep on playing, and jump on the chair" and he got a gun, and they were all -- everybody -- and after we closed up and went up to Small's --
That's Harlem.
Yeah, on 135th Street.
That was bad.
Yeah. And there were those gangsters, and they said, "Well, we have to get money and send up to Sing Sing every so often, that's the only way we could get money".
And then I'll tell you about the band I used to play all around, and I went over to the Cat's Meow in Brooklyn.
That's a club?

That's a nightclub, yeah, where they used to have a show, and we played there, and the boss didn't pay me one week, so I went in the next week looking for my money and he didn't give me any money, so I quit. I told the fellows, don't play no music. He wants some music, let him pay us.
So that fizzled out. Then I went up to Harlem there to 132nd Street down at the end, they had a club there, and this was during the time that Gerald Chapman was caught up
there in Connecticut, and he was electrocuted, and they tried to buy him off, and I never seen so many thousand dollar bills and hundred dollar bills in my life that come up.

So they couldn't buy it off, see, so when he was electrocuted, all I did was play 'The Prisoner's Song.' Da, da, da, da ... The boss said to play 'The Prisoner's Song' all night long, and that's all I played.
Now I don't want to interrupt you because it's your story, but you were telling me about Lucky Roberts. When did you run in to Claude Hopkins?
I didn't run into Claude until after -- Claude was playing down at the Roseland, and this was in '28, and I got the job at the theatre, see, and I got a band and went into the Lafayette Theatre.

And Ethel Waters was the star, and she didn't have any music, and I said, well, you got to have some orchestration -- and she said, 'My piano player will tell them what to play.' So finally, I made some orchestrations for her.
Who was her pianist?
It wasn't Reginald Beame, but who was the girl -- what was the girl's name? Ruby.
Oh? I didn't know here.
Yeah. Ruby was a piano player.
Oh, she had a girl piano player.
Yeah, at first, and then she got
Reginald Beame.
Uh huh.
And I played there ...
Face this way, Tom.
So I played that way until Earl Dancer came in there.
Who was Earl Dancer?
Earl Dancer, he was a playboy around town then.
He married her -- he was one of her many husbands, huh?
Yeah, and he run off -- he collected all the money but $55, that was for the chorus girls and the band.
It wouldn't be like a high class pimp, would he?

Yeah, just like one. And I took Shipman down to the union, and Shipman was ordered to pay all the musicians, so Shipman fired me out of a' job, see. And I used to hang around the theatre there, and one day I caught Shipman out on the side, and I said, 'You act like a kid, when a kid hits you, the kid cries, and you're doing that to me -- I couldn't pay them guys, them guys are looking for the money, and you're letting the man run off with all the money. And just because I took you down to the union, you fired me out of a job.'
So after awhile, let me see, he kept me out of the theatre for nearly a year ...
: Is that so?
And after awhile, I got back in there, and I went from the Lafayette to the Harlem Opera House.
: Harlem Opera House? That was on 125th Street. That's below the Apollo, wasn't it? Closer to 7th Avenue.

Yeah, closer.
