And we used to have Amateur Hour every Wednesday night and these kids used to come in, you know, and I would find out what they would sing -- I wouldn't rehearse them -- I say to give me a key and start singing, and I'd get the key. So Ella came in there, and so she was going around singing everywhere and winning all the prizes, so I said to Ella, "Now you come down here next Thursday when the band rehearses, and I'll introduce you to the band leader" and I introduced her to Chick Webb, see.
: You introduced Ella to Chick, huh?
That's right. I introduced Chick Webb to Ella and his wife, see. And I told him all you have to do is buy some clothes and get a hairdresser and she'll do the rest.
Sure enough, Ella Fitzgerald started out, and Badu Ali said he was the one, and I'd say, shuh, I used to give Ella money to buy some you know, food with, because

she had, you know, just a little orphan kid. And then we went from there, we only stayed at the Harlem Opera House for about two months, and then we moved into the Apollo Theatre, and the Amateur Hour was still on, and Earl Hines was the bandleader of the week, and I said to Earl, hey, we got a kid here, Sarah Vaughn, and she's great.
Sarah? You got Sarah started too? Before you go into Sarah, did Ella win the amateur contest at the Harlem Opera House or the Apollo Theatre?
Harlem Opera House.
Opera House, okay.
Sure.
Okay, so go on with your story about Earl Hines.

Sarah, she came on -- I told Earl Hines that we got a kid here tonight that's great, a Sarah Vaughn, and she won the contest, see, and Sarah had me, I made an orchestration for her. Once in awhile -- and that Johnny Hodges, he took, he made -- obligato, and Duke made a number out of it called -- da, da, da, da ... no.
He made a big number out of it, see, and Earl took Sarah that same night -- they have never looked back, Ella -- and Pearl Bailey came later, see.
Tell us about Pearl.
Huh?
What about Pearl?

Pearl came later on. I missed her because I had a girl playing, see, I put a girl in charge of the amateurs, you know, because I had so much work to do, I couldn't conduct a show because Monday you start a new week, and probably the people that were supposed to be principals in the show, they wouldn't show up until Tuesday or Wednesday, and then I have to sit and get their keys and write an orchestration for them; you know, the numbers that they produce and wanted them to sing.
And I'd have to make an arrangement on that. So I give it to -- I don't remember the girl's name, but she was a pianist. I gave her the job of playing every amateur hour.
Now what about -- we were talking about Claude Hopkins. You mentioned him.
Oh, at the Lafayette Theatre.
Uh huh.

Claude came by -- I had wrote a number, I'd Do Almost Anything for You -- and it became a big hit, Bill Robinson, Jive Smith, Charlie Parker, they all sang it, and the people would start coming up to it and they'd stop.
Now wait a minute -- who did you say wrote that number?
Tom Whaley.
Is that your number?
That' my number. I'll tell you about it.
Okay.

Claude Hopkins came by the theatre, and said, "Hey, Tom give me that number" -- that was next week, see, and I said, "No, I put it on the shelf, we played it enough." So the producer says, Addison Carey, he's a producer, he said, "Yeah, give it to Claude, and Claude will play it down the Roseland Ballroom".
So me, like a dummy, went out and give him the orchestration. About six months later, 'I'd Do Almost Anything For You', by Claude Hopkins, Bob Williams and Joe Davis. So I saw Claude, and I said ...
Oh, Joey Davis -- the guy that had the ruckus around for years.
Yeah, he was a publisher. Joe Davis.
Oh yeah, I know him.

And I said to Claude -- hey, you know, you took my orchestration and you put your name on it. I said to give me $100 -- and you know, he wouldn't give me nothing. So I said, Aha, it wasn't my number anyway, because I'm working for the theatre, and the theatre pays me for all this music.
But anyway, we come along a little while later, and this trumpet player -- he just died a few months ago -- did you know him?
Something red ... did he have a band?
Yeah, he had a band.
Was it Erskine Hawkins?
Huh?
It wasn't Erskine Hawkins -- he's not dead.

No. He was a trumpet player and a singer -- oh, what's his name. He died a few months ago, he was in the hospital a long while, and he had that girl who used to sing with him. Anyway, 'White Cliffs of Dover' was a big number and his band was playing it, and he told all of his band men to copy their parts, and he had somebody in the audience take down the lyrics, and Bobby Caston was a singer.
She was the first one I heard do 'God Bless The Child.' I remember her doing it before Billie Holiday.
Yeah, she was before Billie, and she sang The 'White Cliffs of Dover,' and it was a big hit -- and this guy, he made a record.
This guy, this trumpet player?
Yeah, he went down and made a record on this number.
Oh, a black trumpet player?
No, a white player.
Oh. A white player.
Yeah. He was one of the early bands.
Wasn't he -- didn't he just die recently?

No. I thought I'd never miss that guy's name, but anyway, I saw him downtown, and I said, "Oh, you made a record, got a big record out, huh? 'White Cliffs of Dover'?" I said, "It was my number -- all you did was change the endings!" "Ha ha ha ha!" That's all he said.
Was that your number, The White Cliffs of Dover?
No, but as I said, I made the arrangement.
Oh, I see.

And he took -- he had every member in his band copy their part, and he had somebody come in and sit down in the show and take down the lyrics.

Chick Webb used to do that, sure, take my music, and you go up to the Savoy and you'd hear my music. I used to tell Chick about it.
Now let's get to some other piano players here from that same era. What about The Lion?

Oh, The Lion? There used to be a place on 7th Avenue at 129th Street we used to call A Hole in the Wall, and every Monday night all the piano players would come up there -- Duke, The Lion, J.P. Johnson, oh, all of them, and me, Tom Whaley, we'd all go up there and I'd be up there listening, and The Lion would come in and tap a guy on the
shoulder and say, 'Hey, I got it.' He'd sit down with his cigar and his derby hat and play, and then J.P. Johnson, he would sit down and he'd play 32 choruses and not one the same.
He was great; they tell me he was really fabulous.
Oh, he was a fabulous guy.
Is that so?
He could play. He reminded me of Walter Johnson, you know, played different -- everything was different.
Was there a guy around here named Steel? Was he a piano player or a drummer?
Joe Steele.
Was he a piano player?
He played for Chick Webb.
He was a piano player, though, right?
From Boston.
He's another one from Boston, huh?
That's right. Joe Steele was a conservatory man. He and I went to the conservatory together, and I quit -- but he stayed there. He was in the conservatory nine years.
Uh huh.
And boy, he could tell you why that was F flat and why you go to B flat, like that.
That's him, yeah. And he had a gold tooth in his mouth, didn't he?
I don't know about that, I don't remember. But anyway ...
And a good dresser, right?

Yeah, he used to tell me he wanted to get out of -- he didn't like playing, and I'd say, "Well, why don't you quit? A man of your talent, shish..." He played Rhapsody in Blue, and what's the guy's name who wrote it?
George Gershwin.
George Gershwin jumped on the stage and kissed him after he got through playing it.
Is that so? Where was that at?
At the Lafayette Theatre.
Lafayette Theatre.
Yeah.
Well, did you know anything about -- you know, I used to talk to Will Vodery, the great arranger?
Oh yes.
He told me that George Gershwin used to be his copyist, used to copy for him.
I guess he was. I met Bill, you know, it was in the army, and he's the first guy that I saw

stand up before a whole bunch of people and give me some manuscripts - and write just like a letter, and write. Don't make a mistake, and he said ten dollars for every mistake, and I said that's the greatest thing I have ever heard.
I've told many people in this town, but I'm so happy to hear you say this, it's a matter of record to verify that, because I worked with him at the Cotton Club.
Yeah, that's right.
Downtown.
And he said the same thing, he said if it was a mistake, the copyist made it, because he said that score was correct.
That's right -- and remember, I was down there, too, with him?
That's right, sure, Tom.
Yeah, Bill Vodery, to me one of the greatest.
Great arranger. Great orchestrator.
Yeah, Carl Towne said he was the greatest musician in the world.
Who was that? Earl who?
Earl Towne out of Vanity.
He wrote for Ziegfield -- for 23 years, he did all the Ziegfield shows, didn't he?
Yeah. Oh yeah. He graduated from
the University of Pennsylvania.
Is that so?

We were in the army, see, and all the bandleaders had to take an examination at Shaumont, see, and he did a two hour concert, examination -- he did in 20 minutes. The man said, 'where you going? You ain't finished' and he said, "Yeah, I finished it." Twenty minutes -- Bill Vodery.

I'm so glad to hear you say this, because we don't even have pictures, and especially for our young black people, that they should have some history of some fairly famous black people that came before them, as we don't have anything to tell them about him, so thank you for verifying what I said about him. What a tremendous musician he was.
Oh, everybody -- Bill Vodery. I met him in New York, see, when I used to go up his house, he lived on 141st Street.
That's right, 141st Street.
Yeah.
Up the hill there.
Yeah. And I used to follow him around just like I followed Fats Waller. When I first came to New York, all I did was follow Fats Waller.
Tell me about that.
Fats was playing at the Lafayette Theatre, and I came from Boston, and I had a great, long
overcoat, checkered --and I think I had a derby.
Hold it just a second.
(Phone ringing)
So before the phone rang, you were talking about Fats Waller, and you had this derby, and he had this long coat with the checks.
Yeah, and I had a pocketful of money and I used to hang around Fats and go into theatres and listen to him play and then go out somewhere, I'd be right with him, see.
Uh huh.
And to me, Fats had more harmony in his fingers -- oh, he'd put that hand down and he would sing, and I followed Fats for a long while.

Yep. You know, he lives right by where we're sitting here doing this tape, is right down the street, one block down the street is where Fats Waller's home is, where he lived when he moved out here to Long Island.

Fats was at the theatre, see, and one day I was in there -- and Fats did a crecendo all the way down and he followed it on out the door. I said, 'Why are you running?' and he said, 'Well, didn't you see that man there?' and I said, 'What man?' and he said the man was coming to take him to jail because he didn't pay alimony.
But he was always in trouble about that kind of thing.
Oh yeah. He wrote -- wasn't it Fats who did 'Ain't Misbehavin'' -- $55 or $50 or something like that?
I think so -- $50 and a bottle of gin.
That's right. Then he wrote a lot of numbers.
Surely. What did we say about Woodie? We didn't talk enough about Willie the Lion, I don't think.
Oh, Willie the Lion? Well, see, Willie the Lion was always like -- well, I never did come much in contact with Willie, but I knew he could play.
I had a couple clashes with him. He had a good ego, didn't he?
Oh yeah.
A great ego. But Duke seemed to be -- Duke says he's his mentor.
Oh yeah, Duke and him used to get along great, yeah.

Now what about this -- we mentioned Claude Hopkins. Who else was around -- we mentioned Lucky Roberts. The piano players who were in New York -- we mentioned all the guys in Boston, and we talked about Jelly Roll Morton, when you ran into him at the Lafayette Theatre, and we talked about Lucky Roberts, which you made the $75, and we mentioned Claude Hopkins, when you met him. Now who else was
around here -- piano players -- can you think of anybody, Tom? That was around ...
Well, Joe Steel was around.
Joe Steel, I think we mentioned him. We mentioned him in New York, but he was also from Boston, which is another -- Boston piano players.

At the Conservatory of Music in Boston, he was up there in the conservatory nine years, and I -- see, we used to ride on the train, because he used to work outside, he used to work in one of the clubs, see.
Hold it again, the phone.
We were talking about Joe Steel now, riding the train, you say?

He used to ride the train the same place where I used to work, go, but he'd work at a different see, and he used to talk to me about music, see? And I didn't listen -- there was another piano player, Joe Jordan, and he was an elderly man, and he won a million dollars over there in France, and in between shows, he'd be playing, I don't know what he was playing, but he won a million dollars and came over here and broke the job in Chicago.
You got to be kidding -- a black guy?
Yeah. Joe Jordan.
I heard that name in Chicago -- he went to Chicago, didn't he?
Yeah, he got a building there named the Jordan Building.
He really won that money, huh?
Oh yeah. He went down to where was it -- Monte Carlo? He used to go down there and gamble.
Wait a second. So we're talking about this guy, Joe Jordan and you were saying he went down to Monte Carlo. Now he was a piano player, right?

Piano player -- director of the band. He had the band all down at some theatre on 46th Street. I played the piano and he had a band made a movie picture with Josephine Baker, and he was the director, and I was the piano player. Josephine Baker did -- did I tell you about her?
No, go on, let's hear about that, Tom.
Well, Josephine Baker was a chorus girl in line up in Boston, see?
Uh huh.

And she got out of line dancing, and did a chorus all by herself, and the guy told her to keep it in. Now, she came to New York, and the first thing I know she's over in Europe dancing with the bananas. After ...
She was dancing with what?
Bananas. They used to call her The Banana Girl, dancing with a bunch of bananas, nude like.
: Oh, uh huh.
And Josephine, she was very nice. When I went over there, she entertained me like I was royalty.
: When did you go over there, Tom?
I went over there in -- I think it was in '66.
: With Duke?
Yeah.
: Uh huh.
And I went to see Josephine, and she was in Paris, and I went by and saw her, and when she came over here, Ruth Ellington had a party for her.
: That was Duke's sister.
Yeah. And Josephine came over and spoke to me, and says, told me to keep my chin up. And she left and that's the last time I saw her -- she died, and that was one great girl.
: Great lady, yes she was.
Yeah. Her and Valaida Snow --
: Yeah, let's mention that. We were talking about piano players, but this was a very talented woman.
Oh yeah.
And he had some very talented women there, you know. Name some -- tell them about her.
Valaida Snow was a trumpet player and a singer, excellent, and she -- Russell Smith, one of the Smith boys in the band.
Russell Smith and Joe Smith.
Joe Smith and John Smith.
Oh, there was a John Smith, too?
Yeah, there were three of them.
Is that so?
Yeah, and they --
And all three of them play trumpet?
Yeah, all three were trumpet players, and Russell gave her a car, and she drove to New York with it.
Now where was this with the car? What town was she in?
Oh, she was up in Boston. They were up in Boston.
Oh, I see.
Yeah, and she drove and went to New York -- drove her to New York. And Valaida, oh, she was great to me.
Okay, now what did she do when she got to New York? Russell gave her this car, so now continue with the story.
She went on to New York, and she you know, she played with Lou Leslie and his Blackbirds.
The Blackbirds, right. That's what we want to get to.
Yeah, she played in that show.
What was her part in that show? What did she do? Can you remember?
She had a part just like Florence Mills. Florence Mills had a part and she had a part -- and she ...
Were they both in the Blackbirds?
I think they were. But ...
Valaida Snow played trumpet, huh? Was she a good trumpet player?
Oh yeah, she was a great trumpet player. Yeah. She could play --
And she sang.
And she would sing.
Did she play piano at all, I wonder?
No, I don't think so. I don't remember that.
I remember seeing her.
Yeah. She had a sister named Valeda or something, and anyway, her sister was in the chorus, too, she sang. But she wasn't as talented as Valaida
Yeah.
The Berry brothers were crazy about Valaida.
Yeah, that's another great act peforming there, the Berry Brothers.
Yeah, Berry Brothers.
There was Ananias, James and ...
James and -- Warren.
Warren, right. I think Warren is the only one that's still living.
Yeah, I think so, too.
Yes. But what a great act it was, I tell you.
Well, they were stars -- they were one of the greatest acts going, because they were so smooth and so beautiful.
Who was the greatest of them?
Oh, Ananias. He was the great one -- he was suave, you know?
Right.

Now the Nicholas Brothers -- they came after them, but I was directing a band over in Philadelphia, see, and the man comes to me and says -- no, I was playing piano, I also played piano, and he asked me why didn't I direct the band and let this woman -- and he was talking about Mrs. Nicholas, she was playing piano and her husband was a drummer.
Is that so?
So he says why don't you direct and let her play? And I said, 'Oh, I can't direct' --and this was before
I even started directing.
Uh huh.
So finally, I said okay, and I directed the show and she'd play and her husband was the drummer, and the Nicholas Brothers were in the show. And they were terrific.
Nicholas Brothers? Let's see, I can't recall their names right now.
Anyway, they're still going great yet.
Yep.
That's so nice to know.

See, all those guys I had under me, see, they came through me in the theatre, and the musicians the same way -- I used to tell the musicians, hey, learn to read music, learn to read music -- because they have no place for an ear piano player now, what's the boy that just died?
Piano player?
Yeah.
Oh, Errol Garner.
Errol Garner, see. Errol Garner to me was the only piano player that didn't read that was still playing, see.
Right.
And he played them "off" chords. I listened to him the other day, and I said well, he lasted a long while.
Sure did.
What's the girl down The Cookery now?
Singer?
Yeah.
Oh ...
Eight-five years old. See, I wrote some of her numbers. She used to come to the house and I used to write for her, and oh, what's her name.
Let me stop the tape while I think of her name.
The name that keeps escaping us was who?
Her name was Alberta Hunter.
Right, and what were you saying about her?
And she used to come to the house and I used to -- you know, she used to sing, and I used to put it down and orchestrate it for her and she never mentions me.
Della Reese. Remember Della Reese?
Yes sir.
Well, she's another girl that I used to do her copying. Mostly used to do her arranging, see?
Uh huh. You know, that's unfortunate, but I'm glad we're mentioning it now.
You know, nearly every singer -- Ruby Dee, do you remember her?
: Oh sure.
All right. She was -- I was coaching her singing, and she left me and went somewhere, and all of a sudden, I hear Ruby Dee!
: That's amazing. Okay now, let's go back to these piano players now. Before we get to the great ones, what about Edgar Hays? Remember Edgar Hays?
Oh, Edgar! Edgar was a very good pianist. He had a band, you know, and he went up to the -- he was up at the Cotton Club I think for awhile, with somebody.
And then he -- I remember him down at 126th Street Theatre there down on 7th Avenue, and that's where I first met him down there -- and then he went to, after awhile, he went to California.
: What was his great recording, do you remember?
Edgar Hays -- what was the name?
: 'Stardust'.
Stardust, that's right.
: 'Stardust'.
Da, da da da ...
: Yeah, that's right.
Yeah, Edgar Hays and 'Stardust'.
I just want to get your opinion, your memory of some of these piano players here. We talked
about Jelly Roll and we talked about Edgar Hays and we talked about Claude Hopkins. And the Lion, and Lucky Roberts. What about Casey the photographer? What was his name? Chitteson?
I only came in contact with him once or twice, but he was a very good pianist for singers.
Uh huh.
Yeah. He had a -- I don't remember the girl he had, but he was very good. Chit-teson.

You know, most young people don't -- or wouldn't know, but perhaps you and I talking this over -- would you say that our great black piano player that we consider one of the finest, especially in New York -- Hank Jones -- don't you think he's got --
Who?
Hank Jones, Hank Jones.
Oh.
Don't you think that -- Hank Jones and Chitteson had that smooth type of playing -- don't you agree with me?
Yeah, they were smooth piano players. Hank. And he's got some band now, doesn't he?
He's doing Ain't Misbehavin', he's the musical director of Ain't Misbehavin', Hank Jones is.
He's what?
He's the musical director of Ain't
Misbehavin'.
Oh, he is?
Yes.
Oh, that's great.
Yeah. He plays it. On the stage, he's Fats as far as playing the music.
I see.
And what a great player, right?
Yeah, yeah. Hank Jones.
Now Tom, just in your own words about how you met Duke, in your association down through the years, please.

Well, I came to New York in '21, the last of November, and Robinson's restuarant was a big thing going then, at the corner of 131st Street and 7th Avenue, and all the performers used to go up there, see, and hang out there. Big Jones was at the corner, and Blackie's was around the corner there somewhere, and I'm in there playing the piano one night, and a guy said, "Here's Duke Ellington" and I kept on playing, and said, "Oh yeah?" and then they introduced me to Duke --and we became great friends through the years. And that's where I met my wife.
What was your wife's name?
Up there.
What was your wife's name?
Sue Baker.
Yeah, well my wife and your wife were good friends.

Yeah. And I tell you, Sue came in this place and she had a blue dress on and she was beautiful, and I was playing the piano, and she came up and put her arms around me and I said, 'Take your arms around me!' and she said, 'I'm not married' and I said 'You're not married?' and she said, 'No' -- so I said to give me her telephone number and I would call her up tomorrow.

And I didn't call her up -- no, I called her up and a man answered, and I said, hell, she said she wasn't married. So when I saw her, I saw her walking down 7th Avenue one day and I said hello and told her that I called her up and she said that you weren't married, and your husband answered, and she said that it was her brother. I said, 'Yeah?'
You know, we got married in '27, and she died in '40 or '50 --she lived 20 years, we were married 20 years, rather. She died in '46 I think. She was an epileptic.
Yeah. Now what about Duke -- how did you and he get to be so tight? Tell me.
Oh, Duke -- let me see, Duke was playing at the Kentucky Club, and he --
Is that in New York?
Yeah, in New York here. And he used to ...
About what year was that?
Let me see, that was '22. That was in '22.
Okay, go on.

And well, it wasn't '22. Yeah, I met Duke right after I came -- no, it must have been later. It was about, say, '25. Because it was right before Small's opened up on 135th Street, and the Savoy Ballroom, it was right before then that I met Duke -- but it was at the Robinson Restaurant, see, and I used to go up, when Duke was rehearsing, I used to hang around, you know, I used to hang around his place, and then I went to -- when he went to the Cotton Club, that was in '27, I used to go up there all the time, see, and that's how I -- Jimmy Lunceford's band came in '33 -- no, they came in '28, first, and they didn't do so good. So they came back in '31 at the Lafayette Theatre, and they went from there to Philadelphia, and they made a second one, and the pay jumped 100%.

After they played Philadelphia and came back, their pay jumped --and Duke was at the Cotton Club, and I used to go up there all the time hanging around, listening, and I was rehearsing shows all the time, then, see, and Jimmy Lunceford's show band came in and I rehearsed them, and when I got through rehearsing, I went out in the street and told the guy, man, this was the greatest band in the world. Ah!
And they had a boy playing trumpet and he could hit those high notes and the big number was 'Tiger Rag,' and they
had Willie Smith in there, and they had Louis -- a fellow named Louis on the trumpet, also. But I say that's the greatest band in the world.

So when Jimmy went to the Cotton Club right after Duke left, my man asked him if he had gotten anybody to arrange, so he said there was a boy downtown there at the Lafayette, and they called me up and I went up there and I arranged two numbers -- Here Goes a Fool in Love, and I'm Going To Love You as Long as I Live.
Lena Horne was the ingenue, and what's the boy -- oh, what's his name? Gates or Yates or something. He was in Brown Sugar.
Who's that?
This boy.
Joe Marshall? Which one?
The boy who was in Brown Sugar.
Old Honey Coles?
No.
What's he do -- dance?
Yeah, he dances and sings.
I don't know.
Old timer.
Avon?
Avon Long. Avon Long! He was a singer and Lena was a pretty girl -- she didn't sing then when
I first met her at the Cotton Club. But Avon used to sing that number.
You're talking about Lena Horne?

Yes, Lena Horne. Sing it to Lena Horne, 'I'm gonna love you as long as I love, da, da, da ... yep. Then they had another band number, you know, all the men. 'Here Goes a Fool In Love.' I arranged those two numbers, I charged the man $150, and I had to go up every -- you know, every time trying to get the money. He'd pay me a little, a fellow named Red used to be -- hey, what you want, kid? I said, 'I want my money' and finally I got it all.
It's funny how we have to struggle for our money in show business.
Yeah. And see, Ethel Waters was one of my big stars, that you know, came under me -- Lena Horne.
Where did you meet Ethel?
Ethel? I met her at the Lafayette Theatre. And as I said, Josephine Baker -- Josephine -- was that her name?
Yes.
Huh?
Yes.
Josephine Baker, and Della Reese.
Well, Tom what I want to know now is how did you start to write for Duke now? Score and orchestrate for him?

Listen -- see, I was in the Apollo Theatre, and the girls -- this was in 1940, and the girls wanted more money, see, and the man wouldn't give them any money, so they quit. And that took me out of a job, see. See, I used to arrange and copy all my music and rehearse it for the band, see, and when the girls quit, I quit with them because I didn't have no job, see?
So in '40, Duke called me and I thought I was going to be an arranger, see, and he wanted a copyist. I said okay, I'd copy.
And that's how I started copying with Duke.
How did you get to add the parts, like you were saying Sam Wooding had you add trumpets to his parts -- Duke would say to you, Tom, write this part. How did that happen?
What did you say?
How did Duke trust you with his music and say you orchestrate it the way you know I want it?
Oh, I don't know. I used to write, and if something didn't sound good to me, I'd change it.
Uh huh.
Oh, there's a whole lot of things that went on.
Uh huh.
You know, I was in Los Angeles, Hollywood when we made 'Black, Brown & Beige,' and this thing was -- you know, it stuck in my mind -- da, da, da, da, That's a number that Johnny Hodges made famous.
'Let My People Go.'
'Come Sunday.'
'Come Sunday.'
Yeah.
is that your tune?
No, that's Duke's. See.
Uh huh.

But I orchestrated it for him, and all that show, and I asked Duke, what are you gonna do with this, and he didn't say nothing, see, and in '63 we went to Chicago and that's where he incorporated nearly all -- every tune that was in 'Black, Brown & Beige,' he put in the show. That was great, that was a great show out there.
Oh, I wish I had seen that.

Oh, that was a great show, and I said to Duke, this should go into the World's Fair, this show should be in the World's Fair because it depicted the negro in music from nothing up to lawyers, doctors, preachers and all politicians and everything. He had them all on the stage. Opened up with the -- down in the pit and they were all in rags and then the pit slowly rolls up and -- yeah. They
had this boy they're writing so much about --
At the center?
No, down at the City Center, he's got this dance group. Anyway, this guy and a girl ...
Alvin Ailey.
Alvin Ailey, that's it. He had a girl -- tall, thin, black gal.
Yeah, she's beautiful.

Yeah, and she and him were doing a dance, and they had just a spotlight on her -- everything was black but the spotlight on them, and they danced for about a minute or so and then the pit started rising and showed all these people. Oh, it was beautiful. I used to be copying and I'd run and go in the orchestra and sit down and listen to the music and want to listen to the music and listen to the people singing. Oh ...

Well, that's beautiful Tom, you've really given me some -- I want to get into some depth with you and Duke, how close you were with Duke? How did you get along so well, what did he call you -- the Chairman of the Board.
Of the Board, right.
How did you arrive at that?
Well, see, when I first went into the band, I used to take all of his mail and read it and if he had anything important, I used to tell him.
Uh huh.
That this was important -- you know, like on Christmas, he'd give me so much money and he'd give me the names of all his relatives, and I'd send them that $100, see.
Uh huh.
So that's pretty close, yeah.
Oh yeah.
Yeah, that's pretty close. You were the guy who did that.

Now what are your feelings about Mercer and what he's done with the band? This is for posterity and I think someone that was as close to the father and to the big man as you are and so many of us have these feelings, what do you think what went wrong? What happened to him?
I don't know, Mercer went crazy, I think; he went off his lid when he got all this money from Duke. You know, Duke had left around $200,000, see. Something like that.
Uh huh.
And it changed Mercer all over.
That isn't too much money, for a great man like Duke, considering what his royalties must be like -- $200,000 is not too much money.
No, but Mercer didn't have no money.
Uh huh.

See, and I always thought that I was Mercer's money, see, because when we was in Las Vegas, we shared a room, see. And he'd take my money and go and gamble it and then bring me back money, and you know, I thought I was really his buddy.
But it seems like things change. He wrote that book about his father.
Isn't that too bad? I don't have the book.
No, but Ruth told me about it.
What did Ruth say? Is she upset about it?
Oh yes, she said he shouldn't have wrote it. Somebody else was telling me about how he talked about his father.
Yeah ...

I said that man should never have been talking about him like that -- I thought Duke, when Duke told me he was going to the hospital, he came down my house, he give me $100 and bought some steaks in a pan, see, and he says he's going into the hospital, and I said, 'Where you going?' and he said, 'Up there to Columbia' and I said 'Don't go there.'
Had you lost your sight then?
Yeah.
And so he came by to see you and brought you $100 and some steaks, huh?
And some steaks, yeah. He always used to come -- when he came up to the barbers, he nearly always would come by and see me and say how you doing and all that.
Uh huh.
And I was closer to Duke than Mercer, see, because I used to almost room with him, you know?
Sure.
He'd have a room there and we would have a suite, and I'd have a room there with him and we would stay in the biggest hotels, and oh --
And so you think the memory of a great man like that has been sort of ...
Tarnished.
Yeah.
Because Ruth was never -- you know, Evie was sickly, see.
Who's Evie?
Bee. Bee.
Oh, Bee. She was a chorus girl at the Cotton Club.
Sure, she was a chorus girl ...
Oh yeah, I worked with Bee.
Out in Chicago.
Yeah, and she ended up at the Cotton Club in New York on Broadway and 48th Street. Bee was the lady's name.
Yes, and he took her ...
Wait a second. Okay, so you were saying Duke took Bee and did what?
Like he married her.
Well, she afforded him a great deal of happiness in his lifetime.

Oh yeah, she was great to me. I went down to see Duke when I was blind, and she was -- this was just before Duke was taken to the hospital, and Duke was asleep and she wouldn't let me wake him up. She made me go out of the house.
And he did marry her before he died, right?
That's what he said -- he married her.
Uh huh. Boy oh boy.
He didn't tell me that he married her, but he told somebody else that he married her.
Uh huh.
Because they only let me up at the hospital once up there at the Columbia Center, the Columbia Presbyterian. I went up there only once.
Well, that's a beautiful way to wind this up, Tom. I just want to thank you and if there's anything else you want to say about this great man, who was your friend ...
Head over heels in music.
Is that what he was?
Right.
He was head over heels into music.
Right.
Duke Ellington -- head over heels in music, and talking to Tom Whaley who is the Chairman of the Board.

That's right -- my man, to me one of the greatest. You call the man up, Bill Vodery, I used to think he was the greatest, see, but I didn't hang around Bill too much, see, because he had another guy, the sergeant -- did you remember him?
No.
Sergeant Lofton?
No ...

Anyway, I thought Bill Vodery was great, stand up there and write with all that going on. Well, I did it myself at the Lafayette Theatre; I sat there and I used to orchestrate and Luther Henderson, he says he saw me doing that -- this was before Luther got big, you
know, and Luther said he saw me writing among all that turmoil and he said that was great.

And then he went on and became great himself.
Luther Henderson.
Yeah, he's the orchestrator for Ain't Misbehavin', the Fats Waller Show, Luther is.
Huh?
He's the orchestrator of Ain't Misbehavin', the Fats Waller show. Henderson wrote that.
Yeah. He was around there with Fats and I, and he used to kid me.

Well, to the future generations, long after you and I are gone, they're gonna hear these tapes and know about you and I've taken some pictures of you, so on some of these tapes you can hear some clicks and things, so that they will know what you look like and can hear your voice.
What do you want to say to them, to give them any kind of advice about your times, Tom.
Well, see, I had a very good mother, and she kept us in line, she made us study and take advantage of your opportunities. If you don't take advantage of your opportunities, you'll never get nowhere.
Now I came out here -- in New York, I didn't know nobody, but I met a whole lot of people, see, and

I left Sweatman for a guy I never met, but I knew him from Boston, see, and he had a band he wanted me to join, so I went with him -- and I didn't stay with him but a week, and then I came back and I starved for eight months.
I owed the landlady eight months rent here, but I told her I'll pay her, I'll get the money.
Well, that's beautiful. But what advice do you have for these young people know about music -- what future do you see through music?

Stop thinking of it as black music -- there's no black music. Music is music, all over the world, if you can read them notes, you're all right. Same over there in India, they have music, but it ain't black.
Yeah, yeah.
They didn't call Beethoven's music black, did they? Beethoven was a black man.
That's right -- his grandfather was black.
Sure. That's why I say there is no black music -- it's music all over the world.
That's the most rewarding thing I have heard you say, and we've got to stop thinking in terms of color.
That's right.
Music is a universal art in which
we all participate -- you sitting here, having lost your sight, and me sitting here with my sight -- sight has nothing to do with sound.
No.
We're dealing in sound.
That's right.
It's how you sound. I can recognize you by the sound of your voice, and you recognize me from the sound of my voice -- and not by the color of my skin, because you can't see the color of my skin.
That's right.
But if you did, it wouldn't make any difference.
No -- that's what I say. Music is -- I tell everybody at the Guild, I bawl some of those guys out. And I just thought about something.
Oh? Go.
They were talking about all these people getting killed -- remember? Had the plane crash and the floods, earthquakes.
Uh huh.
I said to myself, next time they bring that up, I'm gonna tell them --well, the Lord gave his only begotten son for the people to save the people.
Uh huh.
He gave his son, see, and he was
crucified, dead and buried for our sins.
Uh huh.
I'll tell you one thing about that -- talk about saving all those people, it's a shame those people were washed away.

Tom, I've got an old Licker piano over here that used to belong to Count Basie, who was my neighbor and when he moved, I kept it -- and I'm gonna turn it on, and I just want you, as a closing thing, just to touch it and play a little something for me so I can have it on the tape.
What shall I play?
No, I'll leave that up to you, but I just want you to do it so that these young people ...
Shall I play 'Come Sunday'?
Yeah, well, we'll talk about that later. Just let me cut this off now.
What'll I play first?

Tom, we're sitting here with you, just to close out our tape -- I got this old piano here that belonged to Count Basie, one of them electric pianos, and it's sitting here in the house, and I just thought I would ask you to play the tune that you conducted for Joe Williams to sing at the White House for Duke Ellington's 70th birthday party -- what was the name of that?
'Come Sunday.'
'Come Sunday' -- will you play a little taste of that for us?
(MR. WHALEY SINGS)
Oh, that was just beautiful. Thank you, Tom -- I didn't know you were going to sing it, too.
This is my number. ("In Love's Garden You Are My Bouquet.")

That's beautiful, Tom. Now just play me a little portion just for the record, see, a number which you hold claim to -- one of the most famous numbers that Claude Hopkins uses as his theme song, which you wrote and didn't get credit for.
What's the name of this?

'I'd do almost anything for you -- I would would swim the ocean line,/cross the Great Divide, I would do almost anything for you! In my heart, there's ecstasy as long as I have you, I'd do almost anything for you.'
(SINGING)
Beautiful. Okay, Tom. We got room for you to play it, so play it right on out to the end.
Thank you, Tom. That's beautiful. This is the most rewarding thing for me.
(CUT)
(END OF PROCEEDINGS AS RECORDED)

segments.chapter: Early life and training in Boston
segments.title: Opening of the Whaley interview, Reel 1
segments.summary: Milt Hinton introduces Tom Whaley, his friend of fifty years, and the Smithsonian oral history purpose, then asks where he was born.

segments.chapter: Early life and training in Boston
segments.title: Birth in Boston, Everett childhood and his parents
segments.summary: Whaley was born in Boston in 1892 and raised in Everett; he recalls a burglary scare, names his parents, and describes his father's Virginia family and supposed Indian ancestry.

segments.chapter: Early life and training in Boston
segments.title: First piano lessons, boy soprano choir and boyhood jobs
segments.summary: His mother gives him piano lessons, a candy-eating first teacher is replaced by a German, he sings in the Malden boys' choir, and he names his siblings and school-age jobs.

segments.chapter: Early life and training in Boston
segments.title: His mother's death and his father's hotel work
segments.summary: His mother dies in his freshman year of high school, and he says his father was a headwaiter at Boston hotels and a cafeteria.

segments.chapter: Early life and training in Boston
segments.title: New England Conservatory, a Russian-trained teacher and early Boston piano jobs
segments.summary: Whaley left the Conservatory, studied with a strict teacher, graduated in 1911, then played cabarets in Boston, learned to transpose for song pluggers and prided himself on sight reading.

segments.chapter: Early life and training in Boston
segments.title: Boston piano players and music-making with neighbours in Everett
segments.summary: He lists Boston's piano players, recalls being told to just 'oompha' in an orchestra, and describes playing with Walter and Leroy Johnson and the Faseoli family.

segments.chapter: Boston roadhouses and the Army band
segments.title: Learn to read, white musicians in Boston, and Caruso directing at a Reading roadhouse
segments.summary: He says Boston jobs were all colored until the 1918 war, and describes a 1912 Sunday job where Caruso directed overtures and tipped $200 to the band.

segments.chapter: Boston roadhouses and the Army band
segments.title: Joining the Lynnfield roadhouse band and the 'Dixie' request
segments.summary: Leroy Johnson recommends him for a Lynnfield roadhouse; he auditions, earns good money and room and board, and a man pays $10 to hear only 'Dixie'.

segments.chapter: Boston roadhouses and the Army band
segments.title: Drafted in 1918 and the Camp Dix band singer Opal Cooper
segments.summary: Whaley is inducted while working at Suntaug Lake Inn, gets sent off with a party, and at Camp Dix plays piano for the singer Opal Cooper.

segments.chapter: Boston roadhouses and the Army band
segments.title: Troopship to France, the torpedo scare and the wet camp
segments.summary: He describes the convoy, being seasick when the ship was thought torpedoed, meeting shell-shocked soldiers and marching in rainy France.

segments.chapter: Boston roadhouses and the Army band
segments.title: Transferring into the Pioneer regiment band under Will Vodery
segments.summary: He gets from headquarters company into the band because he can read, under Will Vodery, and recalls clean-up duty and a 14-piece orchestra.

segments.chapter: Boston roadhouses and the Army band
segments.title: The 807th Pioneer band, Junkman Rag and not Jim Europe's 369th
segments.summary: They play Lucky Roberts's 'Junkman Rag' for the president of France; Whaley clarifies he was in the 807th Pioneer regiment, not Jim Europe's 369th, and mentions a captain who resigned.

segments.chapter: Boston roadhouses and the Army band
segments.title: Touring France, Paris dances and men in the band
segments.summary: The band plays for officers across Europe, Vodery takes the money to Paris, and Whaley names violinist Louie Jones, Gulfport and Joe Stafford.

segments.chapter: Boston roadhouses and the Army band
segments.title: Armistice, Brest delousing, Newport News and discharge
segments.summary: He recalls the armistice shooting, six months waiting at Brest, a Newport News lecture and Chicken Richards's arrest, and discharge at Dix.

segments.chapter: Coming up in New York and Harlem theatres
segments.title: Back at Suntaug Lake Inn, sending trios to Lake George and gambling
segments.summary: After the war he returns to his Boston job, books a trio at Lake George, then works there himself in 1921 and loses his money gambling.

segments.chapter: Coming up in New York and Harlem theatres
segments.title: Joining Wilbur Sweatman, then George Stevens at Larchmont
segments.summary: He tours New England with clarinetist Wilbur Sweatman, reaches New York in 1921, and plays Larchmont with singer George Stevens before returning to Boston.

segments.chapter: Coming up in New York and Harlem theatres
segments.title: Lucky Roberts calls him to New York
segments.summary: Broke in Boston, he is called by Lucky Roberts around 1925 to play a society gig on Fifth Avenue, and Hinton notes Roberts held the society gigs.

segments.chapter: Coming up in New York and Harlem theatres
segments.title: Leading his own bands in Harlem, the Chapman execution night and Casper's
segments.summary: Barred from the Clef Club, Whaley builds his own band, plays a Harlem Italian place on gangster Gerald Chapman's execution night, and recalls Small's opening and Casper's.

segments.chapter: Coming up in New York and Harlem theatres
segments.title: Rehearsing shows at the Lafayette and his first arranging job
segments.summary: After a Brooklyn employer fails to pay, he moves to rehearsing shows at the Lafayette Theatre, arranging a dancer's show in 1928, then for Ethel Waters.

segments.chapter: Coming up in New York and Harlem theatres
segments.title: What jazz really is: tempo, not music
segments.summary: Whaley argues that jazz is tempo and swing, tells how 'jazz it up' became a word, and contrasts it with Paul Whiteman's sweet music.

segments.chapter: Coming up in New York and Harlem theatres
segments.title: Black bands of the 1920s: Fletcher Henderson, Sam Wooding, Charlie Johnson
segments.summary: They discuss Fletcher Henderson's Boston waltzes in 1919, Sam Wooding's European band, Charlie Johnson at Small's and Vincent Lopez.

segments.chapter: Coming up in New York and Harlem theatres
segments.title: Introducing Cootie Williams to Duke and Johnny Hodges in Boston
segments.summary: At Small's, Whaley introduces Cootie Williams to Duke, and recalls first hearing a young Johnny Hodges in Boston.

segments.chapter: Coming up in New York and Harlem theatres
segments.title: Jelly Roll Morton, the Lion's piano night and Joe Jordan
segments.summary: Whaley remembers Jelly Roll outside the Lafayette, piano night at the Famous Door with the Lion and James P. Johnson, Joe Jordan, and the need to read music.

segments.chapter: Coming up in New York and Harlem theatres
segments.title: Meeting Duke Ellington in 1922 and his rise to the Cotton Club
segments.summary: Whaley meets Duke at Robinson's Restaurant, tells how Duke took over Elmer Snowden's band from Sonny Greer, and describes Hardwick, Carney and Bubber Miley.

segments.chapter: Coming up in New York and Harlem theatres
segments.title: Director of music at the Lafayette and Apollo, and discovering Ella and Sarah Vaughan
segments.summary: He becomes theatre music director in 1930, claims to have discovered Ella Fitzgerald for Chick Webb and Sarah Vaughan for Earl Hines, and lists big bands at the Apollo.

segments.chapter: Coming up in New York and Harlem theatres
segments.title: Louis Prima and Keely Smith copying 'White Cliffs of Dover'
segments.summary: Whaley says Louis Prima had his Apollo staging of 'White Cliffs of Dover' copied and published it as his own.

segments.chapter: Coming up in New York and Harlem theatres
segments.title: Writing 'I'd Do Almost Anything for You' and giving it to Claude Hopkins
segments.summary: Whaley wrote the number by reversing 'Nagasaki', gave the orchestration to Claude Hopkins, who published it as his theme, and he got nothing.

segments.chapter: Coming up in New York and Harlem theatres
segments.title: Start of Reel II
segments.summary: The second reel begins, with a brief return to the Riviera and Charlie Ray.

segments.chapter: Apollo years, Eubie Blake and failing eyesight
segments.title: Copying for Russell Wooding at the Riviera
segments.summary: Whaley copied music for arranger Russell Wooding's show at the Riviera across the Hudson, and recalls how Wooding died in a fire.

segments.chapter: Apollo years, Eubie Blake and failing eyesight
segments.title: Moving to the Apollo and introducing Ella to Chick Webb
segments.summary: Whaley recalls the Apollo's productive era, amateur night, and repeats how he introduced Ella Fitzgerald to Chick Webb.

segments.chapter: Apollo years, Eubie Blake and failing eyesight
segments.title: Writing the Apollo shows and the hardest music he could
segments.summary: He wrote all the show music under time pressure, passed some off to an assistant, and says he always wrote difficult scores to learn.

segments.chapter: Apollo years, Eubie Blake and failing eyesight
segments.title: Meeting Eubie Blake in Boston and confusion over Army bands
segments.summary: Whaley met Eubie Blake in Boston in 1918, and they sort out Jim Europe's 369th, Mikell's and his own 807th band.

segments.chapter: Apollo years, Eubie Blake and failing eyesight
segments.title: Eubie Blake, Sissle, Miller and Lyles, and watching Eubie conduct
segments.summary: Whaley recalls Shuffle Along, Brown Skin Models, Miller and Lyles and Sissle and Blake, and Eubie's ritual at the piano.

segments.chapter: Apollo years, Eubie Blake and failing eyesight
segments.title: Arranging for the show 'Eubie' and 'Good Night, Angeline'
segments.summary: He says he arranged numbers for the Eubie show with Roger Sequire, including a song for Louise Johnson, and 'Good Night, Angeline'.

segments.chapter: Apollo years, Eubie Blake and failing eyesight
segments.title: Whether to study Schillinger and his work habits
segments.summary: They discuss Eubie studying Schillinger, Whaley being told he did not need it, and his habit of never listening to other arrangers.

segments.chapter: Apollo years, Eubie Blake and failing eyesight
segments.title: Overwork and copying Strayhorn's symphony in 1968
segments.summary: Whaley recalls tearing up music at the Lafayette, and sitting eleven hours copying a Strayhorn symphony in 1968 and being unable to move afterwards.

segments.chapter: Apollo years, Eubie Blake and failing eyesight
segments.title: Losing his eyesight
segments.summary: He recalls losing the right eye in Portland, Oregon, the specialists he consulted, and the Johns Hopkins doctor who said he would never see again.

segments.chapter: Apollo years, Eubie Blake and failing eyesight
segments.title: Copying for Duke and Juan Tizol's refusal
segments.summary: Whaley says too much copying ruined his eyes, and Hinton calls him the one copyist who could read Duke's handwriting, after Tizol.

segments.chapter: Apollo years, Eubie Blake and failing eyesight
segments.title: Working closely with Duke Ellington
segments.summary: Whaley tells of answering Duke's mail, copying without discussion, and Duke reversing the order of sections.

segments.chapter: Apollo years, Eubie Blake and failing eyesight
segments.title: Last years with Duke and going blind in February 1972
segments.summary: He stayed with the band until 1971, and describes the moment the veil dropped in a doctor's office in February 1972.

segments.chapter: Apollo years, Eubie Blake and failing eyesight
segments.title: Duke's pencil and trust between them
segments.summary: Whaley describes Duke erasing and changing notes on scores, and says they trusted each other completely.

segments.chapter: Apollo years, Eubie Blake and failing eyesight
segments.title: Break
segments.summary: A short break, and Hinton raises Boston and Eddie Cantor.

segments.chapter: Suntaug Lake Inn and Duke Ellington's band
segments.title: Catching Rock and White's show numbers at Suntaug Lake Inn
segments.summary: At Suntaug Lake Inn he learns show songs by seeing every Boston opening, and earns $200 from performers who visit.

segments.chapter: Suntaug Lake Inn and Duke Ellington's band
segments.title: Caruso's Sunday afternoons at Mrs. Eggleston's
segments.summary: Whaley recalls the five-piece band, the club's colored entertainment, and Caruso directing operas for $200 on Sundays.

segments.chapter: Suntaug Lake Inn and Duke Ellington's band
segments.title: Gambling around Suntaug Lake Inn
segments.summary: He tells of gambling with his earnings, the Ferncroft gambling joint, a New York producer's tips, and integrated gambling.

segments.chapter: Suntaug Lake Inn and Duke Ellington's band
segments.title: Song pluggers and his tunes stolen
segments.summary: Whaley says tunes he made up, like 'Japanese Sandman', were taken by others, and that after he arrived in New York his arrangements were heard at the Savoy.

segments.chapter: Suntaug Lake Inn and Duke Ellington's band
segments.title: Ben Webster and Otto Hardwick in Duke's band
segments.summary: He describes Ben Webster drinking and rehearsing one thing and playing another, and Hardwick and Carney controlling the band's dynamics.

segments.chapter: Suntaug Lake Inn and Duke Ellington's band
segments.title: How Duke built up a performance after intermission
segments.summary: Hinton and Whaley describe Carney's reliability and Duke calling the band back with 'A Train', 'Mood Indigo' and 'Satin Doll'.

segments.chapter: Suntaug Lake Inn and Duke Ellington's band
segments.title: Starting to copy for Duke in 1940
segments.summary: After the theatre closed in 1940 Duke wanted a copyist, and in 1942 in Hollywood Whaley copied 'Black, Brown and Beige'.

segments.chapter: Suntaug Lake Inn and Duke Ellington's band
segments.title: Duke's show 'My People' in Chicago and Detroit
segments.summary: He describes 'My People', the education of the Negro through music, which he copied, and the huge crowds in Detroit.

segments.chapter: Suntaug Lake Inn and Duke Ellington's band
segments.title: The 1939-40 Duke band
segments.summary: They agree it was the greatest band, naming Ray Nance, Tricky Sam, Hamilton, Rex Stewart and Ben, and Whaley praises their interpretation.

segments.chapter: Suntaug Lake Inn and Duke Ellington's band
segments.title: Jimmy Blanton and Oscar Pettiford
segments.summary: Whaley never heard Blanton but was close to Oscar Pettiford, and recalls telling Duke Pettiford was a soloist.

segments.chapter: Suntaug Lake Inn and Duke Ellington's band
segments.title: Tricky Sam Nanton and Sam Woodyard
segments.summary: Whaley tells of Tricky Sam's death on tour and his plunger work, and of Woodyard being a loner.

segments.chapter: Suntaug Lake Inn and Duke Ellington's band
segments.title: The Mingus and Tizol fight at the Apollo
segments.summary: They recall Mingus, Tizol and the fire axe, Duke not firing people, and Mingus turning a table over at Earl Hines's club.

segments.chapter: Suntaug Lake Inn and Duke Ellington's band
segments.title: The word jazz, funky and eight measures
segments.summary: Whaley says Duke disliked the word jazz, and he and Hinton talk about how words like funky changed meaning.

segments.chapter: Suntaug Lake Inn and Duke Ellington's band
segments.title: Sacred concerts, conducting at Harvard and the first at Grace Cathedral
segments.summary: Whaley tells how he rehearsed and conducted the choir at Harvard and Texas, and dates the first Sacred Concert in San Francisco.

segments.chapter: Suntaug Lake Inn and Duke Ellington's band
segments.title: Sacred Concert in Barcelona and traveling alone to rehearse choirs
segments.summary: He praises the New York concerts and the Barcelona cathedral concert with 'Father, Forgive', then Paris and Sweden, rehearsing choirs alone.

segments.chapter: Suntaug Lake Inn and Duke Ellington's band
segments.title: Blind before Duke died
segments.summary: Whaley went blind in 1972 while still working a Georgetown show, and notes Duke died in 1974.

segments.chapter: Suntaug Lake Inn and Duke Ellington's band
segments.title: Billy Strayhorn and his Monday visits
segments.summary: He says he could not tell where Duke ended and Strayhorn began, and Strayhorn visited every Monday for a beer.

segments.chapter: Suntaug Lake Inn and Duke Ellington's band
segments.title: 'Lush Life' and Strayhorn's nickname Sweet Pea
segments.summary: They talk about the difficult changes of 'Lush Life', and that no one played it like Strayhorn.

segments.chapter: Suntaug Lake Inn and Duke Ellington's band
segments.title: Mugged the night he missed Strayhorn's funeral
segments.summary: After visiting Strayhorn in hospital he was drugged and robbed near 125th Street and was bandaged and missed the funeral.

segments.chapter: Suntaug Lake Inn and Duke Ellington's band
segments.title: Mercer Ellington's cigars and I.W. Harper bourbon
segments.summary: He talks about expensive cigars, drinking 100 proof bourbon, the Galveston dinner and swapping cigars for whiskey.

segments.chapter: Suntaug Lake Inn and Duke Ellington's band
segments.title: 'A million dollars worth of diamonds' at the Vancouver border
segments.summary: Whaley jokes to a customs officer, who has the bus unloaded, and he is nicknamed 'million dollars worth of diamonds Whaley'.

segments.chapter: Apollo Bar, Apollo managers and Harlem nightlife
segments.title: Junior Raglin, his dirty shirts and Hinton's gin delivery
segments.summary: Whaley and Hinton tell stories about bassist Junior Raglin, including bringing gin to Hinton at Cab Calloway's engagement.

segments.chapter: Apollo Bar, Apollo managers and Harlem nightlife
segments.title: Managing Johnny Hodges at the Apollo Bar
segments.summary: When Duke toured Europe in 1948, Whaley arranges Johnny Hodges at the Apollo Bar, with Billy Eckstine and Hibbler, and Hodges returns to Duke.

segments.chapter: Apollo Bar, Apollo managers and Harlem nightlife
segments.title: Oscar Pettiford as 'the Whaley brothers' and the Apollo Bar
segments.summary: He hired Pettiford for a 46th Street spot, they were the Whaley brothers, and Hinton praises him as the man who followed Blanton.

segments.chapter: Apollo Bar, Apollo managers and Harlem nightlife
segments.title: Mr. Schiffman hires him as Apollo musical director
segments.summary: The Apollo's manager hired Whaley to orchestrate and rehearse shows.

segments.chapter: Apollo Bar, Apollo managers and Harlem nightlife
segments.title: The Apollo basement nightclub and Eddie South shows
segments.summary: He recalls the downstairs nightclub, Trombone Brown, owner Joe Warren, and writers like Porter Grainger.

segments.chapter: Apollo Bar, Apollo managers and Harlem nightlife
segments.title: Rehearsing Leslie Uggams
segments.summary: Whaley and Donald Haywood rehearsed little Leslie Uggams, who went on the road with Cab.

segments.chapter: Apollo Bar, Apollo managers and Harlem nightlife
segments.title: The Nicholas Brothers and Sammy Davis's first Apollo date
segments.summary: Whaley directed the show for the Nicholas Brothers in Philadelphia and arranged for Sammy Davis and the Will Mastin Trio.

segments.chapter: Apollo Bar, Apollo managers and Harlem nightlife
segments.title: Connie's Inn and Jack Leg's Diamond
segments.summary: Whaley recalls Connie's Inn on 132nd Street and begins a story about gambler Jack Diamond.

segments.chapter: Apollo Bar, Apollo managers and Harlem nightlife
segments.title: Band at a Broadway loft nightclub where Jack Legs Diamond sat
segments.summary: Whaley led a band for a 56th Street loft club where entertainers split tips, and quit after white girls replaced them and he learned a customer was gangster Jack Legs Diamond.

segments.chapter: Apollo Bar, Apollo managers and Harlem nightlife
segments.title: Holdup at the Mummers Club
segments.summary: He describes a tiny gunman holding up the Mummers Club on 33rd Street, and seeing the robbers partying at Small's, saying they were sending money to Sing Sing.

segments.chapter: Apollo Bar, Apollo managers and Harlem nightlife
segments.title: Unpaid at the gangster-run Cat's Meow
segments.summary: At the Cat's Meow in Brooklyn the owner owed him a week's pay, hit him in the office, and Whaley told the band not to play.

segments.chapter: Apollo Bar, Apollo managers and Harlem nightlife
segments.title: Break and start of Reel III
segments.summary: The first session ends and the Reel III title and headers begin.

segments.chapter: Show people and family life
segments.title: Avey Hotel in Boston and Eric Brown's clarinet act
segments.summary: At the Avey Hotel a conservatory student, Eric Brown, played the clarinet for money by cackling and breaking it, and Whaley later saw a white act copying him.

segments.chapter: Show people and family life
segments.title: Sweatman's three clarinets and two Boston jobs
segments.summary: He mentions Wilbur Sweatman's three-clarinet act and his two daily Boston jobs, a lunch restaurant and a dance, where gambling cost him his pay.

segments.chapter: Show people and family life
segments.title: Arranging for Marva Louis
segments.summary: Whaley arranged Marva Louis's act, she got $500 a performance, and made a bet she could last six months in show business.

segments.chapter: Show people and family life
segments.title: Boxers Sam Langford, Jack Johnson and Henry Armstrong
segments.summary: He never met Jack Johnson, but was a buddy of fighter Sam Langford and recalls Gunboat Smith and Henry Armstrong watching him play.

segments.chapter: Show people and family life
segments.title: Perry Bradford, Mamie Smith and Bessie Smith
segments.summary: Whaley confirms Perry Bradford discovered Mamie Smith, and recalls Bessie Smith at Carney's Inn.

segments.chapter: Show people and family life
segments.title: Gertrude Saunders and how Ethel Waters got her job
segments.summary: He says Gertrude Saunders would have outshone Ethel Waters but argued with the boss, who then hired Ethel Waters.

segments.chapter: Show people and family life
segments.title: Arranging for Ethel Waters and 'Supper Time'
segments.summary: Whaley first arranged for Ethel Waters at the Lafayette Theatre for $12, and Hinton says he made records with her.

segments.chapter: Show people and family life
segments.title: Alan Drew, the filthy M.C., and Redd Foxx
segments.summary: Whaley recalls Alan Drew's quick repartee, and they compare him to modern foul-mouthed comics such as Redd Foxx and Richard Pryor.

segments.chapter: Show people and family life
segments.title: Milton Berle and his mouthpiece Johnny Bigle
segments.summary: Berle came daily to hear Alan Drew, and Whaley says Berle's jokes came through Johnny Bigle, Clarence Robinson's partner and Berle's driver.

segments.chapter: Show people and family life
segments.title: George Dewey Washington and Paul Robeson
segments.summary: Whaley met singer George Dewey Washington at the Lafayette and the Apollo with Leroy Smith, and says he never knew Robeson but saw him once.

segments.chapter: Show people and family life
segments.title: Josephine Baker and Valaida Snow
segments.summary: He recalls Josephine Baker's start as a Boston chorus girl, Russell Smith's gift of a car, and hanging around with her and Valaida Snow.

segments.chapter: Show people and family life
segments.title: Marrying Sue Baker and her epilepsy
segments.summary: He says he married Sue Baker in 1927, she died in 1946, and tells how he found her ill and took her to hospital.

segments.chapter: Show people and family life
segments.title: How he met Sue, their life together and her death
segments.summary: He met Sue, a chorus dancer, at Robinson's Restaurant, lived with her twenty years, learned only after her death of the family epilepsy.

segments.chapter: Show people and family life
segments.title: His second marriage to Mazie and women on the road
segments.summary: He married Mazie, a West Indian woman, in 1957, she left him, and he boasts of a girl in every town.

segments.chapter: Will Vodery and the road shows
segments.title: Will Vodery as bandmaster, and Whaley playing flute and piccolo
segments.summary: He met Vodery as Army bandmaster in 1918 and learned flute and piccolo from a Frenchman to fill a gap.

segments.chapter: Will Vodery and the road shows
segments.title: Vodery pocketing the band's money and writing parts without a score
segments.summary: Whaley recalls Vodery taking performance money to Paris, finishing a bandmaster exam in twenty minutes and writing parts on the spot, and his Baltimore and Penn background.

segments.chapter: Will Vodery and the road shows
segments.title: Writing a high note for Lamar Wright at Cab Calloway's Cotton Club
segments.summary: Whaley wrote an arrangement for Cab Calloway with a high note that trumpeter Lamar Wright, the iron lip, played.

segments.chapter: Will Vodery and the road shows
segments.title: Vodery's Ziegfeld scores and Bert Williams in Boston
segments.summary: Whaley says Ziegfeld called Vodery the greatest writer, and recalls drinking with Bert Williams at an inter-racial Boston bar.

segments.chapter: Will Vodery and the road shows
segments.title: Bert Williams in blackface and Vodery's orchestrations
segments.summary: Hinton recounts Williams opening the Ziegfeld show with a gloved hand, and notes that Vodery orchestrated his records.

segments.chapter: Will Vodery and the road shows
segments.title: Joe Jordan and Josephine Baker's music
segments.summary: Whaley says Joe Jordan wrote Josephine Baker's music and led the band at the 46th Street Theatre where Whaley played.

segments.chapter: Will Vodery and the road shows
segments.title: Directing 'Red Hot Harlem' with Will Morrissey
segments.summary: Whaley describes Will Morrissey as white M.C. of the black revue 'Red Hot Harlem', the 'Penalty of Love' number whose two singers died, and Mae Barnes.

segments.chapter: Will Vodery and the road shows
segments.title: On the road with 'Stopping the Traffic' and Dewey Wineglass
segments.summary: Whaley toured with dancer-producer Dewey Wineglass, who was hospitalised six months after fighting Elks in Pittsburgh, so Whaley took charge of the show.

segments.chapter: Will Vodery and the road shows
segments.title: The TOBA circuit and Wiley Avenue in Pittsburgh
segments.summary: Hinton and Whaley explain the TOBA circuit, nicknamed Tough On Black Asses, and the show's stop on Wiley Avenue.

segments.chapter: Will Vodery and the road shows
segments.title: How Whaley first became a show director in Philadelphia
segments.summary: He explains Lee Whipper made him direct the show while Mrs. Nicholas played piano and Mr. Nicholas drums, and they straighten out the 1920s timeline.

segments.chapter: Will Vodery and the road shows
segments.title: Acts on the TOBA circuit
segments.summary: Whaley and Hinton try to recall TOBA acts such as Butterbeans and Susie, Flo and Cecil, the Whitman Sisters and the young performers who waited for critiques.

segments.chapter: Will Vodery and the road shows
segments.title: Apollo comedians: Pigmeat, Dusty Fletcher, John Mason and others
segments.summary: They list Apollo comedians, including Willie Green, Aphos and Estrelita, Pigmeat Markham's judge skit and Dusty Fletcher's 'Open the Door, Richard', and Whaley bar-hops after finishing a show.

segments.chapter: Credit, Venezuela and Boston pianists
segments.title: Why Whaley's name is missing from jazz books
segments.summary: Hinton asks why Whaley, who was Duke's 'chairman of the board' and Apollo director, is omitted from books by Feather and Dance, and Whaley says he can't understand it either.

segments.chapter: Credit, Venezuela and Boston pianists
segments.title: Duke's 70th birthday at the White House
segments.summary: They recall the 1970 White House party where Whaley led the orchestra for Joe Williams, sat near Moynihan and Mahalia Jackson, and never received photographs.

segments.chapter: Credit, Venezuela and Boston pianists
segments.title: End of the first session and his great nephew
segments.summary: The first session ends as Whaley's great nephew Randy arrives, and Whaley says they must still do Venezuela.

segments.chapter: Credit, Venezuela and Boston pianists
segments.title: His 1979 operation and stay in the Veterans Hospital
segments.summary: Whaley recalls blood in his bladder, an operation and hernia, two months in the Veterans Hospital and rough nurses before his nephew took him home.

segments.chapter: Credit, Venezuela and Boston pianists
segments.title: Resuming the interview on December 2, 1979
segments.summary: Hinton explains the gap since the last tape and returns to Venezuela.

segments.chapter: Credit, Venezuela and Boston pianists
segments.title: Leaving Duke to arrange for Norma Miller's show in Venezuela
segments.summary: In 1950 Whaley quit Duke over money, wrote the show for Norma Miller and toured Caracas, Maracaibo and Colombia, leaving through Barranquilla.

segments.chapter: Credit, Venezuela and Boston pianists
segments.title: The Venezuela band, Tropical Madness and humming 'Rhapsody in Blue'
segments.summary: He recalls his nine-piece band of New York musicians, pay of $100 a week, playing in a tent, and the 'Tropical Madness' and 'Rhapsody in Blue' numbers.

segments.chapter: Credit, Venezuela and Boston pianists
segments.title: Boston piano players: George Rickson, Dan Carey, Burroughs and others
segments.summary: After mentioning visits to a home for the blind, Whaley names reading and ear pianists from Boston.

segments.chapter: Credit, Venezuela and Boston pianists
segments.title: Will Marion Cook, Abbie Mitchell and the broken violin
segments.summary: Whaley explains who Will Marion Cook was, why he broke his violin in Chicago when denied first chair, and Hinton recalls him conducting in 1933.

segments.chapter: Credit, Venezuela and Boston pianists
segments.title: Boston pianists Sabie Lewis and Walter Johnson, when only black musicians played
segments.summary: Whaley lists Boston pianists, says all clubs used black musicians until the First World War, and recalls his own 1912 jobs.

segments.chapter: Credit, Venezuela and Boston pianists
segments.title: A $500 colonial costume gig in Worcester and a cancelled job
segments.summary: A Harvard student hires Whaley's four-man band for $500 at a colonial party where they barely play, and later a false telegram cancelling a job is settled by his lawyer.

segments.chapter: Credit, Venezuela and Boston pianists
segments.title: Boston piano styles: stride, ragtime and swing
segments.summary: Whaley and Hinton go through the pianists again, including Skinny Johnson and Walter Johnson, and he says ragtime was swing and every pianist had to stride.

segments.chapter: Boyhood and Boston revisited
segments.title: Fish Whaley, learning to swim, and his father's good earnings
segments.summary: Whaley says he was nicknamed Fish for swimming underwater, and describes his Everett playground, his father's hotel tips and the children's good clothes.

segments.chapter: Boyhood and Boston revisited
segments.title: Being one of few black children in Everett schools
segments.summary: He tells of fighting classmates who used racial insults, and he and Hinton note black children got the same schooling as whites.

segments.chapter: Boyhood and Boston revisited
segments.title: Football star Johnny Brinkley and buying stocks
segments.summary: Whaley chums with football player Johnny Brinkley in high school and buys small stocks on tips from stockbrokers at a roadhouse.

segments.chapter: Boyhood and Boston revisited
segments.title: Playing for Caruso at the North Reading roadhouse
segments.summary: He says Caruso came every Sunday to the roadhouse, where the band played opera overtures instead of dance music.

segments.chapter: Boyhood and Boston revisited
segments.title: Joining Suntaug Lake Inn and visiting stars
segments.summary: Skinny Johnson recommends him to Suntaug Lake Inn, where Caruso, Eddie Cantor and Mischa Elman visited, and he begins on Rock and White.

segments.chapter: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
segments.title: Start of Reel IV
segments.summary: The Reel IV headers begin.

segments.chapter: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
segments.title: Singing 'Mississippi' for Rock and White
segments.summary: After a tape change, Whaley retells how he sang the talk-song 'Mississippi' from Rock and White's show when they visited Suntaug Lake Inn and they sent him $200.

segments.chapter: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
segments.title: Pay and bandmates at Suntaug Lake Inn
segments.summary: He explains pay rose from room and board to $250-300 a week, and names Carl White, Leroy Tibbs, Clarence Cummings and Willie Lynch.

segments.chapter: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
segments.title: Caruso's champagne Sundays and Mrs. Anderson at the Inn
segments.summary: Caruso comes on Sunday afternoons and gives $200 to divide, and the owner asks the band to play for ignoring patrons.

segments.chapter: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
segments.title: The 'Dixie' man and Harvard students at the Inn
segments.summary: The man who pays $10 for 'Dixie' returns, Whaley makes money from Harvard students, and he jams on Harvard's Gold Coast.

segments.chapter: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
segments.title: Johnny Hodges and Harry Carney at the Avery Hotel
segments.summary: Whaley says Johnny Hodges came to play at his Avery Hotel gig in 1914-15 and so did Harry Carney, and they name Boston saxophonists.

segments.chapter: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
segments.title: Lessons from a Russian-trained teacher
segments.summary: He returns to the Conservatory and his Sunday $10 lessons with a Russia-trained teacher whose family listened in.

segments.chapter: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
segments.title: His first piano teachers, Fraley and the Italian neighbour
segments.summary: Whaley recounts the candy-eating lady, Mr. Fraley and the Malden choir, an Italian teacher with a baton, and Walter Johnson.

segments.chapter: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
segments.title: Touring with Wilbur Sweatman and George Stevens's firing
segments.summary: He retells joining Sweatman, touring New England, then going to New York where singer George Stevens was fired and the band quit.

segments.chapter: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
segments.title: Jelly Roll Morton at the Lafayette
segments.summary: Hinton asks about Jelly Roll, and Whaley recalls him pacing in front of the Lafayette Theatre.

segments.chapter: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
segments.title: Lucky Roberts's call and the 'Junkman Rag'
segments.summary: Retelling how Lucky Roberts and singer Charles Purcell gave him his start at 666 Fifth Avenue, and Roberts's tune played for the president of France.

segments.chapter: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
segments.title: Loft nightclub, Mummers Club, Cat's Meow and Chapman night
segments.summary: Whaley retells playing the loft club with singer Mary Strange, Jack Legs Diamond, a holdup, the Cat's Meow and the Prisoner's Song.

segments.chapter: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
segments.title: Ethel Waters at the Lafayette, Earl Dancer and the union
segments.summary: He made orchestrations for Ethel Waters, producer Earl Dancer ran off with the money, and Whaley took the manager to the union and was kept out of the theatre for a year.

segments.chapter: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
segments.title: Harlem Opera House amateur hour, Ella Fitzgerald and Sarah Vaughan
segments.summary: Retelling how he introduced Ella Fitzgerald to Chick Webb and Sarah Vaughan to Earl Hines, and why he later left amateur hour to an assistant.

segments.chapter: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
segments.title: Claude Hopkins publishes Whaley's 'I'd Do Almost Anything for You'
segments.summary: Whaley says he wrote the number at the Lafayette, handed the score to Claude Hopkins, and it was published by Hopkins, Williams and Joe Davis.

segments.chapter: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
segments.title: The 'White Cliffs of Dover' copying story again
segments.summary: He retells how a white trumpet-player bandleader copied the Apollo show's 'White Cliffs of Dover' and recorded it.

segments.chapter: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
segments.title: The Lion and J.P. Johnson on piano night at the Hole in the Wall
segments.summary: Whaley repeats the Monday piano night where Duke, the Lion and J.P. Johnson played, with James P. playing 32 different choruses.

segments.chapter: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
segments.title: Joe Steele, the conservatory pianist, and Gershwin at the Lafayette
segments.summary: He describes Boston pianist Joe Steele, nine years at the Conservatory, who played Rhapsody in Blue at the Lafayette, where Gershwin kissed him.

segments.chapter: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
segments.title: Will Vodery's score writing, Gershwin as copyist and his Penn degree
segments.summary: Whaley and Hinton confirm Vodery wrote scores without mistakes, offered $10 per error, passed a bandmaster exam in twenty minutes, and lived on 141st Street.

segments.chapter: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
segments.title: Following Fats Waller around Harlem
segments.summary: Whaley says that on arriving from Boston he followed Fats Waller, recalls him fleeing a process server over alimony, and 'Ain't Misbehavin'.

segments.chapter: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
segments.title: Willie the Lion Smith and Duke
segments.summary: They agree the Lion had a great ego and Duke called him his mentor.

segments.chapter: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
segments.title: Joe Steele on the train, and Joe Jordan's gambling winnings
segments.summary: Hinton asks for more pianists, and Whaley adds Joe Steele and Joe Jordan, who won a fortune at Monte Carlo and built the Jordan Building in Chicago.

segments.chapter: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
segments.title: Josephine Baker from Boston chorus girl to Paris
segments.summary: Whaley played piano in Joe Jordan's band for a film with Josephine Baker, and visited her in Paris in 1966 with Duke.

segments.chapter: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
segments.title: Valaida Snow and the Berry Brothers
segments.summary: He recalls trumpet player and singer Valaida Snow, Russell Smith giving her a car, the Blackbirds, and the Berry Brothers.

segments.chapter: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
segments.title: Directing for the Nicholas Brothers in Philadelphia
segments.summary: Whaley retells how he was told to direct the band for the Nicholas Brothers before he had ever directed.

segments.chapter: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
segments.title: Learn to read music, and singers who never credit his arrangements
segments.summary: He tells musicians to read since there is no place for ear pianists like Erroll Garner, and complains that Alberta Hunter, Della Reese and Ruby Dee never mention him.

segments.chapter: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
segments.title: Pianists Edgar Hayes, Chitteson and Hank Jones
segments.summary: Whaley remembers Edgar Hayes's 'Stardust', the smooth accompanist Chitteson, and Hinton tells him Hank Jones is musical director of 'Ain't Misbehavin'.

segments.chapter: Working with Duke and final reflections
segments.title: Meeting Duke and Sue at Robinson's Restaurant
segments.summary: Whaley retells arriving in New York in 1921, meeting Duke at Robinson's Restaurant and meeting his wife Sue Baker, whom he married in 1927.

segments.chapter: Working with Duke and final reflections
segments.title: Dating his friendship with Duke Ellington
segments.summary: Whaley fumbles whether he met Duke at the Kentucky Club in 1922 or about 1925, and that he followed Duke to the Cotton Club in 1927.

segments.chapter: Working with Duke and final reflections
segments.title: Rehearsing Jimmie Lunceford and arranging for his Cotton Club show with Lena Horne
segments.summary: Whaley rehearsed Lunceford at the Lafayette, called it the greatest band, and arranged two numbers for him at the Cotton Club for $150, with Lena Horne and Avon Long.

segments.chapter: Working with Duke and final reflections
segments.title: Starting to copy for Duke after the Apollo closed
segments.summary: Whaley lost his Apollo job in 1940, Duke called wanting a copyist, and Duke trusted him to change parts that sounded wrong.

segments.chapter: Working with Duke and final reflections
segments.title: 'Black, Brown and Beige', 'Come Sunday' and the Chicago show
segments.summary: Whaley orchestrated 'Come Sunday' and 'Black, Brown and Beige' in Hollywood, and describes the 1963 Chicago show with Alvin Ailey and the rising pit.

segments.chapter: Working with Duke and final reflections
segments.title: Chairman of the Board of Duke's band
segments.summary: Whaley explains how he became Duke's 'Chairman of the Board' by handling Duke's mail and sending Christmas money to relatives.

segments.chapter: Working with Duke and final reflections
segments.title: Mercer Ellington, Duke's estate and Duke's visit before his hospital stay
segments.summary: Whaley thinks the money changed Mercer, that Mercer's book on his father was wrong, and that Duke visited him with $100 and steaks before hospital.

segments.chapter: Working with Duke and final reflections
segments.title: Bee Ellington and being turned away from Duke
segments.summary: Whaley recalls Bee, a former chorus girl, whom Duke treated as a wife, and says she would not let him wake Duke before the hospital.

segments.chapter: Working with Duke and final reflections
segments.title: Duke head over heels in music, and Vodery and Luther Henderson
segments.summary: Whaley sums up Duke as head over heels in music, praises Vodery writing amid noise, and recalls Luther Henderson watching him orchestrate at the Lafayette.

segments.chapter: Working with Duke and final reflections
segments.title: Advice to young people: take advantage of opportunities
segments.summary: Whaley credits his mother for making him study and recalls starving eight months in New York.

segments.chapter: Working with Duke and final reflections
segments.title: 'There is no black music'
segments.summary: Whaley says music is music everywhere, Beethoven was black, and Hinton adds that sound, not sight or color, matters.

segments.chapter: Working with Duke and final reflections
segments.title: Religion and disasters
segments.summary: Whaley says he intends to tell colleagues at the Guild that God gave his son to save people, and laments those lost in floods.

segments.chapter: Working with Duke and final reflections
segments.title: Closing: playing 'Come Sunday' and Whaley's own tune
segments.summary: Hinton asks Whaley to try Count Basie's old electric piano; he sings 'Come Sunday' and his own 'I'd Do Almost Anything for You'.
